The Third Part:
The Sundarī Section.
Homage to the venerable Gurus.
The Śrī Śaktisaṅgama Tantra.
The Sundarī Section || 3 ||
The First Chapter.
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who bestow grace upon your devotees!
I praise that beginningless and endless supreme space, the attributeless and all-pervading Lord.
O Lord, through whose grace the teaching of the Āgamas was known by me,
when a later time arrived, I questioned you again, O All-pervading One.
"But how has the initiation of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā) come to possess this state of differentiation?
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Great Goddess, at the beginning, Bālā is proclaimed as the foremost of all."
Without which, on the fifteenth day, there is indeed no qualification whatsoever;
O beloved, the three peak-syllables (kūṭa) reside within the Imperishable (akṣara), supreme and suited for the Kali age.
Because it is contrary to dharma and because of its fallen nature, success is certainly not achieved through the recitation of any other [mantra].
For a young girl, there is the purification of the mouth; from that, she attains eligibility for the Vidyā.
When eligibility for the Vidyā has been established, there is eligibility for the Ṣoḍaśī;
but when eligibility for the Ṣoḍaśī is established, there is eligibility for everything. (1.6)
Then, on the fifteenth day, during the rite of the fifteenth [tithi], O Śivā,
one should perform the placement (nyāsa) in ten ways, first placing the Mātṛkā and likewise the placement of the Vidyā.

Having again performed the *cakranyāsa*— both the abbreviated (*laghu*) and the extensive (*mahā*) sixfold rites, as well as the external and internal sixfold rites— one should then perform the *śaktinyāsa*.
The practitioner of mantra who is intent on the deposition of power (śaktinyāsa) is, without doubt, the very form of the deity;
thereafter, by means of that deposition, he shall immediately become one who possesses supreme authority. (1.9)
Following that, there is authority over the *parāprāsādika* nyāsa;
then, by means of the *prāsādaparā*, there is the initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*) into the *caraṇa*.
Indeed, from that [state] arises the Śāmbhava state, beginning with the practice of Nirvāṇa;
the practice known as Nirvāṇa is said to be the highest among the Śāmbhava states.
If one is qualified for the Bālā [vidyā], the wise man should install those prescribed for the Bālā;
if one is qualified for the Pañcadaśī, he should perform that which exceeds the Pañcadaśī.
O Goddess, after the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsa), one should then perform the unlocking (utkīlana);
having performed the placement of the Dīpinī, one should thereafter contemplate the Kulluka.
If one is endowed with the initiation of the Ṣoḍaśī, one should perform the Mahāṣoḍhā and other rites;
if one is endowed with the supreme (parā) initiation, one should install the Ṣaḍadhvā and other elements.
If one is endowed with Parā-prāsāda, one should perform those respective nyāsas; if one is endowed with Prāsāda-parā, the wise one should perform those very same ones.
The initiation of the four feet, however, has the Parā-prāsāda as its domain;
O Pārvatī, there is no difference between the two, yet there is some slight distinction.
Then there shall be initiation into the Śāmbhava state, and worship directed toward the Śrīcakra;
the worship of all [deities] must be performed, or else their ritual placement (nyāsana) is prescribed.
First, the ritual placement (nyāsana) is proclaimed; thereafter, worship (pūjā) is extolled.
O lady of pleasant speech, the worship within the Śrīcakra should be performed for all.
O Goddess, in the place of the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya), one should then perform the sixfold Śāmbhava rite;
having established the locus of the six, one should then worship Saṃvarteśa.
O Goddess, having performed the worship of all [the deities] and likewise of the water-pot (kalaśa), those desiring all perfections should worship it with diligence.
Endowed with all initiations, one should perform all the ritual depositions (nyāsa).
O Goddess, however, without the Ṣoḍaśī [initiation], there is no qualification for anything else.

The rites beginning with the initiation into the Parā-prāsāda and others that follow the Ṣoḍaśī [initiation] are performed according to the rules prescribed in their respective Tantras, being joined with those specific initiations and so forth. (1.22)
One should perform each respective rite; otherwise, it is not the word of Śaṅkara.
That which is proclaimed as the initiation of the feet (caraṇadīkṣā) is indeed celebrated as the supreme one.
(3) However, having set aside the Śrīvidyā, no qualification is recognized [for other paths].
But in the Śrīvidyā, O Dear One, one becomes complete in all paths. (1.24)
Having drawn the Śrīcakra by first drawing a triangle with a bindu in its center,
one should then draw a circle and immediately after that, a four-petalled lotus.
Then, having drawn a square consisting of four or five spokes,
one should thereafter draw the body in the form of the thirty-six principles (tattvas).
In this way, however, the body [of the deity] is to be meditated upon; indeed, meditation itself is the drawing.
That which precedes the temple is declared to be the Supreme (parā), whose form is the venerable reality (śrītattva). (1.27)
O Goddess, one should worship the lineage succession all around the circle of the Śrī Mahāṣoḍhī Vidyā, which has the form of the embodiment of mantra. 1-28.
O Maheśvarī, the sequence of the Parāprāsāda-vidyā has been declared;
now listen attentively as I shall explain the primary sequence. 1–29.
Then, one should visualize above the *bindu* an auspicious eight-petaled lotus,
and thereafter one should draw a lotus consisting of thirty-six petals.
O Śivā, one should draw an eight-and-thirty-petaled lotus outside of that; O Śivā, one should then draw the lotus known as Bhuvana outside of that.
Having thus drawn [the lotus] with fifty petals, endowed with the number of the moon (sixteen),
one should meditate there upon the Supreme Mother according to the prescribed rule.
Having thus first meditated upon [the deity], one should then [meditate upon] the Vidyā of Parāprāsāda, whose body consists of the thirty-six principles (tattvas). || 1.33 ||
In the Śāmbhava [tradition], the drawing of the yantra and the meditative visualization (bhāvanā) therein are indeed prescribed;
having performed the external worship, one should then meditate upon the Supreme Mother (Parāmbikā).
O Great Goddess, when the authority regarding rites such as the worship of others has been completed, then indeed the authority regarding the sixfold Śāmbhava [initiation] arises. (1.35)
O Maheśānī, the Ṣaṭśāmbhava is declared to be the supreme of all;
the initiation should be performed either as that which transcends the Ṣoḍaśī or as this very one.
"O Supreme Goddess, what should be recited by those who are endowed with initiation and the like?
Whatever devotion one has toward whatever [deity], that very thing should be recited by him. (1.37)
According to the tradition and by means of the yoga of devotion, the initiation of the sixteenth power occurs; this is called the second [initiation], so listen.
But the supreme *vidyā* of Parā-prāsāda consists of Śiva and Śakti;
she is declared to be Ardhanārīśvara, hidden in all the tantras. (1-39)
"Thus has this been told, O Goddess; what else do you wish to hear?
Śrī Śiva said:
'O Supreme Goddess, as for the doubt that arose in you regarding what should be chanted (japya)..."
That very [matter] is now being declared, O Maheśānī; listen with care.
The abiding of all the gods within the Śrīcakra has been proclaimed. (1.41)
This is the Great Sovereign of the Śrīcakra, the supreme Mahāśrīṣoḍaśī;
she is the Vidyā who is the grace of the Supreme, the Great Mistress of the Śrīcakra. (1.42)
The initiation of the Upper Tradition (ūrdhvāmnāya) and others, however, pertains to the Supreme Palace (parāprāsāda);
it is the placement of the mantra of the Supreme Palace within the Śrīcakra. (1.43)
The placement of the sixfold Śambhaveśa-vidyā within the Śrīcakra, and its worship in the Binducakra—O Maheśānī, listen with reverence. (1.44)
O Śivā, one should worship Mānasa in the southwest within the Bindu-cakra;
O Goddess Śivā, one should not worship Nāda here, from the northwest of the Bindu.
O Dear One, one should indeed worship the Maruta [element] in the east of the Bindu-cakra;
O Śivā, one should worship the Taijasa [element] in the southeast of the Bindu-cakra.
One should worship the Śāmbhava element, which is watery, in the western direction of the Bindu-cakra;
then, one should worship the earthly element in the northeastern direction of the Bindu-cakra.
Having worshipped the [deities] with their rays of light according to the prescribed method,
O Dear One, one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) within the body, which consists of thirty-six wheels (*cakra*).
Thus has this been told, O Goddess, regarding the ninefold mandala;
indeed, the ninefold mandala is proclaimed as the primary one.
O Goddess, one should worship with effort the Mahāsaṃvarttakeśvara, who consists of nine wheels; this has been taught in brief, O beloved.
The morning rites, meditations, worship, and other such rituals have been explained in detail within the illustrious *Pañcakrama* tantras. (1.51)
The yantra known as Ṣaṭśāmbhava is said to consist of nine parts;
O Supreme Goddess, the principal worship is prescribed within that yantra.
The five pretas are in the Śrīcakra, while six pretas are considered to be in the Śāmbhava;
seven pretas are spoken of in the Guhyakālī—listen now.
The one known as Hiraṇyagarbha is proclaimed in the Śāmbhava [Tantra]; those named Indrabhairava and [Indrāṇī] are said to be in Guhyakālī. (1.54)
The mudrā known as Saṃghaṭṭanā is indeed proclaimed to be of three kinds; having joined the two hands together with the palms facing downwards, it possesses excellent characteristics. (1.55)
Having joined the nails to the nails so that the five fingers are positioned below,
and having thus properly joined the hands, this is the mudrā known as Saṃghaṭṭanā.
Having properly joined the previous mudrā and separated the two little fingers, this second mudrā is proclaimed as that called Saṃghaṭṭanā (the Collision). || 1.57 ||
In this case as well, there are two positions for the little finger when joined separately;
thus the third mudrā arises, while the fourth is the most excellent of all.
One should join the thumbs, ring fingers, and middle fingers in the shape of a womb;
having thus formed both hands facing downward in a most beautiful manner.
The index finger should be joined with the index finger, and the little finger with the little finger;
one should join the two index fingers and the two little fingers together at their tips, pointing upward.
This mudrā, called Saṃghaṭṭanā, bestows all accomplishments at the end of the recitation;
it is used in the Vidyā of the Four Feet as well as in the sixfold Śāmbhava rite.
O Great Goddess, O Śivā, the primary [lineage] has been declared; one should demonstrate it with effort.
Thus has this been told, O Goddess; what else do you wish to hear?
Śrī Śiva said:
Now, therefore, O Śivā, I shall fully declare the sequence of the lineage;
distinguishing it according to its focus on the complete initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā), I shall explain it to you.
In the beginning, Śaṅkara was awakened by Paraśiva himself;
then Śaṅkara will descend [to earth] together with four disciples.
The Goddess was awakened by Śiva, and by the Goddess all were awakened;
even Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva were awakened by Īśvara.
The Guru who has entered the lineage of Śiva is the lineage of Śiva;
O Goddess, the lineage of the Goddess follows the path of Kālī’s instruction.
Even here, there is a multiplicity of powers (*śakti*), so that no fixed number of doctrines exists.
Now, from Ānandabhairava comes the succession of the Goddess’s doctrines (*devīmata*).
O Goddess, the previously mentioned triad is divided within the Kāmarāja [cakra]; according to the doctrine of Ānandabhairava, this is the sequence of the eighty-five doctrines. (1.68)
O beloved, the initiation of the Śiva-lineage comes from Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
in every case there is this lineage-transmission. Now listen, O beloved, to that which is in the middle.

Those engaged in the three streams beginning with the Divine (divya), as well as those impelled by the Śaiva and Gāṇapatya [traditions]—even here, the great multiplicity of views cannot be described by me. (1.70)
In that Tantra, there are the divine lineage (divyaugha), the lineage of accomplished masters (siddhaugha), and the human lineage (mānavaugha) as the third;
[these apply] to Sundarī, Śrī Mahākālī, Tārā, and the Kālikā-mantra.
On the fifteenth day, during the *lopikā* [observance], with the mantra of the *manvagastika*,
when the *parā* is joined with the *śaiva*, and so forth, through the inversion of the beginning and the end.
O Great Goddess, the three currents have been declared within the Ṣaṭśāmbhava;
all three currents have been explained—what do you wish to hear from this point on?
O Dear One, the lineage of the *ogha* is said to consist of divine and perfected beings;
the lineages of the *ogha* have emerged from Śiva, and the succession of the worship of the *tvaugha* [has followed]. (1.74)
Likewise, through the form of Dakṣa, there is the Gaṇeśa [group,
beginning with Baṭuka], and then the group beginning with Ānandabhairava— all of which resides within the middle current (augha).
These traditions have indeed been proclaimed;
O Goddess, in the Ānandabhairava, ten million divisions are proclaimed.
O Dear One, Ānandabhairava and the others are indeed included within the Hādi [group];
however, because they are the initiators of the paths, their preeminence is proclaimed. (1.77)
Therefore, O beloved, Virūpākṣa and the others attained the status of sages;
Sarasvatī is considered the pen, and Gaṇeśa the scribe. (1.78)
This is the doctrine of the Supreme Śiva; the Lord Maheśvara is its speaker.
O Great Goddess, the Earth is its leaf, and the Nāthas are the binders of the scripture.
The Brahmāstras and other weapons, as well as the Śarabhas and other protectors who set the floods of tradition in motion within the world, are in every way worthy of worship. (1.80)
Transmitted through successive lineage, they are proclaimed to be diverse;
they are eternally divine in the presence of the gods, and likewise perfected here upon the earth as well.
The multitude of human beings among men is said to be the threefold flood;
from Śiva down to one's own guru, [one should practice] knowledge and the unsurpassed worship. (1.82)
(7) O Dear One, knowledge extending from the Goddess down to one's own respective guru is considered the supreme worship;
then, O Beloved, that which extends from the one named Ānandabhairava down to one's own guru [is likewise so]. 1.83.
This alone, O Great Goddess, is esteemed as Dakṣiṇāmūrti;
listen with care, O Queen of the Gods, to the truth up to your own Guru, my dear. 1-84.
Worship is declared to be supreme; now listen to that which begins with the *ogha* and ends with the *guru*.
O Goddess, knowledge beginning with the *ogha* and ending with the *guru* is proclaimed as worship. (1.85)
This primary knowledge is said to exist somewhere in the Kali age;
O Goddess, the first four [ages], however, are considered to belong to the Tretā and Satya ages.
O Maheśānī, in the absence of all [these], that which ends with Parameṣṭhin is considered [the rule];
or else, the group of four should be known [as the rule], for otherwise it creates an obstacle to accomplishment. (1.87)
The lineage of instruction for the Goddess extends back to her own Guru;
likewise, O Mistress of the Gods, it is proclaimed that in every case it begins with Bhairava. (1.88)
At the feet of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, one should worship [the lineage] ending with one's own guru.
Let the twenty-first [chapter], known as the Guru, be performed quickly.
The various distinctions regarding the multiplicity of gurus are many in the Ānandabhairava;
O Goddess, without this knowledge, a man shall become a partaker of sin.
How should initiation be given to women, and how does womanhood exist therein? This is when the instruction is that which has been pointed out by the lineage of goddesses.
Then, by observing his own [vow], a man becomes a partaker of merit;
however, the initiation for renunciants (saṃnyāsins) is according to the tradition of Dakṣiṇāmūrti.
One should perform initiation everywhere among the auspicious and bliss-bestowing gods;
for Śiva, it is named "Śivāntaka," but for Viṣṇu, it is "Tadantaka."
In the Śākta [tradition], however, there are indeed divisions regarding the gurus of power;
in the Saura, the Saura [guru]; in the Gāṇapatya, the Bauddha; and in the Dharmāntika, it would be the same. (1.94)
"O Goddess, in this way, regarding the Pāśupatas and other [sects], the name mentioned there for initiation must be performed with great effort"—thus spoke Kālikā. (1.95)
Alternatively, O Maheśvarī, having worshipped Dakṣiṇāmūrti, initiation for women should be bestowed by his presence; that indeed is considered the [proper] method.
O Śivā, if women were indeed obstructed by their karma, then how could a son—who ought to be nourished through his sons—exist when there is no son? (1.97)
First, she must indeed perform the rite with the syllables; thereafter, one should initiate her.
Now I shall explain another matter; listen to that which was previously mentioned, O beloved. (1.98)
But when the Kali age has arrived, no one at all will perform [the rites];
having resorted to secondary sciences (upavidyā), the lowest of men will merely mutter prayers.
They do not attain success; they all become partakers of suffering.
O Goddess, in the Kali age there will be no doubt that they will be subject to censure.
Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Sundarī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī, Bhuvanā, Lakṣmī, Dhūmrā, and Tripurabhairavī. (1–10, 1)
These very Mahāvidyās are perfected vidyās from another age;
however, O Great Goddess, their status as vidyās is due to the influence of their respective ages.
Due to being devoid of the lineage of gurus, due to employing inferior sciences,
due to misconduct, and due to disparagement, they indeed do not partake in accomplishment.
Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, and Sundarī are indeed of one form;
and any other Great Goddess as well is of one form—of this there is no doubt. (1.104)
One should practice the ten sciences, including the secondary sciences (upavidyā) and so forth;
otherwise, having seized all one's possessions, the yoginīs devour him.
Now I shall further explain the description of the various differences of opinion regarding Kālī,
Tārā, Mahāvidyā, Dīpinī, and Kulasundarī.
If the wise one desires accomplishment, he should recite it at all times,
O Dear One, [including] the Pāśupata-triśūlya and others such as the Vīra-kaula.
Within this very auspicious procedure for the Great Vidyā,
those who are proclaimed as Vīraśaivas and those previously described as Vīravaiṣṇavas will be included.
Within this very *mantra* of Kālī, Tārā, and others, the various divisions such as the Cārvākas and these divisions of the Cīnas will be included. (1.109)
The Cārvākas, Ārhatas, Buddhists, Chinese, Jains, and others [worship] Śiva;
O Goddess, O Beloved, the Śākyasiṃhas and others worship the Lord of Gods, and the Devīputras and others [worship] the Goddess.
They will be included right here within the auspicious fire of Mahātārā.
Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the discernment of the complete initiation (pūrṇadīkṣā).
In the initiation of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), many varieties are indeed considered;
[it may be performed] with the *parā-prāsāda* mantra, or with the *prāsāda-parā* mantra.
In the Śaiva system, she who consists of the *kāmakalā* becomes endowed with the *bindu* as the creative source (*sargī*).
Likewise, in the supreme form of the *Prāsāda* mantra, there is that which consists of both the *bindu* and the creative source. (1.113)
The supreme initiation (*parā-dīkṣā*) is likewise another, [arising] from the emission of the point (*bindu*) and the principles (*tattva*) and so forth;
then the sixfold *śāmbhavī* initiation has been proclaimed in many ways.
There is also the Garbhaśāmbhavaka and the Keralaśāmbhava;
there are many varieties within the Kerala [tradition], and they shall now be described here.
O Goddess of gods, there may be six lineages, or five, or even four lineages, or three; or indeed, in their absence, there may be only one.
When the rays of Śiva and the rays of Śakti are of the nature of Śiva and Śakti,
they are called the fifteen rays known as Tripurā, which are the supreme light.
Or are these the supreme rays (raśmi) said to exist within those called the Sixfold Lineage (ṣaḍanvaya)?
Or is this the initiation of the feet (caraṇadīkṣā), which takes the form of the four quarters? || 1.118 ||
Nirvāṇa, however, is the fourth state, having the nature of the mixture of red and white;
it is the initiation of the three steps, the Nirvāṇa that is supreme among all.
O Goddess, there is no knowledge superior to Nirvāṇa within my tradition;
one who is devoted to the oral lineage should perform the full initiation on the sixteenth lunar day.
O Goddess of the Gods, for those who perceive [the truth] within their respective mantras according to the tradition,
the sixfold lineage (ṣaḍanvaya) is also recorded in the case of Guhyakālī.
The initiation of the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka-dīkṣā) is proclaimed for Kālī;
likewise, the full initiation is proclaimed for all the Vidyās. || 1.122 ||
Likewise, in the Śrīsundarī and Kālī traditions, the principal [deity] is proclaimed;
one should perform the worship of each according to their respective lineages. (1.123)
In the *Pañcadaśī* as well, the complete initiation (*pūrṇadīkṣā*) is proclaimed for Śiva;
however, in the *Mantragastalopikā*, the bestowing of the name is treated separately.
O Maheśvarī, the name should be given according to the tradition;
in the case of Śrī Dakṣiṇakālī, however, it is Kālī, following the path taught by the Guru.
O Goddess of gods, Tārā also [is worshipped] according to the path taught by the Guru;
as is Kālī, so is Tārā, for she who is Tārā is indeed Kālikā herself. (1.126)
Because it has been stated thus, O Maheśānī, initiation is also performed in Tārā;
O Mahādevī, Śivā, it is likewise performed in Guhyakālī according to the sequence of the six rays.
O beloved speaker, fifteen *mālikās* are taught here;
by means of the sequence of their rays, the worship of names and so forth is considered [to be performed]. (1.128)
O Maheśvarī, the name should be given according to the sequence of the six Śāmbhava [methods];
she is considered to be Mahākāmakalā Kālī, the Sovereign of the Kings of Kings.
In this [tradition], however, the auspicious *pūrṇadīkṣā* (initiation of completion) has been proclaimed for Śiva;
it proceeds according to the path taught by the Guru and through the sequence of the lineage of human masters (*mānavaugha*).
One should cause the name of command to be bestowed upon the disciple who is devoted to the Guru;
she who is Kāmakalā-Kālī is considered the Mistress of the Yoga-paṭṭa. (1-131)
That is declared to be the Yoga-initiation (yogadīkṣā), which has the nature of Great Nirvāṇa;
likewise, in the Haṃsakālī [tantra], one should bestow the name Ājñā.
That Kāmakalā who is known as Kālī, the Mistress of the Yoga-band (Yogapaṭṭeśvarī), is the supreme form of Prāsāda;
she is the supreme Mahākāmakalā.
The initiation of the feet (caraṇadīkṣā) within Haṃsakālī consists of the four-fold form;
there is no initiation superior to the Haṃsa-initiation, which is the complete consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
Then, indeed, one should cause the name of the *ājñā* to be bestowed by means of the sequence of the swans (*haṃsa*).
Here too, O Goddess of the Lord of Gods, is the lineage of Śiva and the Goddesses.
O Goddess Śivā, you have spoken of Bhairava Ādinātha;
O Great Goddess, the lineage of all [these teachers] is considered to be the succession of the Oghas. (1.136)
Because of the knowledge of the succession of lineages (augha), that very lineage is primary within the ogha;
O Goddess of the gods, the lineage beginning with Śiva is the Virūpākṣa lineage.
O Maheśvarī, from Ādinātha down to one's own guru, O Deveśī, the first guru everywhere is the one who bestows the mantra. (1.138)
O Goddess, this lineage and so forth belongs to Maheśa alone and not otherwise;
the gurus are proclaimed to end with the one named Ānandanātha. (1.139)
Even women who possess the form of a guru are proclaimed to be included among the mothers;
O Śivā, having first worshipped one's own guru, one should then worship [the lineage] ending with Śiva.
Thus, O Goddess, it has been proclaimed as before regarding initiation and other rites; indeed, it is proclaimed in exactly the same way for Ānandabhairava and the others. (1–141)
O Śivā, one should perform worship beginning with one's own guru and ending with the divine [deities].
Then, at the initiation for Kālī and other rites, one should bestow the name of the Command (ājñā).
(11) O Goddess, listen now as it is described according to another method, O Beloved, beginning with the bliss of Prahlāda and ending with the bliss of awakening. (1–143)
This should be caused to be bestowed upon those who lack knowledge by way of the path taught by the Guru;
it has also been proclaimed by me to you in brief regarding Tārā. (1.144)
Śrī Śiva said:
Now I shall further explain the nature of the spiritual traditions (sampradāya).
First, indeed, the Vaidika was proclaimed, and after that, the supreme Vaiṣṇava.
After that, the Gāṇapatya is proclaimed; after that, the Saura is celebrated.
O Maheśvarī, the Śaiva scripture is superior to the Saura, and the Śākta is superior to the Śaiva.
O Maheśānī, that which is Vāma is proclaimed as superior to Śākta;
the Dakṣiṇa is superior to the Vāma, and the Vīra is indeed superior to the Dakṣiṇa.
Now, from the Vīra comes the Avadhūta, proclaimed as being prior to the Kaula;
from the Avadhūta comes the Divine Path (Divyamārga), and there is nothing superior to the Divine.
The venerable Pāśupatas and others will be included within the Śaiva [tradition],
while the Pāñcarātras and others, O Goddess, indeed arise within the Vaiṣṇava.
Those systems approved by the heretics and the Chinese will be included within the Śākta;
the various divisions of the Rudras are within the Kāpālika, and eight are proclaimed to be within the Kaula.
O Goddess, the Vīra [system] is considered to have five divisions; in China, it is considered to have two hundred.
There are one hundred divisions among the Buddhists, and seven are recognized in the Pāśupata [tradition]. (151)

O Goddess, there are two divisions in the Divine [tradition], while the Paśus are considered to be of three kinds; however, in the lineage of the Sampradāya, there are seven divisions in the Avadhūta.
Ānanda is declared to be the first, while the second is indeed Nātha;
Ānandanātha shall be the principal, and after him comes Prakāśa. (1.153)
Prior to that [initiation], he possesses his own essential nature; thereafter, he possesses consciousness.
Furthermore, he is proclaimed as an Ācārya (teacher) worthy of worship due to his excellence in knowledge. || 1.154 ||
One who knows the six scriptures beginning with the Śāmbhava is proclaimed as worthy of worship.
The syllable *gu* signifies darkness, while the syllable *ru* is its illuminator. (1.155)
He is declared to be the Guru by means of two [qualities]; he alone is indeed the Illuminator.
The Lord (Nātha) is endowed with the attainments (siddhis) and so forth; he is Ānanda, possessing the power of Śambhu. (1.156)
The term Ānandanātha is a designation for Paraśaiva;
he who is called Mahāvīra is declared to be a Māheśvara. (1-157)
In the Kali age, the Vīra style generally exists somewhere in an arrogant manner;
however, its specific variety known as the Kerala style is considered to be characterized by gracefulness (vilāsa). || 1-158 ||
Its division is said to be the Draviḍa, which bestows the status of an Ācārya;
that very same [division] is called Caitanya, declared to be established in self-sovereignty (svārājya). (1-159)
Those who proclaim the tradition of the Master (Svāmī-sampradāya) will be included within the Draviḍa school;
he who is called Gauḍa Svarūpa is indeed that very one named Ānanda.
There are many divisions in Kerala; I shall speak of them, so listen attentively.
One is known as Bhavasiddha, and the one called Hara is proclaimed as Siddhākhya.
Through the distinction of the permutations of place, there are four marketplaces;
through the distinction of the permutations of mantra, there is the accomplishment of the ritual procedure, and from that, the sequence.
Through the distinction of the succession of time, the lineage of the Siddhānanda school consists of Kalahaṭṭa, Gomukha, and after him, Vijñānin. (1.163)
O Maheśānī, thereafter came the king of Draviḍa known as Utpāda;
this is considered the sequence of the tradition according to the divisions of the passage of time.
The first shall be Pūrvakerala, while the second shall be Uttarakerala;
here too, there is a multiplicity of names according to the tradition. (1–165)
O Śivā, he is divine, perfected, true, consciousness, a mass of pure awareness, supreme,
known as the Omniscient One, and bears the names of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra.
Then, O Goddess, the designation "Ādi" (the First) should be applied to Sarasvatī;
for first come the words beginning with "divya" (divine), and then the goddess Sarasvatī.
First, the sequences (krama) are to be known, and after that, the tradition (sampradāya);
then, O Maheśvarī, having understood the names and so forth, one reaches the state of command (ājñāpada).
Now, listen as I shall describe the Dravidian divisions in their proper order:
the one called Advaita, Pūrṇanātha, and the third, named Cidambā. (1-169)
O beloved, the tradition known as Advaita belongs to Avadhūtamata; it ends either with Sarasvatī or with Ānanda.
Or, O Maheśānī, it may end with Nātha; there are three triads in the three [locations].
But that which is called Īśa, O Maheśānī, is situated within Kerala. (1–171)
O Dear One, he becomes a Māheśvara known by the name Viśvarūpa;
O Goddess, these [others] are indeed included within the Kerala [tradition]. (1-172)
Thus, one endowed with knowledge should perform worship preceded by the knowledge of Kuṇḍalinī; otherwise, success will certainly not be attained. (1.173)
O Goddess, due to ignorance of this, one shall not attain the perfection of the Vidyā;
indeed, one who desires the perfection of the Vidyā should practice preceded by knowledge. (1.174)
"O Goddess, whatever is performed out of ignorance shall all be fruitless.
Thus it has been briefly declared; it must certainly be carried out, O Beloved. (1-175)
O Goddess, in the ritual of offering the sacrifice, in the act of arranging the vessels, and in the procedure for their application, everything becomes clear; it is not otherwise.
Śrī Śiva said:
Now what do you ask, O Śivā? Speak quickly regarding Kāśmīra;
he who is declared to be the most divine of all is celebrated as Kāśmīra.
The Lord of Meditation, the Lord of Action, and likewise the Lord of Knowledge; the Supreme Consciousness, the Lord of Cognition, and the one known as the Lord of Siddhas.
And then Ṛddhinātha— thus, O Maheśānī, these eight have been proclaimed by me for the rites of worship and so forth, as well as for the ritual of placing the vessels.
O Maheśānī, this is the division; everything is proclaimed as one.
O Deveśī, there is the path known as Gauḍa, as well as that which is approved by Kāśmīra.
O Goddess, that which is within Kerala is not otherwise than the word of Śaṅkara;
indeed, at some time or place, a distinction has been proclaimed according to the tradition.
O Maheśānī, the fourfold division consisting of Trijaṭā and Eka-jaṭā, as well as the trident adorned with a dot, is all contained within this Śaiva [tradition]. (1-182)
O Goddess, the illustrious Pāśupata and other systems are included within the Śaiva tradition.
There are indeed seven divisions of them; I shall speak of them, so listen attentively. (1.183)
First is the one with a topknot (śikhin), then the shaven-headed (muṇḍin), and the third is the one with matted hair (jaṭin);
then the one with two staffs (dvidaṇḍin), the one with a single staff (ekadaṇḍin), and finally the one with three staffs (tridaṇḍin) is recorded.
The Vīraśaiva is the seventh; thus the Pāśupatas are remembered as being sevenfold.
In the Vaiṣṇava tradition, however, there are eight divisions, of which the Vaikhānasa is traditionally considered the first.
O Goddess, Śrī Rādhāvallabha is the first, Gokuleśa is the third, he named Vṛndāvana is the fourth, and Pāñcarātra is the fifth. (1.186)
Then [the one] named Vīravaiṣṇava is proclaimed;
Rāmānandī, Harivyāsī, and Nimbārka is remembered as the eighth. (1-187)
O Goddess, these Smārtas and Bhāgavatas are the founders of paths; O Śivā, the Cīnas and Kāpālikas are included within the Śākta [tradition].
Then, O Goddess Śivā, there are the Buddhists, the Jains, the divine Kaulas, and likewise the Vīras and Paśus; their characteristics are now described. (1.189)
There are two hundred varieties of the Chinese [script], but that [system] is for the method of cutting through the stars (tārā).
These are: Tārādhīśa, Parādhīśa, the one called Kṣema, and Prematāraka. (1-190)
Known as Sāgara, he was devoted to others and likewise intent on compassion for living beings;
he was long-lived and named Siddha—thus he has been briefly proclaimed.
O Śivā, we shall now describe those five divisions among the Kāpālikas:
the Indrajālī, the Devajālī, and the Rudrajālī as the third; || 1-192 ||
Vidyājālī, numbering four, and Siddhijālika as the fifth—these are declared to be the five Kāpālikas. Now listen with diligence to [the description of] the Buddhists.
The hair-cutter, the tree-cutter, the drinker of intoxicants, the defiled one, and the fifth, the breaker of vows— thus they are considered to be of many kinds.
O Goddess, listen attentively as I describe the two divisions of the Jaina [tradition]:
Pārśvanātha, Kalānātha, and Padmābhogavatīrata. (1-195)
O Śivā, there are two divine divisions: the primordial divine (ādidivya) and the secondary divine (upadivya).
O Goddess, the bound souls (paśus) are of three kinds: those who know, those who do not know, and those who revile [the teachings]. (1.196)
It is said that there are five types of *vāra*; hear their distinctions, O Pārvatī:
Śrīcakravīra is the first, O Goddess of Gods, and the second is named Ūrmilā.
The third is the Cūḍācakra, the fourth is the Puṣpacakra, and the fifth is the Jīvacakra; thus five divisions have been proclaimed.

The yoga of contemplation (*bhāvayoga*) is in the *jīvacakra*, the yoga called action (*kriyāyoga*) is in the *puṣpacakra*, the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is in the *śrīcakra*, and the yoga of dissolution (*layayoga*) is in the *ūrmile*. (1–199)
"In the Cūḍācakra, what else do you wish to hear regarding Rājayoga?
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear that which was previously mentioned and is exceedingly secret."
The illustrious Śiva said:
From a mere insect up to the limits of the universe, the world consists entirely of Śakti.
O Goddess, by the worship of Śakti, the entire universe becomes worshipped.
By the power of Śiva, indeed, the fourteen worlds exist within his body;
the three worlds, beginning with the world of the gods, reside in the place of Kalā within Śiva. (1.202)
The mountains, minerals, lakes, oceans, and likewise rivers—whatever exists within the sphere of the cosmic egg and upon the surface of the earth. (1.203)
All that, O Pārvatī, clearly resides within the body of Śakti;
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are born from the body of Śakti.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Śrīcakra Yoga and Other Practices," in the third section of the northern portion of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 1 ||
The second chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, if I am dear to you, speak that which was mentioned previously."
Śrī Śiva said:
One should worship Gaṇapati when desiring wealth, and Divākara (the Sun) for the sake of health.
One desiring glory should worship Tārāpati; one desiring liberation, Janārdana;
one desiring all things, Nārāyaṇa; and one desiring glory, Puruṣottama.
The mantra-practitioner, for the sake of attaining mastery over mantras, should worship Śrī Kālikā; one desiring knowledge, Mātaṅgī; and one desiring all desires, Vārāhī.
One desiring sovereignty should worship Bhuvaneśī, as well as Nīlasarasvatī,
and likewise Tripura, who manifests the peak-syllables (kūṭa) within each peak.
In the Kali age, one should worship Sarvakāma; in the Kṛta age, Puruṣottama; in the Dvāpara age, Śivabheda; and in the Tretā age, Vāmana Hari.
Now, she who is praised in the Kali Yuga is called Bālā;
Lalitā is praised in the Tretā Yuga, and Pañcakūṭagā in the Dvāpara Yuga.
In the Kali age, the Ṣaṭkūṭā is praised; it is concealed in all tantras.
O Supreme Goddess, Sundarī fulfills every desire in the Kali yuga.
The jackal is for the sake of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*), especially for the purpose of paralyzing (*staṃbhana*);
*Dhūmāvatī* is for the purpose of killing (*māraṇa*), and the *śarabha* is considered suitable for suppression (*nigraha*).
Pratyaṅgirā is proclaimed for the purpose of subduing [enemies] through fire-weapons and the like.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, I shall tell you another thing, if I know it. (2.9)
One who desires prosperity should constantly worship Tripurā in the Kali age;
likewise, one who desires eloquence should worship Kālikā, the Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā).
One who desires heaven should likewise worship Bhuvaneśī and Tārā;
and one who desires spiritual luster should fully worship Brahmā.
One desiring health should worship the Sun; one desiring wealth, the Fire-god;
one desiring prosperity, Kamalā; and one desiring knowledge, Sarasvatī.
In the Kali age, by [worshipping] Nīlapatākā and likewise Nīlasarasvatī, the perfection of speech arises quickly; there is no doubt that the perfection of desires is attained. (2-13)
One who desires the accomplishment of ritual actions (karmas) should indeed worship Vināyaka;
one who desires enjoyment should worship Śaśin, and one who desires strength should worship Samīraṇa.
One should worship Śiva with effort for the sake of liberation from all saṃsāra;
likewise, if one desires meditation, yoga, liberation, and imperishable knowledge. (2.15)
He should worship Virūpākṣa, Hara who consists of all beings,
as well as Chinnamastā, Rājapūrvā, Mātaṅgī, and Kāmakālikā.
O Śivā, one should worship the goddess Śmaśānakālikā, who bestows all siddhis, as well as Aśvārūḍhā, Kukkuṭī, and Bhogavatī. (2.17)
O Dear One, one should worship Nityaklinnā and Bheruṇḍā for the purpose of bringing women under one's control;
however, one who desires to attract all beings should worship the single-syllable Kālikā.
Likewise, O Dear One, one should worship the Madhumatī Vidyā for the sake of attracting all things; as well as the Parā-prāsāda Vidyā and the Ṣaṭśāmbhaveśvarī. (2.19)
For the sake of accomplishing all desires, one should worship Sundarī with diligence;
she is the giver of wealth for those desiring prosperity, and the beloved for those desiring spiritual accomplishments.
Bhairavī grants the desire for form, while Hayagrīva bestows eloquence.
Śrī Śiva said:
He now describes the lineage of initiation (*dīkṣā-paraṃparā*) by which one becomes identical with the Goddess.
Whether in Gauḍa, Kāśmīra, Draviḍa, Kaula, Vāma, or Dakṣiṇa, the beautiful [Prakṛti] is indeed to be applied everywhere according to the respective path. (2.22)
O Goddess, by the power of their respective offices, when the Kali age—filled with sin—has arrived, all indeed fall away from their state. (2.23)
But there will undoubtedly be the destruction of the lineage;
with the agitation of the guru and the loss of the primary [teacher], accomplishment does not proceed from this. (2.24)
O Goddess, under the influence of ignorance they indeed wander here and there;
thus they have become lost from the path and are considered to be like those who have strayed into the branches.
Even after ten million yugas, they shall certainly not partake in spiritual accomplishment (siddhi).
O Maheśvarī, I shall now describe the lineage of initiation (dīkṣā-paramparā) pertaining to Śrīvidyā.
Likewise, even in the Kālikā [tradition], there is a division into Gauḍa and Kāśmīra;
now, therefore, I shall fully explain the initiation into the various forms of Śrīvidyā. (2-27)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, she who is worshipped by those who have attained limited authority is the Bālā;
O Goddess, she who is worshipped according to desire by those with full authority is the supreme (Parā).
Beyond that should be the Ṣoḍaśī, and beyond that the Parā-vidyā;
beyond that should be the Parā-prāsāda-vidyā, which has the form of the supreme Prāsāda.
O Dear One, one should cause initiation to be performed according to the tradition;
thereafter, the sixfold Śāmbhava [initiation] is proclaimed in accordance with the tradition. (2.30)
Then the initiation of conduct (caraṇadīkṣā) is proclaimed; after this, no other initiation exists.
O Goddess of the gods, the initiation of liberation (nirvāṇadīkṣā) is considered the most excellent of all. (2-31)
One who is devoted to the initiation of nirvāṇa has no other initiation;
one endowed with the initiation of nirvāṇa attains the supreme Brahman, without a doubt. (2–32)
O Maheśvarī, the initiation into the three steps (caraṇatraya-dīkṣā) should be performed on certain occasions;
mantras such as Bālā and others are proclaimed as Vidyā-mantras.
That which is the fifteenth goddess, O Goddess, is proclaimed as the sixteenth;
and the sixteenfold installation (ṣoḍhānyāsa) and so forth consists of eighteen thousand [verses].
The ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed with effort, as well as devotion to the Name;
all of this has been proclaimed in the Parāprāsādavidyā.
Furthermore, there are those who are constant regarding time and so forth, as well as those who are constant regarding the succession of the yugas;
likewise, there is the practice of the recitation of mantras and the practice of the recitation of the nāḍīs.
One who is endowed with the sixteenfold knowledge (ṣoḍaśī-vidyā) is indeed qualified in every respect;
O Śivā, initiation, ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, and so forth, belong to the lineage of the sixfold transmission (ṣaḍanvaya-krama).
It has already been stated that [the procedure] is distinct; now the specific details are being told again.
In the initiation of the four-fold system (catuścaraṇa), the ritual placement (nyāsa) and other rites are considered to be distinct.
O Beloved, there is a specific distinction in the science of Parā-prāsāda;
O Goddess, the worship of all [deities] is proclaimed to take place within the Śrīcakra. (2-39)
O Maheśvarī, it should be applied according to one's qualification;
[then] Mahādeva is undoubtedly endowed with all initiations and the like. (2.40)
Know this, O Maheśvarī, to be increasingly superior at each successive stage;
by the power of this knowledge, O Goddess, one becomes directly identical with Brahman. (2.41)
At the beginning, the single-syllable [mantra] is proclaimed; it is celebrated as being like Bālā.
Siddhakālī, the fifteenth, is celebrated as being like Vidyā. (2.42)
Now, indeed, Kālī is celebrated as the Ṣoḍaśī who is present at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
thereafter, she is considered to be Kāmakaḷākālī, like the supreme grace (parā-prasāda).
Just as the initiation of the feet (caraṇadīkṣā) has been described, so too is Haṃsakālikā;
thereafter is Guhyakākālī, O Supreme Goddess of the six Śāmbhavas.
In the *Ṣaṭśāmbhava* and in the *Guhyakālī*, it is proclaimed as being distinct;
here too, the knowledge of Kāla-nityā and so forth has been declared by me to you. (2.45)
O Goddess, there is the recitation of mantras (maṃtrapārāyaṇa), likewise the recitation of names (nāmapārāyaṇa),
and the recitation of the channels (nāḍīpārāyaṇa), as well as the eternal cycles and so forth, O Śivā.
O Goddess, everything beginning with the daily time-periods and likewise everything beginning with the daily rites has already been explained by me in detail.
But at the beginning of the Yuga, according to the sequence of the eternal time-cycles, it is said to be twenty thousand and eight hundred and thirty-six [years]. (2.48)
Furthermore, the means of accomplishment, beginning with the rules for the times and constellations, is now described.
Thus, O Goddess, this has been told by me to you in brief. (2.49)
One who follows this procedure will undoubtedly attain success in the world.
During the initiation of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), one should perform the recitation of the *Nāmapārāyaṇa*.
In a Śaiva [initiation], the name should end with "Śaiva"; in a Vaiṣṇava, however, it should end with "Vaiṣṇava";
and in the Saura, Gāṇapa, Bauddha, and other traditions, it should be according to the name prescribed in their respective scriptures. (2.51)
In the Śākta [initiation], the name extends up to the end of Śakti; in the Śākta, abundance is said to be present.
In the Śrīmacchāmbhava initiation and others, the Śāmbhava [state] is indeed accepted here.
Or it may be situated within its own rays, or positioned in the midst of the Guru,
or even located at the junction of two seasons, according to the sequence of the traditional transmission.

Due to the distinction between the pair of Śiva and Śakti, [the mantra] resides precisely within the *mālāmantra* in the sixteenfold and fifteenfold [kalās], as well as in the *lopāmudrā*, *agastika*, and *śiva* [mantras].
This name proclaimed by the Guru should be bestowed with effort during initiation;
it should be placed either within the *parā-prāsāda* or by means of the *prāsāda-parā*.
The name ending with Śiva and Śakti, or alternatively ending with Śiva and Śakti, or the name beginning and ending with Nirvāṇa—this is established by the Guru in the feet [of the disciple]. (2.56)
O Maheśvarī, this which resides within the Guru of that [wisdom] has been declared in the *Medhā*.
Now I shall explain another [teaching], the supreme essence of essences. (2.57)
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you, tell me that: what difference would there be between the extraction of the curse and its opening?"
Śrī Śiva said: Unbolting (utkīlana) is bondage; it is a curse that obstructs one's splendor (tejas).
O Great Goddess, when there is bolting (kīlana), coming and going (gatāgata) is said not to occur.
O Great Goddess, the coming and going occurs during the removal of the curse, out of a desire to bestow grace upon devotees in the presence of the goddess and her practitioner. (2.60)
Having gone there, O Goddess, the boon was granted; yet it has indeed become false.
Because the consciousness of the mantra was obstructed, O Maheśvarī, it became false. (2.61)
This curse has been declared, and likewise the "unbolting" (utkīlana) is spoken of;
for, O Śivā, out of a desire to bestow grace upon devotees, a boon must indeed be granted.
When there is liberation from bondage, at that very moment, coming and going cease;
yet the power of the Goddess persists in granting boons, O Maheśvarī.
Just as a cow’s affection for her calf persists even when the calf is older, so too does the mother’s milk continue to flow only when the calf is released from its bond. (2.64)
Kālī, Tārā, and likewise Chinnā are considered to be like masses of splendor; for who indeed would be capable of obstructing the radiance of these three? (2.65)
Therefore, O Maheśvarī, there is no curse or the like in Kālikā;
Kālikā is the Tāriṇī Vidyā, the liberator from bondage.
Just as a cow, having broken her tether, goes toward her calf, so too does this supreme Kālikā act out of a desire to bestow grace upon her devotees. (2.67)
Tārā is the severer, the mistress of paralyzing, and the liberator from all bonds;
yet there is no flow [of power] in the case of cursing, whereas indeed there is a flow in the case of pinning.
O Great Goddess, there is indeed a constant flow in Kālikā at all times;
now listen with diligence to the explanation regarding the removal of the curse. (2.69)
The calf may be nearby and the cow may be nearby;
O Great Goddess, due to the absence of milk, what fruit could there be in proximity? (2.70)
When the appointed time has arrived again, just as milk may appear once more, so too does their splendor manifest again through the very release from the curse. (2.71)
For by being released from the calf-tether, the fruit indeed becomes accomplished;
for in the case of "untying" (utkīlana), O beloved, the binding itself bestows the attainment of the fruit.
Therefore, *utkīlana* is declared to be distinct, and the *śāpa* is proclaimed to be distinct;
O Goddess, the transposition of syllables is prescribed in the rite of *utkīlana*.
Since mantra is of the nature of consciousness, there is no deviation from consciousness; by abandoning this non-deviation from consciousness, a person becomes a partaker of sin. (2.74)
Prāṇāyāma is proclaimed for the purpose of removing that sin;
for the nature of the limbs of the body resides within the auspicious syllable (akṣara). (2.75)
O Goddess, through the transposition of syllables, a deficiency of limbs arises;
however, O Great Goddess, when free from such a curse, every limb is indeed perfected.
Furthermore, O Maheśvarī, how the rite of tethering the calf may become perfected, and how the rite of uprooting may likewise be perfected— [this shall now be told].
O Great Goddess, upon the pronouncement of a curse, there is indeed an absence of consciousness;
O Maheśvarī, it is just as a cow, though present, has no milk. (2.78)
O Maheśānī, O Śāmbhavī, there is no consciousness in the bestowing of the curse;
O Mahādevī, in the act of unlocking (utkīlana), consciousness is indeed already perfected.
"Thus has it been explained according to its divisions; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
'The ritual concerning the lamp-lines and so forth was previously indicated by you.'"
"O Lord, what offense have I committed that it has not been revealed to me?
Śrī Śiva said:
"The knowledge concerning the lines of the lamp and so forth is considered the most essential of all essences. (2.81)
The "flame-line" (dīparekhā) is proclaimed for the purpose of establishing the metaphorical expression of illumination;
it begins from sunrise and extends over an interval of sixty vighaṭikās.
Through the yoga of emanation and withdrawal, the rule for the line of the lamp is established;
indeed, beginning from the point (bindu) and ending with the hour (horā), the Illuminator (dīpinī) arises. (2.83)
O Goddess of the gods, the illuminator indeed arises for all mantras;
O Goddess of the gods, through the sequence of the jar (ghaṭakrama), the emergence of the mantra occurs there.
(22) O Śivā, this convention has been declared by me regarding the mantra alone, O Maheśvarī, beginning with a single syllable and ending at a thousand. (2-85)
O Goddess, impel the syllable through the application of the sequence of the ghaṭikās;
there the syllable eternally arises, and from the knowledge of that, one shall obtain the fruit. (2.86)
O Great Goddess, just as the movement of the swan always proceeds, that very [movement] is called Ajapā; however, through volitional intent (saṃkalpa), it yields fruit.

O Śivā, having ascertained the day that marks the beginning of a Yuga and the count of elapsed days (ahargaṇa), O Goddess, know that the emergence of the mantra-syllables is firmly established therein. (2.88)

O Goddess, by means of the conjunction with each individual ghaṭikā, the syllable arising from the bindu and the line (rekhā) within the hour (horā) must be diligently known by one who desires auspiciousness. (2.89)
Starting from the door up to the point of the Bindu, there is again the syllable of single emergence;
O Goddess of Gods, by being pervaded in this way, one attains the state of Virāḍ-rūpa.
O Goddess, without pervasiveness, the state of being Virāṭ is not recognized;
for the very nature of having the form of the universe is proclaimed to be the form of Virāṭ. (2.91)
O Goddess, without the line of the lamp (dīparekhā), it is certainly not considered "illuminating" (dīpinī);
indeed, the illuminating power arises within the central portion of the line of the lamp.
Having worshipped Dīpinī in that very place, one should [worship] the letter of emergence (udayākṣara) right there;
indeed, by means of the conjunction with the letter of emergence, it is the Saṃjīva mantra itself.
O Goddess, one should not contemplate a mantra that lacks an *udayākṣara*, for it is indeed cursed;
one should contemplate the *udayākṣara* for the purpose of removing the curse from the mantra. (2.94)
O Goddess, the syllable arises as mantra, and likewise the line arises;
by the union with the arising syllables, what on this earth cannot be accomplished? (2.95)
O Goddess, just as there is the arising of mantra, so too is there the arising of the lines;
for the arising of the lines occurs within the mere mantra, and indeed, the arising itself exists there.
"Thus it has been told by me, O Goddess; what else do you wish to hear?
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord, O Master, the meditation on the yantra was previously indicated by you."

How is it to be meditated upon? What is its specific character? Is it indeed both the object of meditation and the non-object of meditation? Is its nature like that of a wall, or is its nature like that of a girdle? (2.98)
Is it to be meditated upon as consisting of lines, or as having the form of Mount Meru, or should one remember it as the universal form? Tell me all of that. (2.99)
Śrī Śiva said:
O Maheśvarī, meditation on the mere yantra is said to be threefold.
First, it consists of the form of Virāṭ, whose nature is the eye of the universe. (2-100)
O Goddess, one should contemplate the yantra; this has indeed been taught for all cases.
O Great Goddess, in the case of the Śrīcakra and so forth, there is equality with the form of the Virāṭ.
O Maheśvarī, tell me how the second [line] is to be meditated upon: it is a line resembling a mass of light, the very form of universal consciousness. (2.102)
One should contemplate everything as being like a mirror, having the nature of self-luminosity; one should contemplate all consciousness, from the bindu up to the outer enclosure (bhūpura). (2.103)
O Dear One, one should meditate upon the third [center] at the root as inseparable from the light of fire; O Goddess of Gods, now hear of the eternal form of Meru.
One should contemplate the progressively higher seeds, beginning from the *bindu*;
and below the *bindu*, O Goddess Śivā, one should contemplate each [seed] in successive order.
Or, O Maheśvarī, one should meditate upon her according to the sequence of nine;
O Goddess, in the ritual of the Kālī-vidyā, she is the embodiment of the nine jewels.
O Goddess, one should fashion the lines either like the Meru-prastāra;
O Supreme Lady, the Śrīcakra, when conjoined with the seed-syllables, is freed from all curses.
But that wheel which is devoid of seed-syllables does not bestow accomplishment;
first there should be the wheel of emanation (sṛṣṭicakra), and the wheel of maintenance (sthiticakra) is the second.
The third is the layacakra; thus the wheel is declared to be threefold.
O Goddess, the drawing out of the seed-syllables has been described by me as being of three kinds.
But without the seed-syllable (bīja), it is proclaimed to be lifeless like a corpse;
when joined with the seed-syllable, the yantra becomes free from curses and bestows accomplishment (siddhi).
In the absence of the seed-syllables, one should write the letters of the alphabet adorned with the nasal bindu;
having written them in the center of the yantra, O Śivā, one should worship that yantra.
(24) However, if the yantra is in the form of petals, that yantra bestows success;
in the Kali age, the petal-shaped [yantra] is to be worshipped, for no other grants success, O Śivā. (2-112)

O Goddess, the consciousness of the mantra, likewise the consciousness of the yantra, and the consciousness of the guru—O Goddess, one should cultivate the realization of these three within oneself. (2.113)
In that [state], there is no visualization of the form of meditation or a mass of fire;
rather, it is the Śiva [principle] within the insubstantial world of manifoldness, which is like a vow of ill-conduct.
Meditation alone has been fully proclaimed; meditation is considered the bestower of accomplishment.
If meditation is perfected, how could this [world] not be so? (2.115)
O Goddess Śivā, the impelling toward meditation is performed by destiny;
O Sovereign of the Gods, hear now the conviction which is always practiced by all. (2.116)
Kuṇḍalī may be of diverse forms, and its liṅga is likewise of diverse forms;
it is called the *svayambhū-liṅga*, O Maheśvarī, established by itself. (2.117)
O Goddess, Kuṇḍalī consists of the root-vidyā and has the form of Śakti;
Kuṇḍalī takes the form of a serpent, while the deity possesses a distinct form. (2.118)
Because Śiva is of non-differentiated nature, his form is proclaimed to be threefold.
O Maheśvarī, the mūlādhāra is declared to be the seat of Kuṇḍalī.
The heart is proclaimed to be the abode of the Śrī-devatā;
O Maheśānī, the thousand-spoked [lotus] is proclaimed to be the abode of Śiva.

O Maheśvarī, O Great Goddess, since there are differences of place, differences of name, and differences of form, how can there be unity? Therefore, it is held that [the deity] is a mental conception (bhāvanā).
O Goddess, I have no concern whatsoever with differences of place, differences of form, or differences of name; rather, my intent is solely the contemplation of pure consciousness. (2.122)
All primary ritual actions lead to the Guru; Nirvāṇa has the form of the Guru.
Nirvāṇa is the supreme Brahman, and Nirvāṇa is the state of the Guru. (2.123)
The Guru is Śakti, the Guru is Vidyā, the Guru is the Lord Maheśvara;
the Guru is Brahmā, the Guru is Viṣṇu, and the Guru possesses the form of Virāṭ. (2.124)
For the guru and the mantra are indeed consciousness; what more need be said? They are nothing but Brahman.
Consciousness alone is the ultimate goal, for meditation is truly nothing other than creative contemplation (bhāvanā).
By whom has the form of meditative concentration been seen, which is the domain of mere mental cultivation?
When one is endowed with firm cultivation, direct perception arises. (2-126)
O Goddess, consciousness must always be directed toward the Guru; of this there is no doubt.
Without the Guru, there is no attainment of knowledge, nor indeed the attainment of mantras. (2.127)
The position of the guru is supreme; one should cultivate the realization that everything resides in the guru.
With the intellect, one should contemplate the identity of the guru, the deity, and the mantra. (2.128)

Having ascertained the meaning of the mantra in one's heart and contemplating the form of the Guru, and indeed knowing that everything is dissolved in the Guru, one should then recite it, O Beloved. (2.129)
Having conceived the threefold [set] within each of the three as non-different from oneself—
[the deity who is] the eye of all, the face of all, and the very essence of all— (2.130)
One should recognize only the guru; meditating upon the guru, one should perform the recitation (japa).
O Śivā, the three states of being have been previously described by me.
What indeed is described regarding the divine state beyond the states of the animal, the hero, and the divine?
Having meditated upon the mass of splendor, one should then perceive everything as having a single essential nature. (2.132)
Then, having contemplated consciousness, one should remember the Great Splendor within Śivā;
O Goddess, may there be the grace of the Guru, for the Guru is remembered as being of the very form of the God. (2-133)

The self should be conceived as the form of the Guru, and the mantra should be conceived as the form of the self; having thus meditated upon everything as being the form of the mantra, one performs the visualization of the [divine] image.
Having meditated upon the deity described in the context of dhyāna, one shall accomplish everything in an instant.
O Goddess, through such meditation, the state of being identical in form [to that deity] arises. (2.135)
But when one has attained identity with that [Supreme], one reaches the state of being the Supreme Power;
"I am of the very nature of the Supreme Power"—this is the imperishable conviction. (2.136)
Having meditated upon the embodiment of consciousness, what on earth cannot be accomplished?
For there, the three [powers] are unified as a single radiance; therein lies the conceptualization of the Form (mūrti).
Having meditated upon the deity described in the context of dhyāna, one should contemplate her as being of one's own essential nature.
Having conceived the triad within the three, there follows the visualization of the desired form therein. (2.138)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, according to the stability of the mind and according to the task at hand,
one should meditate upon her essence as being of equal flavor (samarasa), resembling a mass of radiant energy.
Even regarding Ardhanārīśvara, who is the embodiment of the mantra’s consciousness,
the wise practitioner should not visualize the letters of the mantra as pervading his own body.
"O Śivā, one should contemplate [Kuṇḍalinī] as being like a garland of forest flowers and resembling a mass of radiance;
thus has the form of Kuṇḍalinī been briefly described. (2-141)
O Goddess Śivā, just as it is conceived within the triad of Kuṇḍalinīs, so has this meditation been taught here; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the second chapter, titled "The Description of the Arising Syllables," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā.
The third chapter. The Goddess said:
O God of gods, omniscient one, promulgator of all scriptures!
O Dear One, knowledge such as the emergence of mantras, as well as the lines of the lamp and so forth, [is to be understood]. (3.1)
The end of cultivation (bhāvanā) has been mentioned, but what was previously stated has not been revealed.
Śrī Śiva said:
That very thing is now being told; listen with diligence at this time. (3-2)
The first is the doctrine known as Kerala, the second is that of Kashmir, and the third is the one called Gauḍa; these are the systems regarding the method of meditative cultivation (bhāvanā). (3-3)
But first, O Goddess, Kerala is pure and esteemed by all;
one should contemplate with the intellect the unity of the Guru, the deity, and the mantra. (3-4)
One should contemplate the consciousness of the three as a mass of light;
O Goddess, the Guru is the instructor regarding the awakening of consciousness within the mantra.
One should indeed contemplate the nature of consciousness as being the form of the Guru;
O Goddess, just as the luster of the nine gems is united in one place. (3.6)
O Goddess, from a distance of one yojana in one place she has a radiance equal to a blazing Mount Meru; from a distance of one yojana in another place, her radiance is equal to ten million suns.
Within that radiance, O Great Goddess, one should meditate upon the Guru, whose nature is Śambhu, who bestows boons and fearlessness, who is peaceful, two-eyed, and two-armed. (3.8)
For by that splendor, the entire world—both stationary and moving—is indeed dissolved;
one should contemplate the Guru in this manner within the tradition known as Kerala. (3-9)
All ritual actions have the Guru as their primary focus; therefore, the Guru is supreme above all.
O wise one, listen to that which is called Kāśmīra, by means of which one attains identity with Him. 3-10.

Indeed, contemplating with one's intellect the identity of the mantra, the deity, and the guru, [one perceives] everything as having the nature of the syllable, resembling a mass of radiant light. (3-11)
One should contemplate the mass of light, the syllables, and everything else as one in a single place;
for indeed, the triad of consciousnesses is dissolved within the imperishable Śiva.
All this light born of consciousness has a splendor equal to ten million suns;
these syllables are indeed masses of light, like a collection of peaks of jewels.
Having honored [the deity], one should mutter the mantra that bestows the attainment of desired goals.
The Krama known as Kāśmīra has been declared; now hear the Gauḍa-krama. (3.14)
Perceiving with one's intellect the identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra,
one should contemplate the entire world, both stationary and moving, as consisting of pure light.
O Goddess Śivā, the consciousness of the three [deities] became a single mass of splendor, resembling a heap of light as vast as Mount Meru. (3.16)
One should contemplate the Great Goddess, together with her weapons, within that fire;
having meditated according to the procedure prescribed for meditation, one should visualize her in all her forms.
For one who meditates in this way, the deity will become a granter of boons.
This indeed is declared to be the meditation; what else do you wish to hear? (3-18)
The Goddess said: "O God, if I am indeed dear to you, let that very intention which was indicated by means of the three lineages be told."
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen with reverence to the *saṃkalpa* (formal resolve) within the tradition known as Kerala;
this *saṃkalpa* is proclaimed for the sake of pleasing the deity. (3.20)
At the very moment that joy arises for the deity, first there is clarity, and from that, joy proceeds. (3.21)
O Goddess, when joy has arisen, there is no doubt regarding clarity;
this application for the sake of joy is proclaimed as the primary one. (3.22)
O Goddess, O beloved, hear now the application of the sequence known as Kāśmīra, for the purpose of the direct vision of the deity, O Maheśvarī. (3.23)
O Maheśānī, in the Gauḍa tradition, for the sake of attaining all siddhis,
when there is pleasure in the deity, then everything proceeds.
O Goddess, direct perception indeed exists dissolved within bliss;
likewise, the perfection of speech and other faculties indeed exists dissolved within bliss. (3.25)
Therefore, O Great Goddess, it has been declared that joy is the primary element, and its application is for the sake of joy; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear how the Nityā is fivefold.
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim the definitive teaching regarding the Kālanityās.
The Tithinityā comes first, followed by the Dinanityā;
thereafter the Yuganityā is proclaimed, and after that the Kālanityā is considered. (3-28)
Therefore, it would be eternal by way of succession; thus, the Nityā is considered to be fivefold.
The daily worship of the Nityā is held to be twofold, according to the sequence of the bright and dark fortnights.
O Dear One, having first worshipped Kāmeśvarī in the bright fortnight and Citrā and the others in the dark fortnight, one should then worship the Tithinityā and the two primordial goddesses.
Having again performed the beginning and the end according to the tradition of Dakṣiṇāmūrti, this is the daily rite for the first day according to the system of Ānandabhairava. (3.31)
Following the sequence of the bright and dark fortnights, one should worship her in her entirety at the end of that period;
thus has the Tithinityā been described, preceded by the Dinanityā.
The Yuganityā has been described, and the Kālanityā is as before.
O Goddess of gods, the *paryāyanityā* is described, preceded by the *kālanityā*;
listen, O Goddess of gods, and hear with an attentive mind. (3.34)
Having extracted the two void-creations (śūnyasarga), one should then utter the Kāmakalā.
Having extracted "Haṃsaḥ so'ham," listen as the reversal is described. (3.35)

O Goddess, [the mantras are formed] with the vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣ*, joined with the "sprouts" *u*, *ṛ*, *i*, and *e*, auspiciously combined with one another in pairs or triplets.

Then, by means of those vowels and so forth that have been taken up, and by those very same [consonants] joined with the vowels, which are mutually intertwined, there is the one called the Nāmapārāyaṇa. (3.37)
The auspicious one is said to be eternal through its manifestations (paryāya-nityā) and endowed with eternity through time (kāla-nityā).
O Goddess, the manifestation of its own nature occurs through the revelation of the eternity of time (kāla-nityā-prakāśataḥ). (3.38)
O Maheśānī, that which is called *tattat-pārāyaṇa* is proclaimed as difficult even for the gods to attain; it is known by the name of the *Nityā* cycle within the *Kālikā*. (3-39)
Kālī, who is indeed eternal in her various manifestations, has been revealed in brief;
she is said to consist of twenty thousand [verses] divided into thirty-six hundred parts.
Regarding this, some maintain that there are seven hundred [verses] in the Nāga [recension],
and that which is proclaimed as the Akṣarodaya is indeed manifold.
The *Ṣaṣṭipārāyaṇa* has already been proclaimed previously;
distinct from it are the *Nāmapārāyaṇa* and likewise the *Mantrapārāyaṇa*.
That which is called *mantrapārāyaṇa* is proclaimed as distinct;
however, the *akṣarodaya*, being the sixtieth, is proclaimed as one and the same. (3-43)
O lady of excellent vows, that which is called the Kālī-pārāyaṇa has been proclaimed to you;
O Maheśvarī, listen as I describe how it differs from the Sundarī [pārāyaṇa]. (3-44)

O Śivā, [the mantras are formed] with the vowels beginning with *ā* and *ī*, joined with the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa* in groups of two or three syllables, combined with one another. O Śivā, [these are] joined with the *pallavas*.
O Śivā, O Tripurā, your names indeed arise from those vowels and consonants, along with their respective vowels, when they are enumerated. (3.46)
Indeed, this secret beyond secrets, which has not been revealed anywhere else, consists of twenty thousand, one hundred and thirty-six [verses]. 3.47.
Either the letter *a* is first, or this letter *ā* is first;
O Goddess, the letter *a* is indeed first, and the letter *ā* follows immediately after that. (3.48)
First is the form of Virāj; thereafter, it is considered to have limbs.
The form of Virāj is called Kālikā, beautiful with the face of Sundarī.
Therefore, the letter *A* is indeed primary; it is considered the principal [seed-syllable] in the ritual of Kālī.
In the system of Kālikā, the letters beginning with *Ka* are used, whereas in the tradition of Śrīsundarī, those beginning with *Ha* are employed. (3.50)
In the true nature of the phonemes (varṇa), that form does not exist as something belonging to me;
the letter 'ka' is proclaimed to be the Virāṭ, whose nature is emptiness. (3.51)
The letter *ha* is the primordial sound (*hādi*), the Śrīvidyā, the digit of consciousness (*citkalā*), and Kāmasundarī;
the Mahākāmakalā-vidyā shines within the letter *ha*. (3.52)
The nature of Virāṭ has been proclaimed as belonging solely to Sundarī;
nevertheless, O Goddess of gods, it is established as being primarily present in Kālī. (3.53)
O Goddess, that essential nature is revealed in the Nāmapārāyaṇa:
the letter *a* joined with the *bindu*, and the letter *a* joined with the *sarga*. (3.54)
The pair of syllables *aṃ* and *aḥ* is the nature of the Unsurpassed (*anuttara*).
The fifty-two known as the Vidyās are proclaimed to be the Unsurpassed. (3.55)
Thus the Vidyā of Kāmakalā has been shown according to the different schools of thought;
O Goddess, the letter *ī* alone is considered the Great Kāmakalā.
p. 31) For this very reason, in Kāmarāja, when there is the letter *ka*, it possesses primacy;
whereas in Lopāmudrā, the letter *ha* is indeed proclaimed as being of the nature of *ā*. (3.57)
O Goddess of gods, having made [the self] half of Hara, one who meditates upon Jagadambikā,
enclosed by the two mantras, with the contemplation of absolute non-difference— 3-58.
O Śivā, the Nāmapārāyaṇa has been proclaimed in the ritual procedure of the Kālī-vidyā;
for this very reason, O Maheśvarī, it is declared to be the nature of consciousness itself.
O Goddess, the letter *a* is indeed the first, and the letter *ā* is the second; the letter *ā* is declared to be all-pervasive by virtue of its pervasiveness. (3.60)
O Goddess, the half-measure of the letter *ha* is proclaimed as the letter *ī*;
thus united, O Mistress of the Gods, she is the supreme Mahārājeśvarī.
O Great Goddess, O Śivā, the *Mahārājeśvarī-vidyā-pallava* is considered supreme; it has been taught in brief regarding the *Śrīvidyā*. (3-62)
The Virāj-Uttareśvarī Vidyā is proclaimed in the Kālikā [Tantra];
the letter 'A' is proclaimed within both the letters 'Ka' and 'Ha'. (3.63)
O Goddess, the utterance of the letter *a* is not considered to be among the *ka*-group or the *ha*-group;
where there is a combination (*kūṭa*) of both, it is proclaimed as having the meaning of a *kūṭa*.
In the Kali age, whose will be the practice of pronouncing the *kūṭa*?
Therefore, for the sake of pronunciation, the letter *a* has indeed been proclaimed [as the substitute]. (3.65)
The letter *ka* is indeed considered the first syllable, and the letter *ha* the last;
O Goddess, in this matter there will be conviction regarding the extraction of the letters.
He in whose speech this great mantra "Kaha" proceeds is blessed, he is wise, and he is indeed worshipped by the gods. (3.67)
Upon seeing him, one should offer salutation; through knowledge, one obtains the fruit, but through ignorance, there would be the destruction of the fruit. What else do you wish to hear?
The illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord, [please explain] the method for the recitation of the Ṣaṣṭhī, as well as the Pārāyaṇa of Names, the Pārāyaṇa of Mantras, and likewise the Akṣarodaya."

O Lord of Gods, who has the authority regarding the cognition of the lines of the lamps and likewise the arising of the syllables of the mantra? By whom should it be performed, and who might that person be? (3.70)
"Tell me that, O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
"One who has received the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), whose inner self is pure, who is devoted to the Guru, and firm in his vows... (3.71)
One who has renounced impermanent actions and is intent upon eternal practice, being devoted to the traditional succession of teachers, indeed reaches the very end of the six Śāmbhava stages. (3.72)
O Goddess, he who indeed possesses authority over the four junctions (sandhyās),
O Great Goddess, he indeed possesses authority over the office of the teacher (ācārya).

The knowledge of the future, the knowledge of the three times, and the vision of discernment; the fifteen-fold [knowledge] beginning with the ignorant, and then the sixfold supreme ignorance (avidyā). (3.74)
Then follow Parā, Prāsāda, and Nirvāṇa, along with the sequence of the six lineages;
thus, it is joined with the tradition and endowed with names, designations, and so forth. (3.75)
O Goddess of the gods, O Śivā, his authority extends from the recitation of the names (nāmapārāyaṇa) and so forth,
beginning with the chanting of the Ṣaṣṭhī mantra up to the name-mantras.
O Maheśvarī, he who performs such a rite as the Pārāyaṇa—O Goddess, is he a mere human? For he is indeed Śiva himself in person.
The Pārāyaṇa of the Sixty, as well as the Pārāyaṇa of Names,
the Pārāyaṇa of Mantras, the Knowledge, and likewise the Dīparekhā and so forth.
The convention of giving names and so forth is not the fruit of a minor action,
O Goddess, by which Sundarī was perfectly worshipped for twenty million aeons.
Indeed, eighteen thousand nyāsas were performed by him upon his own body,
accompanied by preliminary rites (puraścaryā) and other practices, as they are honored by the Lord of Gods.
Therefore, O Goddess, this may indeed be obtained, or it may not be obtained;
O Maheśānī, I know this truth only slightly through diligent effort. (3.81)
O Great Goddess, he who possesses complete knowledge is Kālikāmbikā herself;
she indeed appears in the form of Sundarī, whose very body is the nectar of youth.
O Goddess Sundarī, you alone know this, O Maheśvarī;
O wise one, you conceal my exceedingly great fortune.
The Goddess said:
"O Śiva, Lord of the Universe, you who show the further shore of all things, you are blessed!
O Śambhu, without Śiva, the state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya) is not seen within Śakti. (3.84)
Śrī Śiva said:
O Great Goddess, there is no difference, just as the sprout arises from the seed;
she is indeed I in the form of a male, and I am indeed she in the form of a female. (3.85)
(33) "Indeed, there is no difference between the two of us; difference arises only from ignorance.
O Mistress of the Gods, I have been instructed in the ocean of unsurpassed qualities. (3.86)
"By your grace, all of this has indeed not been forgotten.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord, the analysis of dreams and mantras was previously indicated;
yet it was not told to me, O Lord, for indeed there was no fitness in me. (3.88)
"O Lord, if I am dear to you, let everything be told to me.
Śrī Śiva said:
"Until this time, it has not been revealed anywhere."
Out of affection for you, O Great Goddess, I shall speak; listen now.
Indeed, fifty great lotuses are proclaimed as the scriptural texts (āgama-granthas).
In that regard, O Great Goddess, all mantras are established therein:
thirty nikharvas, six vṛndas, ninety arbudas, and [ninety-six] koṭis. (3.91)
The mantras have been proclaimed, O Maheśānī; but where and how does the Āgama reside?
Listen to that, O Maheśānī, if I am indeed dear to you. (3.92)
In the great fifty-fold lotus, twenty-six are situated on the earth;
fourteen are situated in heaven, and ten belong to the realm of the netherworlds.
Thus, O Goddess of the gods, the Āgama has been narrated by me in due order;
O Great Goddess, the dream-mantras are indeed established in three ways.
In the netherworld (pātāla) is the Virāṭcakra, and in heaven is the Tāṇḍavacakra;
O Goddess, there is a second pair of wheels in heaven known as Tripura.
O Goddess, first is the Virāṭ, then the Śivatāṇḍava, and the third is that named Tripura; thus the dream-mantras are established in three ways.

But therein, O Great Goddess, those [mantras] ending with the heart-mantra are within the scope of the Virāṭ-cakra; whereas those ending with the weapon-mantra are within the scope of Śiva’s Tāṇḍava dance.
These mantras, situated in the center of the Tripurā-cakra and ending with the wife of Fire (svāhā), are considered to have become manifest on earth through intense longing and dreams. (3.98)
O Goddess of gods, they have indeed been instructed by Śiva through the path of dreams;
O Goddess, listen now with diligence to their characteristics. (3-99)
(p. 34) Now listen to the characteristics of the mantras of the netherworld cycle (pātālacakra): collyrium, pills, concealment, and likewise the accomplishment of the command (ājñāsiddhi). (3-100)
Now hear the characteristics of the Śivātāṇḍava-cakra:
