the accomplishment of the sword and the vetāla, as well as the entry into another's body. (3.101)
O Pārvatī, listen now to the characteristics of the Tripura-cakra-mantras, as well as the state of moving and non-moving beings and the eightfold powers beginning with *aṇimā*.
And for one who has no affliction regarding their desires within the wheel-diagram of Tripurā,
having become a lord of the sixty siddhis on earth, in heaven, and on the surface of the world— 3.103.
O Pārvatī, as for those mantras belonging to Triśaṅkara, where are they established? They reside within the Ardhanārīśvara-cakra.
O Goddess, they have indeed attained the state of Śaṅkara in three ways within the maṇḍala of Paraśiva, possessing characteristics like those of a beautiful woman. (3.105)
For the mantra of Parāprāsāda is indeed formed either by [reversing] Prāsāda with Parā, or else by [reversing] Parā with Prāsāda;
and in that case as well, O Maheśvarī, it attains a twofold nature.
O Goddess, that which is the primordial is considered to be Ādyashankara;
he is Shankara who is Parā—what else do you wish to hear? (3.107)
The Goddess said:
O Great Goddess, how is it that the seer, meter, and so forth are [required] for what is obtained in a dream?
O Maheśvara, why is it that the seer, meter, and so forth are not declared for that which occurs in a dream?

Likewise, O Maheśvara, regarding the meditation on the seats and so forth that has not been declared—O Mahādeva, in a case where it has not been stated, what should it be and how should it be performed? (3.109)
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, the seer is declared to be Śiva, the meter is said to be Gāyatrī, and the deity is the form of consciousness (cidrūpa); there is no preliminary *kīlaka* or other such elements.
The doctrine known as Draviḍa has been proclaimed; now listen with diligence to that of Kāśmīra.
O Maheśvarī, when the seer, meter, and so forth are not mentioned, Brahmā is the seer.
O Pārvatī, who knows that the Gāyatrī meter has been prescribed [for this], that the vowels are called the Śaktis, and that the unmanifest (avyakta) is considered the Kīlaka? (3.112)
The seat (pīṭha), however, is the Mātṛkā-pīṭha; meditation and so forth are as described for the Mātṛkās.
O Maheśānī, O Śivā, in the Gauḍa-krama, [this is established] by virtue of being a perfected mantra. (3.113)
O Goddess, there are no requirements for ṛṣis or meters, nor any restriction regarding worship, O Śivā;
success shall come through mere recitation—no deliberation is required in this matter. (3.114)
O Maheśvarī, for one whose mantra is perfected, there is no need for the purification of the wheel and so forth;
if there is doubt regarding a perfected mantra, that very doubt becomes its perfection.
There is neither debt nor wealth; success is granted by mere recitation alone.
O Goddess, the preliminary rites (*puraścaryā*) and so forth have been described as before. (3.116)
O Great Goddess, there is no six-limbed [rite]; Caitanyeśī is the deity.
As for the meditation on the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), it is proclaimed as mere meditation.

One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) by means of the sixfold repetition of the root mantra, which is a meditation on the syllables of the mantra as a mass of splendor that grants the accomplishment of all goals. (3.118)
O Goddess, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) at whichever location [is prescribed], or else one should perform it by means of that [mantra];
wherever the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and so forth are taught, there indeed one should perform them accordingly.
O Dear One, when no seat is mentioned, it is the Śaktipīṭha; when no visualization is mentioned, it is Mātṛkā;
and when no preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) and so forth are mentioned, one should perform a thousand-fold recitation in each direction.
Up to twenty-two syllables, it is proclaimed as a thousand directions; beyond that, O Great Goddess, is a thousand Gajāntakas.

O Goddess, what difference could there possibly be between that which is obtained in a dream and that which is given by a woman? In the case of a mere consecration of a jar, O Goddess, there is equality in the ritual refinement.
O Goddess of the gods, one should purify the *siddha* and *ari* wheels by means of their names alone;
then, having contemplated the *ṛṇa* wheel, one should install the Rudra wheels. (3.123)
Indeed, the wheel known as Debt and Wealth has been described by me everywhere;
having set aside the wheel of debt, one should then recite [the mantra] ten billion times.
O Goddess of the Gods, there is no success for him; he shall incur the curse of the deity.
For he owes nothing to the god himself, yet the fault is attributed to him. (3-125)
One should not give directions to the gods, and one should always recite [the mantra] as a creditor;
he who, relying on the "debtor-mantra" (ṛṇimantra), recites various mantras. || 3-126 ||
Having become a lord of accomplishments (siddhīśvara) in this world, one shall become equal to Śiva in the next;
yet, O beloved, when a mantra is being purified, a debt is indeed observed.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord, since perfection arises from one's own experience alone, what else remains there?
Śrī Śiva said:
A mantra that has been previously accomplished but not yet fully realized is called "one who owes a debt. || 3-128 ||
By the name of the station situated in that yuga, he is established as a debtor;
through its power, O Maheśānī, that mantra bestows accomplishment (siddhi).
But when one has entered into the midst of the dream, no wonder exists;
when the great wheel is being purified, no debtor is clearly seen. (3.130)
"O Goddess, that mantra is indeed wealthy; one should instruct it to the disciples.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Lord, O Master, you previously spoke of those obtained in dreams and so forth. (3.131)
O dear one, those mantras and so forth obtained in a dream or given by a woman are called "accomplished mantras" (siddhamantra); otherwise, they are explained differently.
"In this regard, a doubt has arisen within me; tell me that, O Maheśvara.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Maheśānī, this is true; your state of perfection is clearly manifest. (3.133)
O Goddess, he in whom there is conviction is proclaimed as a perfected one (siddha);
O Mistress of Gods, he in whom there is no conviction is proclaimed as a wealthy man.
O Goddess, regarding the state of being perfected in a mantra, not all have attained perfection;
other mantras are proclaimed to be so by virtue of their prior impressions (saṃskāra). (3.135)
O Śivā, these have been transmitted through successive lineage by the power of conditioned formations (saṃskāra);
therefore, one who desires auspiciousness should clear his debts and wealth and recite the mantra. (3.136)
Indeed, by one's former name there is debt, and likewise, there is existence;
such a person, O Great Goddess, is obtained through great good fortune. (3.137)
But having attained [birth] through past conditioning (saṃskāra), he has now become a debtor;
even he, O Goddess, is considered such a one, not a wealthy man. (3.138)
O Maheśvarī, this should indeed be applied within the midst of the five wheels;
thus has it been briefly declared, proclaimed as the conclusion of the sādhana.
"O Goddess, male, female, and neuter [mantras] are traditionally remembered as *phaṭ* and *svāhā*, applied to the heart [and other limbs] in sequence.
Thus the practice has been briefly declared; listen as it is now explained. (3.140)
In the midst of the weapons are the weapon-mantras, ending with "vahnike" (O Fire) for the feminine forms;
in the case of the Śiva-mantras, they are said to be included within those that end with "namaḥ" (salutation).
"O Pārvatī, some indeed desire the meditation taught in the *Dvimātṛka*;
others say, 'Let the Kashmiris perish'—thus the twofold division has been proclaimed. (3.142)
O Maheśvarī, by means of the yoga of the five seats and the meaning of the mantra,
O Goddess of gods, they indeed become internally contained within the pallava.
But as for those mantras that exist on earth, if they are joined with [mere] sprouts, they are indeed attained only in dreams; what purpose do they serve? (3-144)
Some [mantras] have been declared in the *kavaca*, and some have been proclaimed in the *stotra*;
O Supreme Goddess, all of them should be recited as if they were the primary ones.
Whatever rite has been declared as primary is proclaimed in all cases;
O Goddess, remember the example for this in the case of Nīlasārasvata.
O Goddess of the gods, the *puraścaryā* has been proclaimed as taught by the Guru;
in that regard, O Beloved, the sequence of the path has been described as before. (3.147)
In Kerala, however, the *puraścaryā* is proclaimed to have ten limbs;
whereas in Kashmir, the *puraścaryā* has been described by me as having eight limbs. (3.148)

O Maheśānī, the five-limbed *puraścaryā* is proclaimed in the Gauḍa tradition; however, when [the mantra] is obtained in a dream, the performance of the preliminary rites (*puraskriyā*) is considered to consist of only one limb.
Recitation, fire sacrifice, and feeding Brahmins—these three are considered [the means for purification].
When [a mantra] is obtained in a dream, the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) serves to ward off the two-fold defect.
If there is birth-impurity at the beginning and death-impurity at the end [of the recitation], that mantra, being joined with both types of impurity, will not succeed at all. (3.151)
The Goddess said:
"O Mahādeva, tell me by what means the defect of birth-impurity (jātasūtaka) may be averted."
Śrī Śiva said: One should draw an auspicious eight-petaled [lotus].
Having placed a water-pot in the middle of that [area], one should place a banyan leaf there;
indeed, having written the mantra upon the banyan leaf with saffron.

Having placed the water-pot in front, one should establish the vital breaths of the Guru; from the presence of the Guru comes the reception [of the teaching] and the warding off of birth-impurity. (3.124)
The Goddess said:
"O Supreme Lord, what indeed is the nature of the impurity caused by death and birth?
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, a mantra without the preliminary rites (puraskriyā) is said to be dead.
Just as a body devoid of life is incapable of any activity, so too is a mantra proclaimed to be ineffective when it lacks the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa). (3.156)
Therefore, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaryā) for the pacification of the defect of death;
that mantra which is endowed with consciousness is the mantra that bestows success.
Consciousness is indeed the preliminary rite (puraścaryā), and consciousness is the guru as well;
O Goddess, there is the consciousness of the yantra and likewise the consciousness of the mantra.
The consciousness of the Guru and [one's own] consciousness—this is considered the triad of consciousness.
A mantra devoid of this triad of consciousness does not bestow success.
O Goddess, if one should become wealthy through what was obtained in a dream, then what should be done? One should perform the *puraścaraṇa* rite according to the specific mantra. (3.160)
One should perform the rite of homa according to each respective cakra;
however, when no specific substance for the homa is mentioned, the offering is prescribed to be made with sesame seeds.
O Goddess, it is likewise declared that [the oblation] may be made with ghee or even with barley;
by the mere offering of ghee, all the powers become bestowers of boons.
Having thus performed the preliminary honors and having ascertained his spiritual accomplishment,
one should then examine the end of the mandala, or alternatively, the end of the sun's solstice.
Having observed [the results] for the end of a year, one should recite it a thousand times every day;
if no miraculous effect (*camatkāra*) arises, then the disciple should speak to the guru.
O Śivā, having first investigated matters such as debts and so forth, one should then speak to the disciple;
otherwise, the disciple would become impaired and the fault would fall upon the guru. (3-165)
O Goddess of the gods, one should not abandon [the mantra]; by abandoning the mantra, poverty ensues.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (3.166)
The Śrī Devī said:
"The great mantra has appeared within a dream while I was situated in the world of mortals.
What should be done there, and what kind of maṇḍala should be present there? (3.167)
Śrī Śiva said:

"O beloved, one should practice a mantra after due consideration—whether it was previously mastered by someone else or given [to oneself] unaccomplished; for such a person may be either a debtor or a creditor."
However, O Dear One, one should perform the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) according to the method prescribed in the respective Kalpa,
because of the lack of lineage and due to previous practice.
O Dear One, one who has obtained a mantra through a dream should practice that mantra;
but if an enemy's mantra is obtained in the midst of a dream, what should be done? (3.170)
O Śivā, one should either attach the *pallava* or discard it with effort;
for he who is joined with the *pallavas* has entered into another mantra. (3-171)

O Goddess, everything has been explained by me to you according to the nature of the primordial source (mūlaprakṛti); for, O Goddess, within the section on weapons (astraprakaraṇa), there is a specific application regarding the midst of weapons.

O Goddess, one should employ [the mantra] within the midst of the mantra according to the section on mantras, by way of the primary expansion (mūlaprastāra) and through the sequence beginning with vision (darśana). || 3.173 ||

O Śivā, by means of the sequence of the six traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) and through the method of expansion (prastāra), there is the accomplishment of expansion for every mantra as well as for every vidyā. (3.174)
O Maheśvarī, listen to the number previously mentioned by me,
according to the divisions of mantras, vidyās, and so forth, as well as the various traditions of the Āgamas.
O Maheśvarī, mantras numbering as many as the higher half (parārdha) have appeared;
however, because they are devoid of the *prastāra* method in the Kali age, they are proclaimed to be merely the limbs (*aṅga*).
O Śivā, that knowledge which exists in the form of a grid (prastāra), more secret than the secret, Ādinātha alone knows; I do not know it, O Pārvatī. (3.177)
The Śrī Mahāsundarī Vidyā is Kālī, who is indeed Kāmakalā;
Ādinātha and Paraśiva are like a seed and its sprout. (3.178)
Likewise, O beloved Pārvatī, Kāmakalā, Kālī, and Śrī Mahāsundarī—thus has everything been declared in brief; now hear the secret. 3-179.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, the lineage of the illustrious Goddesses was obtained through a woman;
O Great Goddess, the lineage of Dakṣamūrti was obtained in a dream. (3.180)
O Maheśvarī, one should worship Dakṣiṇāmūrti as the Guru;
first, one should worship the Tetrad. What else do you wish to hear?
O Śivā, regarding the enumeration of the expansions of the mantras of the six Āmnāyas:
there are thirty "Nikharvaka" clusters of expansions for the six Āmnāyas.
O Maheśvarī, in the Eastern Tradition (Pūrvāmnāya) there are five hundred million mantras;
O Maheśānī, in the Southern Tradition (Dakṣāmnāya), there are nine hundred and ten billion.
O Maheśvarī, mantras joined with the five *kharvas* have been proclaimed;
O Goddess, in the Western Tradition (*paścimāmnāya*), there are thirty *arbudas*, *padmas*, and [other units].
The mantras have been declared, O Maheśānī; now listen with respect to what follows: fifty, five hundred million, six hundred and thirty million. (3.185)
(40) O Great Goddess, hear the enumeration of the *prastāra* in the *Ūrdhvāmnāya*: it is proclaimed as eight *arbudas*, ten million (*koṭi*), and fifty *śaṅkhas*. (3-186)
Now listen with diligence to the enumeration of the traditions of Pātāla:
ninety-three crores, one hundred million, and one thousand million, together with a lotus.
O Supreme Goddess, O Daughter of Śaṅkara, the mantras situated within the central pavilion of the netherworld (pātāla) are declared with effort to be the arrays (prastāra) of the six Āmnāyas.
O Śivā, those who know the calculation pertaining to the Śiva-siddhānta are not to be revealed anywhere; they are merely within the scope of enumeration. (3.189)
O Dear One, he who possesses knowledge of the twenty-eight Siddhāntas, O Goddess, indeed possesses the knowledge of the *prastāra* within the venerable Siddhānta doctrine. (3.190)
O Maheśānī, indeed one who knows the *prastāra* is very difficult to find in the Kali age.
O Goddess, the calculation has been described; now listen as the method is being told. (3.191)
One who understands this expansion is undoubtedly the very form of Śiva; O Dear One, whatever issues from the mouth of one who knows the expansion is [Śiva himself]. (3.192)
Each of those [teachings] is equal to the word of Śiva; what need is there to mention the praise of their fruits?
Thus it has been briefly stated; now the supreme *prastāra* is described. (3-192)
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Mahādeva, that which was previously indicated should now be told; tell me how one should indeed meditate upon the mantra and its conduct."
"Tell me how the rites of oblation and libation are to be performed.
Śrī Śiva said:
"That which is circular at the base of the petal is declared to be situated upon the support (ādhāra)."
O beloved of my life, listen now to the circular [arrangement] situated above the petals;
it is proclaimed as consisting of the moon, sun, and fire, arranged in reverse order. (3.196)
O Queen of the Gods, these well-known ones are not proclaimed to be moons;
rather, it is there that the crores, billions, and fractions of the Goddess eternally arise.
He is called the Moon, he is the Sun, and he is said to be the chief Fire;
O Maheśānī, these have been declared by me to you within the Ṣaḍanvaya.
O Maheśvarī, the triad of circles possessing the three forms is of the nature of fire;
that which is called the Virāṭ-svarūpa is established as being precisely that. (3.199)
(41) Otherwise, indeed, one should remember the meditation on the enclosure wall along with its function, not as an action;
O Goddess, resembling a mass of light, one should always remember the moat. 3-200.
O Goddess, in the practice of meditation upon qualities, as one contemplates a progressively higher state, O Maheśvarī, there is a successive ascent. (3.201)
O sweet-spoken one, the presence of all [the elements] exists together, just as all the cycles are considered to exist in high and low positions. (3.202)
Thus, O Goddess, the primary Meru-prastāra has been described according to its cause;
likewise, the Prastāra known as Kailāsa has been proclaimed.
The third arrangement, known as Ratnagarbha, has been fully described.
O Goddess of the Gods, in the first arrangement, the vision of all is equal.
O Maheśānī, in the region called Kailāsa, they are considered the obstacles for some; in the expanse known as Ratnagarbha, they are proclaimed to be the foremost.
But the cycles (āvṛttayaḥ), O Goddess of gods, have come to possess a threefold division;
otherwise, for what purpose would there be this threefold nature, rather than simply the form of the universe itself? (3.206)
O Maheśvarī, it has been proclaimed everywhere before that this is indeed the truth;
O Goddess, by virtue of one's qualification, one takes refuge in those respective places.

Listen, O wise one, to the rite of fire-offering (homakarma), which is the answer to your previous question: one should employ "svāhā" in the fire-offering; the heart-mantra is prescribed for the act of satiation (tarpaṇa). (3.208)
Likewise, O Goddess of the Gods, the heart-mantra is proclaimed for the consecration;
that which is called the wife of Agni (Svāhā) is established as the mantra for the fire-oblation.
O Lord, when two fire-born wives (svāhā) occur in the middle of the mantra, and likewise the heart-mantras and the beloved of fire (svāhā) at the end of the mantra, O All-pervading One; 3-210.
The ritual procedure is indeed accomplished by the mantra alone; why then should a second [mantra] be employed?
For that which is the "wife of fire" (svāhā) at the end of a mantra is itself the very nature of the mantra.
I have indeed declared to you that the accusative case is used when [the mantra] is an auxiliary part of the fire-oblation (homa);
know that it is likewise in the case of libation (tarpaṇa), whereas the heart-mantra (hṛnmantra) takes the second case.
O Śivā, he who does not act in this manner shall have a short lifespan;
however, the rite of *homa* must be performed, for when the mantra is mastered, the fruit [of success] will arise.
O Beloved, if that very wife of Agni is employed in the homa, O dear one, the mantras become moistened and he attains mastery over himself. (3.214)
(42) For the purpose of removing the defect of dampness, *svāhā* is uttered by me in the fire-oblation (*homa*).
For the purpose of attaining one's own bliss, the heart-mantra (*hṛnmantra*) is intended for the libation (*tarpaṇa*). (3-215)
O Maheśānī, when there is agitation in the mantra, the syllables *huṃ* and *phaṭ* and so forth are employed;
nevertheless, O Maheśvarī, they should be applied again as mere pallavas (supplementary extensions).
O Maheśvarī, O Śivā, when the encapsulation is performed with the heart-mantra,
the agitation of the mantra is entirely stilled.
O Goddess, O Beloved, although the *nati* (salutation) occurs in the middle of the mantra,
nevertheless, O Maheśvarī, it should be given again by way of encapsulation (*saṃpuṭatvena*).
"Listen as the preliminary practice for the six weapons, beginning with the Heart-mantra, is now described;
thus it has been taught in brief. What else do you wish to hear? (3.219)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the secret concerning the sequence of meditative realization (bhāvanākrama).
Śrī Śiva said:
Ending with *svāhā* for all purposes; ending with *phaṭ* for fierce rites.
The fruit of a collection of mantras used for killing and other such purposes is traditionally held to end with the word "namas.
O Śiva, one should avoid the rudrākṣa in the case of powerful mantras, women, and [mantras] dedicated to Rudra.
Now, O Goddess of gods, I shall explain the contemplation of the unity of the four: the contemplation of the Guru, the Deity, and the Mantra as being non-different from oneself. (3.222)
One should indeed contemplate the single peak-syllable as the very nature of the Guru’s splendor;
one should contemplate the peak-syllable of divine consciousness as being of the form of light.
The consciousness of the mantra-syllables is like a blazing mountain;
indeed, the peak of one's own inner consciousness is likewise equal to Mount Meru.
O Śivā, the fourfold fire has become one, pervading the entire universe;
it resembles ten million fires of cosmic destruction and possesses a radiance equal to the sun of Yama.
O Goddess, one should contemplate the form of Virāṭ as being like a mass of moons;
then, having visualized it as a mass of light, one should fashion the image therein.

There, having meditated with a concentrated mind upon his chosen deity— who is beautiful, resembling ten million Cupids, and described according to the rules of meditation— he should perform the recitation.
Alternatively, O Śivā, one should meditate on the entire [universe] as resembling a mass of light;
and that light, O Maheśvarī, one should always meditate upon as having become one.
Now I shall describe the internal *mātṛkā*, which has come down through the lineage of succession;
the nature of the six petals, however, has already been proclaimed.

O Śivā, O Goddess who bestows the tradition of playful grace, I have explained to you everything, beginning with the pronunciation of the phonemes (varṇa), as well as the sequence for the ritual placement (nyāsa). (3.230)
Listen, O Goddess of gods, as I speak this most secret of secrets:
from the cosmic egg down to the smallest insect, everything is certainly composed of Śiva and Śakti.
On the path consisting of Śiva and Śakti, which is the domain of the Parā-prāsāda, there is also the Śrī-prāsāda-parā; for she is indeed endowed with both the Bindu and the Sarga.
O Parameśvarī, the supreme mantra of the Śrīprāsāda, conjoined with the power of laughter (hasa), accompanied by the bindu and nāda, and joined with [the syllable] śive, has been proclaimed. 3-233.
Having first extracted the letter beginning with *ha*, joined with the middle vowel and the *bindu*,
and having then uttered the letter beginning with *sa* at the end, it should be deposited in due order.
O Goddess, one should assign [the mantra] syllable by syllable and perform the external yoga;
one should utter "sādya" and "hādya" at the beginning of each syllable in the sequence "sādya-hādya."
Then, O Maheśvarī, the knower of mantras, having uttered the phoneme,
should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa), encasing it with the letter *ha* alone.
Having encapsulated [the syllable] with the *sādi* alone, the knower of mantras should then place the syllable according to the *sādi*-yoga in its proper sequence, O Goddess. (3.237)
Then, O Goddess, one should place the syllables of the *hādi-yoga* in their proper order;
having extracted the *śrī-bīja*, one should then follow it with the *śrī-prāsāda-parā*.
Again, having extracted the seed-syllable Śrī, one should then utter the syllable ŪṂ;
having encapsulated [the mantra] with this, O Śivā, one should place it in its respective location. (3.239)
Then one should extract ŚRĪ/ SRĀ/ TATAḤ ŚRĪ/ VAIR VARṆAṂ, and then ŚRĪ/ TU;
having again extracted the seed-syllable ŚRĪ, one should utter HASAU/ ŚRĪ/. || 3-240 ||
O Maheśvarī, in this manner it should be deposited by means of the *saṃpuṭa* (encasement) yoga;
one should then utter the syllable beginning with *ha*, encapsulated by the seed-syllable of Śrī.
O Dear One, one should first place the seed-syllable (bīja) and then the letter in their respective positions;
thereafter, one should utter the Śrī-bīja together with the syllable 'sa', and again utter the Śrī-bīja.
Having encapsulated [the syllables] with this, one should carefully perform the placement (nyāsa) according to the Śāmbhava method;
then one should utter the letter preceded by "Sa" and encapsulated by the Śrī-bīja.
By this sequential yoga, Sundarī becomes well-pleased.
O Maheśvarī, one should then recite the syllable [of the deity] encased within the Śrī-bīja.
One should utter the seed-syllable *hrāḥ*, encased by the seed-syllable *śrīṃ*, at the end of each letter;
having performed this placement with effort in this manner, one will become a master of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) in person. (3.245)
(44) The first letter, encapsulated by the seed-syllable *Śrī*, and likewise the last letter, encapsulated by *Śrī*;
then, O Maheśānī, one should utter the phoneme and the preceding seed-syllables. (3-246)
Thus, having encapsulated [the mantra] in this manner, one should practice the *sadyoga*:
first the syllable *sa* encapsulated by the *śrī-bīja*, and then the syllable *ha* encapsulated by the *śrī-bīja*. (3.247)
Then the best of practitioners should again assign the color and the seed-syllable;
or else, O Goddess, having performed the union (yoga), it should be assigned, O Maheśvarī. (3.248)

Having encapsulated the seed-syllable *Śrī* with the letter *Ha*, and having likewise encapsulated that [seed-syllable] with the letter *Sa*, one should form the syllable by encapsulating it with those [syllables] and then practice the yoga. (3.249)
One should practice the conjunction of the syllable *sādyaṃ* enclosed by the seed-syllable *śrī*, and likewise *hādyaṃ* enclosed by that same [seed-syllable];
indeed, one should perform the yoga with these syllables thus enclosed. (3.250)

O Goddess, one should utter the syllable *hā* encased by *śrī*, then likewise the syllable *sā* encased by *śrī*, again the syllable *hā* encased by *śrī*, and thereafter one should pronounce the [target] letter. (3.251)
Having encapsulated [the mantra] with these, one should again perform the yoga;
O Goddess, the syllable *sā* is encapsulated by *śrī*, and likewise the syllable *hā* is encapsulated by *śrī*.
Again, the letter beginning with *sa* is encased by *śrī*; then the letter as before;
the letter beginning with *ha*, O Goddess, is encased by *śrī*, joined with *sa* and *śrī*. (3-253)
Furthermore, the syllable beginning with *ha* is encased by *śrī*, and it is likewise enclosed by those [syllables];
or else, having first performed the union (*yoga*), it is then preceded by *sa* just like that which begins with *ha*. (3.254)
O Goddess, [the mantra] beginning with *hā* is encased by *śrī*, likewise that beginning with *sā* is encased by *śrī*;
again, *hā* is encased by *śrī*, and it is further encapsulated by *hasa* at the end. (3.255)
Or else, O Goddess, having performed the *yoga*, one should [place] *hasau* or *śrī* as an enclosure;
likewise, each syllable should be enclosed by these, or by *hasau* and *śrī*.
O Śivā, [the mantra] may be *śrī-ha-saumiti* with *ha-sau* in the middle, or *ha-sau-śrī-miti*;
O Goddess, it may likewise have *hādyam* (beginning with *ha*) enclosed by *śrī*, or similarly have *sādyam* (beginning with *sa*) enclosed by *śrī*.
Furthermore, O Goddess, having performed the union (yoga), one should enclose *hā* with *śrī*, and enclose it with *hasauṃ*; or alternatively, one may enclose *shauṃ* with *śrī*.

O Śivā, when a phoneme or a conjunction is encapsulated by these [mantras] as before, O Goddess, it is "encapsulated by Śrī" (śrīpuṭita) when preceded by *sā*, and likewise "encapsulated by Śrī" when preceded by *hā*. (3-259)
Again, the syllable *sā* is encased by *śrī*, and then encased by *śauṃ*;
or the letter [is] encased by these, or *śauṃ* is encased by *śrī*. (3-260)
"O Dear One, O Maheśvarī, having joined the *bindu* and the *sarga*, one should install either *śrīṃ* or *śaṃ* in the middle, or *śauṃ* or *śrīṃ*. (3.261)
O Maheśānī, it should be accompanied by *hādyam* (the letter *ha*) and *sādyaṃ* (the letter *sa*), conjoined with *śrī*, or enclosed (*puṭita*);
O Parameśvarī, this may indeed be enclosed by the previously mentioned [syllables] or otherwise combined.
They know the method of pārāyaṇa as that which is encapsulated or joined by successive application, according to the sequence beginning with *ha* and ending with *sa*. (3.263)
O Śivā, all the sequences for the Pārāyaṇa were previously taught by me;
this sequence, O Maheśānī, is difficult even for the gods to obtain. (3.264)
"This should not be told anywhere else; otherwise, one would incur a curse.
O Śivā, this Krama known as Anantapādukā has been proclaimed by me. (3.265)
O Goddess, through other methods of recitation (*pārāyaṇa*), [the goal] is achieved in a short time;
thus has the recitation regarding the piercing of the six wheels (*ṣaṭcakra*) been described. (3.266)
Only he who possesses the initiation of *medhā* has the qualification for this very [practice].
O Goddess, without the initiation of *medhā*, one may perform the *cakrapārāyaṇa*. (3-267)
He meets his death and shall go to the Raurava hell—he in whose hand the [power] of entering another's body and so forth resides. (3.268)
O Śivā, the initiation of intelligence for him has indeed been described by me;
O Maheśānī, it was performed by me previously six times.
"I know only a little, which has been revealed before you;
O Goddess of gods, Sundarī, the supreme deity, knows it in its entirety. (3.270)
No other knows it, O Goddess of Gods; I have spoken this in brief.
Indeed, one who is endowed with the full initiation likewise [performs] the recitation of the Names.

O Goddess, one who is endowed with the purification of the intellect and other qualities should perform the recitation of the mantra, the recitation of the channels (nāḍī), and so forth, as well as the recitation of the wheel (cakrapārāyaṇa).
O Goddess of the gods, in the Kali age, due to short lifespans, unrighteousness, and harsh speech, I have declared that others have no qualification for the auspicious [path]. (3.273)
O Goddess, he who is qualified for the stage of the child possesses the qualification for the Vidyā;
once the qualification for the Vidyā is accomplished, he becomes qualified for the Ṣoḍaśī.
Endowed with the sixfold knowledge and so forth, he possesses the authority for supreme knowledge; joined with the authority of the supreme, he becomes a possessor of the supreme palace. || 3-275 ||
One who is devoted to the Śrīprāsāda [mantra] shall become a lord of Nirvāṇa;
when joined with the initiation of Nirvāṇa in the rite of the six lineages (ṣaḍanvaya) within Śiva. (3-276)
He indeed shall be the qualified candidate; listen to the reality of this, O Maheśvarī: one who is endowed with the six lineages and possesses the authority for the initiation of wisdom.
Having brought about the end of the six lineages, one should perform the initiation of *medhā*.
If one is joined with the initiation of *medhā*, one should perform the *cakrapārāyaṇa*. (3-278)
In the Cakrapārāyaṇa, the number ending with the feet of Sundarī is stated;
likewise, the number for the external pārāyaṇa is declared in the third [section] as well. (3.279)
In the same way, that which ends with the venerable feet (Śrīcaraṇāntakī) was proclaimed for Kālikā;
as soon as the vision occurred, at that very moment it was completed.
O Śiva, the difference between the external and the internal is only this much:
in the Kali age, one should perform the recitation (pārāyaṇa) ending with the sixteenth square of the grid (prastāra).
In this regard, O Supreme Goddess, the practice called *pārāyaṇa* is the ritual deposition (*nyāsana*).
O Supreme Goddess, he who performs it by force against those who are unworthy [is at fault].
O Goddess, his destruction would occur and he would incur the curse of the deities;
one who is endowed with wisdom and the initiatory consecration (dīkṣā) should perform [the rite] extending sixteen [years] beyond that.
O Supreme Goddess, it should be understood through the application of the sequence of the grid (prastāra);
one who is joined with the initiation of a child (bāladīkṣā) should perform the placement (nyāsa) joined with the lunar grid (candraprastāra).
Endowed with the initiation of knowledge (vidyādīkṣā), the best of practitioners should perform the placement [of mantras] that extends from the beginning to the end of the sādhana;
the supreme adept should perform this placement precisely according to the sequence of the tradition.
For one who is endowed with the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka) should [employ] the enclosures of the fire-extension (vahni-prastāra);
for one who is endowed with the higher initiation (parādīkṣā) should [employ] the enclosures of the elemental-extension (bhūta-prastāra). || 3-286 ||
One who is devoted to the Śrīprāsāda [mantra] should employ the Muniprastāra-sampuṭas;
one who is engaged in the Nirvāṇa initiation should employ the Nandaprastāra-sampuṭas. || 3-287 ||
O Pārvatī, one should perform the conjunctions joined with the six lineages and the enclosures of the *kalā*-expansion, both at the beginning and at the end.
Having placed the seed-syllable (varṇa) in the middle, one should deposit it encapsulated by the syllables;
for one who is endowed with the full initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka), O Śivā, is equal to the six lineages (ṣaḍanvaya). || 3-289 ||
Whatever ritual procedure is prescribed for the six lineages (ṣaḍanvaya), that same one is proclaimed for this [initiate] as well.
O Goddess, after the six lineages, one should perform the initiation of intelligence (medhādīkṣā).

O Goddess of the Gods, joined with the initiation of wisdom (medhā-dīkṣā), one should perform the recitation of the cycles (cakrapārāyaṇa) according to the method of placement (nyāsa), beginning with the *prastāra* and increasing by sixteen [syllables]. (3.291)
The summoning of the three worlds, the accomplishment of the command of subjugation, the entry into another's body, and the accomplishment of the medicinal pill. || 3-292 ||
The immobilization of the wind and the mastery over vetālas come within the reach of one's hands;
thus has it been briefly explained. What else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who bring about the existence of the world,
O Śaṅkara, tell me that which was previously indicated to me.
"O Mahādeva, why has even this much been hidden from me?
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Mahādevī, O you who are worshipped by the supreme, O you whose form is the cause of all! (3.295)
Now listen as the secret of *prāṇāyāma* is being told;
*prāṇāyāma* is fivefold—listen attentively to its sequence. (3.296)

One should perform the inhalation (*pūraka*) with [sixteen] *kalās*, the retention (*kumbhaka*) with the great [sixty-four], and the exhalation (*recaka*) with half of that; one should repeat this triad again.
One should perform the triad three times; this is proclaimed as *prāṇāyāma*.
O Goddess of the Gods, when performed in direct and reverse order, it is proclaimed as the second [type].

O Maheśānī, for ascetics who follow the left-hand path, the practice is said to be twofold: either ending with *kumbhaka* (retention) or consisting of *recaka* (exhalation) or *pūraka* (inhalation). (3-299)
O Maheśānī, I have already described to you the division known as the intermediate; now listen as the third is being told. (3-300)
O Supreme Goddess, having first established the increase of the *kalā* and half of that,
one should proceed with the other [halves] from the beginning onwards in this sequence.
As before, the third [round] should be performed; thus one should practice three times.
At the end of those two, there should be two breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) beginning with the retention (kumbhaka). || 3.302 ||
By means of the application of the sequence previously described, that which is other than it has been proclaimed;
by the very sequence called the second, the second [member] has been proclaimed. (3.303)
By the very sequence called the third, the third [chapter] is fully established;
it is proclaimed as the third due to its connection with the garland and the chain. || 3.304 ||

(48) Listen with reverence to the etymological explanation of the *mālāśṛṅkhalikā-yoga*: O Goddess, one should proceed from the beginning to the end, and indeed, one should proceed from the end to the beginning. (3-305)
Furthermore, the first and likewise the last is breath control (prāṇāyāma), the lord of the digits (kalāpati).
Having performed the first three here, it is proclaimed as the "spreading" (prastāra).
Furthermore, from the end to the beginning and so on up to the third [cycle], this is proclaimed as the prāṇāyāma known as the "Chain of Parts" (kalāśṛṅkhalikā). || 3-307 ||
O Goddess, another method of breath control (prāṇāyāma) involving numbers such as *kalā*, *vasu*,
and *veda* has thus been proclaimed by me to you in the ritual of the Great Mantra.
Eight, two Vedas (four), and then more than that are proclaimed; O Maheśānī, for those exceeding that, [the number] follows the sequence of Vedas, eyes, and moons (14, 24, and 34).
The prastāras have been described, O Goddess; now listen to them according to the sequence of the letters.
This [practice] is proclaimed to be of two kinds, beginning with the kumbhaka (retention).
The multiplicity of divisions has been described through the previously mentioned varieties of fire;
the expansions [of mantras] resulting from the application of the chain of digits (kalā-śṛṅkhalikā) have been indicated previously.
O Great Goddess, the sequence of the letters is now being told; listen.
Having performed the inhalation (pūraka) with the vowels, the retention (kumbhaka) should be performed with the consonants. (3.312)
The first is said to be the nose; then, O Goddess Śivā, having performed the *kumbhaka* breath-retention thirty-four times, one should repeat it twice with the vowels.
O Goddess, O Śivā, one should perform the exhalation (recaka) as part of three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma);
the sequence of the expansion (prastāra) has been declared according to the previously mentioned method.
By means of the tone alone, conjoined with the six kalās of the Vedas,
it becomes here, through the previously mentioned yoga, a vessel for the various divisions of the prastāra.
By means of the *īḍā* [nāḍī], the yogi should draw in the external air with sixteen *mātrās*;
he should then retain the inhalation (*pūraka*) for sixty-four *mātrās*. (3.316)
The best among those who know yoga should properly exhale this [breath] slowly through the piṅgalā channel for thirty-two mātrās, while it is correctly situated within the suṣumṇā.
Those expert in the scriptures of sacrifice call this *prāṇāyāma*;
one should perform it repeatedly and gradually, alternating its sequence. (3.318)

The wise know that [practice] which is properly joined with recitation, meditation, and so forth, according to the sequence of increasing duration, for twelve or sixteen [muhūrtas], as "with embryo" (sagarbha). || 3-319 ||
The supreme ones know that [practice] devoid of that [breath] to be breath-control (prāṇāyāma) without the core.
For men who practice it in due order, perspiration and dizziness arise in the body. (3.320)
O Maheśānī, this is indeed without a core (agarbha); hear now another, O beloved:
the middle [level] is joined with trembling, while the other is considered the abandonment of the ground. (3.321)
The middle [type] is with a pause (sasandhi), while the next is called "to be accomplished" (sādhyākhya).
O Goddess, this fivefold sequence of prāṇāyāma has been described by me.
One who is devoted to breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recitation (japa) shall become a master of perfected yoga.
What on this earth cannot be accomplished through the practice of breath control and recitation alone? (3.323)
One should calculate the units known as *palas*, *nāḍīs*, and *muhūrtas*—two of each in the sequence of watches (*prahara*)—by means of the conjunction of day and night, with a steady mind. (3.324)
For a person practicing in this manner, all yogas come into their hands;
O Goddess, breath control (prāṇāyāma) and recitation (japa) are proclaimed as the primary ones. (3.325)
In the absence of that, O Maheśānī, one should perform *prāṇāyāma*;
O Śivā, it is to be employed in the rite of elemental purification (*bhūtaśuddhi*) during the procedures of drying and so forth.
One should perform [the practice] either three times or once by means of the sequence of breath control (prāṇāyāma);
when the count reaches nine, one should then perform the breath control.
O Goddess, in the tradition known as Kerala, drying is not prescribed;
O Goddess, in the tradition known as Kashmir, one should perform the rites beginning with drying.
The Gauḍa [system] is equal to the Kāśmīra, while Caitanya is the fourth;
O Goddess, such is the sequence of prāṇāyāma and also the sequence of bhūtaśuddhi.
This should be applied according to what is appropriate. What else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the third chapter, titled "Breath Control and Recitation," in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, within the third section of the latter part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*.
The Fourth Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
"That which was previously indicated by me, the determination of the expansion of mantras—"
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess Pārvatī, it is more secret than the most secret, like one's own womb;
therefore I shall tell it to you here, but it must not be spoken by you, O Śivā.
The four Śiva-cakras and the five Śakti-cakras,
through their state of aesthetic equilibrium (sāmarasya), become the Śrīcakra, which embodies all forms.
O Maheśānī, the wheel of power (śakticakra) is proclaimed to extend from Bindu up to Manava; beyond that, up to the door, is the wheel of Śiva (śivacakra).
This is declared to be the Pure Wheel (śuddhacakra), and it itself becomes threefold:
the earth, Kailāsa, and Meru, by way of their extension, O Pārvatī.
O Goddess, the arrangement of the earth (bhūprastāra) is twofold according to the sequence of the netherworlds and the upper realms;
likewise, the arrangement known as Kailāsa is proclaimed to be of two kinds.
The one known as Ardhakailāsa, as well as Pūrṇakailāsaka,
and likewise Meruprastāra— these have been described by me to you.
Indeed, there are exactly eighteen [syllables] according to the sequence of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal;
and by the sequence of writing the seeds of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.

The number of expansions (prastāras) is equal to the number of seasons and fires; the movement of the numbers is from left to right, and there is an identity with the eternal in the expansion known as Meru.
The identity with the Mātṛkā is proclaimed as that which is called Kailāsa;
the identity with the Goddess of Speech is proclaimed in the Bhūprastāra.
This yantra, known as the Pure Eighteen-fold, has been described by me to you on the sixteenth [day], according to the sequence of writing the Mātṛkās.
In the rites of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal, there is a reversal of the arrows and the Vedas;
or else, one should have a proven yantra made in the shape of petals. (4.12)
Thus, by means of the arrays previously described— beginning with those of emanation, maintenance, and dissolution—
I have proclaimed to you this yantra which is free from all curses.
O Maheśvarī, O Goddess, many *prastāras* arise for Lalitā through the nine varieties of numerical divisions; I shall describe them to you. (4.14)
The twofold nature [of the letters] is proclaimed according to the systems of the *kādi* and *hādi* groups;
there are six divisions within the *kādi* group of six, and likewise six within the *kāmarāja* group of six. (4.15)
O Goddess, listen quickly as this awakening is described;
O Mistress of the Gods, it is differentiated within the Kāmarāja [cakra] which has fourteen spokes. (4.16)
When the six beginning with *la* are purified, the others are divided according to the second [group];
however, in the six beginning with *ka*, as well as in those beginning with *ha*, they are the locus of division within the ten-spoked [wheel]. (4.17)
In the ten-spoked [cakra] called Netra, which consists of the six beginning with Lopa, there is the vessel of differentiation.
Thus, O Mistress of the Gods, twelve prastāras are declared when combined.

But for each [deity], O Maheśānī, according to the divisions of the previously mentioned grid (prastāra), there is a sequence of writing based on emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, O Śivā. (4.19)
O Pārvatī, through the application of the sequence of emanation, maintenance, and withdrawal, each [element] becomes a vessel for differentiation according to the very order of the petals. (4.20)
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, on each individual petal there are one hundred and eight [mantras];
thus the arrangement (prastāra) is proclaimed to consist of thirteen varieties.
The moon, the moon, and six marks, and the sage, the seasons, and the marks.
And the diagrams (yantras) have been extracted here according to the sequence of their arrangement.
Indeed, out of affection for you, this most secret of secrets has been spoken here;
by the mere remembrance of which one shall become Rudra in person. (4.23)
O Goddess, the arrangements previously indicated have been recounted by you;
all of them have been told, O Goddess, but they must be kept secret like one's own private parts.
O Goddess, whether out of ignorance or deluded by knowledge,
wherever one may dwell, O Goddess, and wherever one may be a worshiper— (4.25)
That poor man becomes powerful; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
For he who is a worshiper of Śrīvidyā is like another Devendra (Indra). || 4-26 ||
O Great Goddess, the Siddhalakṣmī of the Lord of the Gods has been proclaimed;
now, O Beloved, hear the name Lakṣmī of the worshipper of Śrīvidyā. (4.27)
The sovereign fortune of all enjoyment resides in his house;
O Goddess, how can he be poor, being the lord of the glorious universe? (4.28)
(52) O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, through ignorance of this, or even through knowledge of it, O Great Sovereign, poverty certainly comes to pass; of this there is no doubt. (4.29)
He shall fall into poverty; there is no need for deliberation on this point, O Goddess of the gods, even if one should speak [of this] anywhere after having learned it.
Having fallen into poverty at the end, he shall go to the Raurava hell,
if he does not utter the name during the sequence of the Pārāyaṇa in the Full Initiation (pūrṇābhiṣeka).

O Goddess, he in whose hand shines the initiation that extends from the recitation of mantras (*maṃtrapārāyaṇa*) as well as the recitation of the wheel (*cakrapārāyaṇa*), and which culminates in the initiation of intelligence (*medhādīkṣā*).
O Goddess of gods, his authority lies in the determination of the layout of the yantra;
no one else has such authority, for whoever should perform it otherwise shall go to hell.
A living being dies from poverty and sinks into the depths of poverty;
O Goddess, he who always desires the removal of poverty [should worship you]. (4.34)
He should first be one who has undergone initiation and afterwards be a perceiver of the ritual expansion;
he who knows this correctly is Śiva—of this there is no doubt.
Śiva is truth, Śiva is truth, Śiva is truth; there is no doubt.
O Goddess, Śiva alone is supreme; one should worship him in every way.
By the mere worship of that [mantra], one becomes equal to the Lord of Lakṣmī.
What is the use of much speaking, O Queen of the Gods? [The mantra] consists of the letters beginning with *ka* and *ha*, and so forth.
O Great Goddess, it must be kept secret like one's own womb or another's; O Maheśvarī, one should give away a kingdom, one should give away one's head, and one should give away a wife.
But one should not give this scripture; rather, one should conceal it from everyone.
Thus has it been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (4.39)
O Dear One, he who recites this hymn named Yantraprastāra becomes a master of all accomplishments, like a second Mahādeva in person.
Likewise, there is the Mahendrajāla, the weaving of the illusions of Indra and others,
as well as the attainment of the powers of the Pātālakhecarī, and the medicinal pill and collyrium.
The accomplishment of the yakṣiṇīs and the sword enters his hand—whatever [power] exists within the cosmic egg or upon the surface of the earth. (4.42)
All accomplishments (siddhis) indeed belong to him, there is no doubt;
for whatever accomplishments he possesses arise simply from the recollection of the *prastāra*. 4-43.
They come of their own accord before one; what need is there to mention their arrangement?
O Goddess, this hymn is proclaimed by the name *Yantrapārāyaṇa*.
The *nāḍīpārāyaṇa*, the *nāmapārāyaṇa*, the *mantrapārāyaṇa*, and likewise the *cakrapārāyaṇa*. (4-45)
O Goddess, O Beloved, one should perform the recitation of the Yantra every day;
by even a single recitation, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds.
By merely performing two recitations, the Lord of Śrī becomes the embodiment of the three qualities; indeed, there is no need for further deliberation on this point. (4.47)
By merely performing it five times, one becomes a sovereign lord of kings;
O Supreme Goddess, this shall continue for as long as the vision persists.
And the boundary of the ocean has been proclaimed, O Supreme Goddess;
whatever desire one contemplates, one should then always recite this hymn.
Whatever desire one attains, a person becomes of that very form.
What is the use of much speaking, O Goddess of the gods? She is indeed the Sovereign Queen of the Kings of Kings.
Just as Chinnā is, so is Kālī; likewise is Sundarī Parā;
and Tārā is likewise ordained—there is indeed no difference among these four. (4-51)
In the Kālikā [Tantra] as well, one should practice the recitation of the Yantra in that same way;
its twofold nature is proclaimed according to the systems beginning with 'ka' and 'ha'. (4.52)
Having seen this [mantra] endowed with knowledge, one should prostrate like a staff and perform worship as if to a deity; otherwise, it will certainly not succeed. (4.53)
O Maheśānī, it is known by the names Yantraprastārarāja, the supreme Yantrapārāyaṇa, and likewise as Śivaśaktyātmaka.
O Goddess, whatever exists on the surface of the earth consists of Śiva and Śakti;
therefore, O Goddess, this world of moving and non-moving beings is essentially Śakti. 4-55.
I have explained everything; what more remains to be specified?
O Maheśvarī, hear now the numerical figures for the purpose of establishing the expansion of the divisions.
Indeed, it is proclaimed in the sequence of the night, the eight corpses, the name, the sign of power, Viṣṇu, the banner, and the elephant-turn. (4.57)
The determination of the lines for the first Daśāra has been declared;
thus, these five types with four divisions each bestow all spiritual accomplishments.

The determination of the lines and marks for the second Daśārha is as follows: [they are determined] by the seasons (6), the number eight (8), the groups (3), and the final letter (m), followed by the meanings of the first letters (vīra, etc.). (4.59)
(54) It is accomplished precisely through the sequence of the Path of the Lord by means of the piercing of the days.
One should pierce the line with a pair of rays, the sixth [taste], and the five [arrows]. (4–60)
Thus there would be five divisions; now listen regarding the *mantrasre*.
The eternal speech (*nityā-vāṇī*) shall indeed arise through the attainment of the *mātṛkā* by means of the numerical cycle.
O Maheśānī, the second [cakra] possesses the moon of the qualities (guṇavāk); it is proclaimed as the second by way of the conjunction of its digits (kalā). 4-62.
Thus, O Śivā, the description of the fruits has been briefly told;
even with thousands of crores of tongues and hundreds of crores of mouths, [it could not be fully recounted].
O Maheśvarī, I am unable to describe his greatness;
thus it has been spoken in brief. Now listen to the sequence of the placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa).
One should perform the deposition of the principles (tattvanyāsa) with the principles of Ātman, Vidyā, and Śiva.
The principle of Ātman is proclaimed to extend from the feet up to the navel. (4.65)
Indeed, the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) is proclaimed to extend from the navel to the heart;
the principle of Śiva (śivatattva) is proclaimed to extend from the heart to the point between the eyebrows (bindu). || 4.66 ||
Having uttered all the mantras, O Śivā, they pervade all the limbs;
this is declared to be the totality of reality (sarvatattva), which brings about the state of being all the deities.
O Goddess of gods, the principles of the lunar days (tithitattva) indeed reside within the principle of the Self (ātmatattva);
the twenty-five principles indeed reside within the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva).
Indeed, the thirty-six Śiva-tattvas are contained within the Śiva-tattva;
furthermore, indeed, the fifty tattvas are contained within the Sarva-tattva. (4.69)
In the rite of installation, one should contemplate the principles of the Vedas; in purification, the five principles;
and in the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi), one should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) three times in sequence according to the three principles.

O Great Goddess, in every mantra one should perform the ritual sipping (ācamana) according to the Vedic principle; what would be the use of placing the name in the middle of the seed-syllable, or indeed making it confused? (4.71)
Or rather, what is the conceptualization of reality (tattva) in a mantra that is pervaded by a name—such as a single syllable or three syllables—which is devoid of any locus for reality? (4.72)
O Goddess, O Maheśvarī, one should not conceive of anything else for the ritual of the perfected Vidyā, namely the Śrīvidyā, than that which has been established in the *Tattvanyāsa*. 4.73.
All the principles known as the divisions indeed reside within the three principles;
one who possesses full knowledge of the three principles becomes a master of the descent of power (śaktipāta).
(55) Through conversation, sight, touch, giving, and even through acts of favor;
through contact with objects touched by him, through the imparting of mantras, and even through recitation—4.75.
Through the inscription of the mantra upon the tongue, by consuming the remnants of betel, by means of mouthfuls of water from a cloth, and through the application of consecration; || 4.76 ||
O Śivā, by the mere remembrance of His name— even from a distance of a hundred krośas— whatever is uttered,
whether a curse or a favor, shall come to pass exactly so.
One becomes a knower of the secrets of all scriptures and likewise possesses a retentive memory;
O Goddess, such is the eighteenfold descent of power (śaktipāta) that occurs in Śiva.
Alternatively, I am unable to describe the multiplicity of accomplishments;
if one desires that multiplicity of accomplishments therein, one should become devoted to the power of will (*icchā-śakti*). (4.79)
O Śivā, by the mere contact with Śakti, everything becomes purified;
without Śakti there is indeed no liberation, for Śakti is considered the bestower of liberation.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (4.80)

Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Array of Mantras," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā.
The Fifth Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the great definitive conclusion previously mentioned."
The illustrious Śiva said:
Now listen as that which is a secret, even more secret than a secret, is being told. 5-1.
All primary ritual acts are preceded by bathing, and the bath should be performed for the deity during the morning, midday, and evening recitations of hymns.

Whenever there is mental distress, one should perform a bath at that very moment; furthermore, upon speaking with a fallen person, one should perform a mantra-bath. In the case of Śrīvidyā, this should be done four times a day, and for Kālikā, three times a day.
At the very moment the mind becomes weary, one should perform a ritual bath;
for he who recites the Vidyā while remaining unbathed and having already eaten [incurs a fault].
O Maheśānī, his vidyā shall be lost and he shall go to the Raurava hell, if being impure he should perform the recitation of the vidyā. (5–6)
O Goddess, its destruction occurs and the Vidyā will certainly be burnt.
The times for bathing have been fully declared; now listen, O beloved, to the various types of baths. 5–7.
Bathing is said to be fivefold, by which one becomes identical with the Goddess:
the Vāruṇa, the Nābhasa, and the third is remembered as the Bhasmaja.
The fourth, O Goddess, is Taijasa; the fifth shall be Daivata.
[These correspond to] Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva.
These five great gods are established in the five ablutions:
Parā, and after that Taditā, Tatparā, and immediately following that, Tadanantaram.
The fifth is proclaimed as Citparā and that which transcends it (Tadatītā).
Vāruṇa is said to be of two kinds: Vaidika and likewise Tāntrika.
The Vedic bath is prescribed according to the procedure taught in one's own Vedic branch;
one should perform the Tantric bath according to the procedure taught in one's own respective Tantra.
O Pārvatī, listen now to the three [measures] that are for the *vīras*;
O Maheśānī, the best [measure] is proclaimed everywhere. (5-13)
But the middling [method], O Maheśānī, is preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma); having duly performed the assignment of the seers and so forth, it is preceded by the seven mudrās. (5.14)
O Goddess of gods, having taken water and reciting the root mantra over all limbs,
one should cleanse the body ten or seven times, O Śivā.
O Goddess, one should then apply the *tilaka* mark using either *kuśa* grass, *dūrvā* grass, or a heated seal, while remaining restrained in speech in ten ways.
The *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is of three types, while the *tripuṇḍra* is of two types;
there is also the shape of the *agasti* leaf and the *paṭṭabandhana*.
O Goddess, one should fashion the shape of an Agasti leaf using vermilion, saffron, or red sandalwood, according to the path of yoga. (5.18)
This [procedure] applies to the previously mentioned mantra alone, as well as in the Śrī Kālikā-mantra;
it should be performed for every deity with its own respective yantra, O Pārvatī. (5-19)
O beloved Śivā, in the ritual procedure for Tārā and Chinnā, one should wash the hands below the wrist and the feet below the ankle, O Goddess, and likewise wash the face. 5-20.
One should perform this bath, for it bestows purification of the five limbs; O Goddess, this is called the Vāruṇa bath. Now hear, O Pārvatī, about the Nābhasa bath.
O Goddess, the eighteenfold [mantras] pertaining to the ether (nābhasa) have been proclaimed;
they end in *namas*, *svāhā*, *tarpaṇa*, and *jaya*. (5.22)
The garland-mantra is fivefold according to the sequence of Śiva and Śakti;
through the application of that twofold sequence, fifteen mantras are traditionally taught.

O Goddess of the gods, the practitioner [should proceed] from the first day of the dark fortnight until the end of Phālguna, following the sequence of rays even as he moves through the sequence of the six cakras.
The eighteen-fold bath known as the celestial (nābhasa) has been described;
it consists of contemplating [the flow] from the mūlādhāra up to the aperture (bilam), reaching as far as the vicinity of the Ājñā-cakra.
O Great Goddess, the rays here are proclaimed to be three hundred and sixty;
for one full year, the ritual bath in the Jāhnavī was performed at the three junctions of the day.
O Goddess, one shall obtain that fruit; there is no need for deliberation here.
By means of the sequence beginning with the seasons, using the waters produced by each respective season, [one attains the result]. (5.27)
O Goddess of the Gods, whatever fruit is obtained by performing the ritual bath, that shall be attained all at once through the sequence of rays, as one directly assumes the form of Śambhu. (5-28)
O Great Goddess, having become disciplined, one should meditate upon the deities within that wheel in the secondary wheel (praticakra), from the root-support (mūlādhāra) up to the end of the cavity.
This is declared to be the internal bath (antaḥsnāna), which bestows the vision of the deity;
O Goddess of gods, one should perform the dissolution of all [elements] into the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra). (5.30)
Furthermore, having contemplated the true nature of purification, one should perform the recitation (*japa*).
The ethereal bath (*nābhasa-snāna*) has been described; now hear, O beloved, about the ash-bath (*bhasma-snāna*).
O Goddess, fire, water, and earth, as well as wind and space everywhere—by means of these three, which have the appearance of clouds, bathing removes the fever of death. (5.32)
The second [form] is proclaimed by means of the five Śaiva Ṛks;
O Goddess, the third [form] is within the Śrīvidyā by means of the Śrīmālinī and others.
The Sūrya mantra is placed in the midst of the ashes; with it, one should smear all the limbs.
As described in the meditation, that which resides in the sacrificial fire-pit (homakuṇḍa) becomes the fifth [application] by means of the ashes.
There are also many other varieties arising from the vital breaths (prāṇa).
Now I shall describe the luminous [breath] by which the supernatural powers (siddhis) are accomplished. (5.35)
Meditating with the intellect on the unity of the Guru, the deity, and the mantra— namely,
the splendor of the Guru, the splendor of the mantra, and likewise the splendor of the deity— (5.36)
Having unified the threefold consciousness, one should conceive of that as its form;
the place of the deity is in the heart, and the mantra is considered to be in the throat.
The Guru is said to reside in the thousand-spoked [lotus]; one should contemplate that threefold consciousness within one's own body, according to the sequence of its own constituent parts.
One should honor it, O Maheśānī, for it bestows the vision of the deity;
this, O Goddess, is declared to be Taijasa. Now listen, Pārvatī, to the description of the Daivata [fire]. (5.39)
O Supreme Goddess, O Śivā, beginning from the mūlādhāra up to the end of the aperture,
one should meditate upon the deity, [uniting] one's own mouth with [Her] mouth, O Goddess.
O Goddess, one should place all her limbs within one's own body according to their respective locations;
O Maheśānī, one should likewise place the Gaṅgā and Yamunā at the region of the door.
But if all [these] are already present, what fruit would there be from the Gaṅgā?
The Iḍā is renowned as the Gaṅgā, and the Suṣumṇā is the river Yamunā. (5.42)
Sarasvatī is Piṅgalā, and Prayāga is situated in the middle of the body. O Goddess, without knowledge of the body, what is the fruit of external knowledge? (5.43)
One should meditate on the lineage of gurus in the thousand-petaled lotus, the limbs [of the mantra] between the eyebrows,
and all the deities of the enclosures from the root of the throat up to its end, O Goddess.
O Goddess, one should diligently meditate upon the deity; this is declared to be the ritual bath.
By means of this method of bathing, what is there that does not come into one's hand? (5.45)
"O Pārvatī, by this bath the deities beginning with Brahmā and the Siddhas [are purified].
Thus has the ritual of the twilight (sandhyā) been briefly declared; listen, O beloved. (5-46)
O Sundarī, one should perform the twilight worship (sandhyā-vandana) four times a day:
in the morning, at midday, in the evening, and also at midnight.
O Pārvatī, one should recite the fourfold Gāyatrī with effort:
that which has the form of a diagrammatic arrangement (prastāra), and likewise that which is designated as the ritual salutation (upasthāna).
O Goddess, the fourth is proclaimed as Vāñchākalpalatā;
it consists of sixty recitations in the morning and that which is known as Nāma at midday.
One should perform the recitation of the mantra (*maṃtrapārāyaṇa*) at night during the period known as the *cakra*;
however, at the third watch, namely at midnight, one should perform the *tūrya* twilight ritual (*saṃdhyā*).
This is declared for Kālikā, excluding the formal attendance (upasthāna);
because of her sovereignty over wisdom, initiation, and so forth, there is a fourfold twilight rite (sandhyācatuṣṭaya) for Kālī. || 5.51 ||
The three twilight rituals (sandhyā) for Tārā and Chinnā are of three kinds;
indeed, there is no difference between them, and one who perceives a difference shall go to hell.
Thus has it been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (5.52)

Thus ends the fifth chapter, titled "The Determination of the Varieties of Ablution," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 5 ||
The Sixth Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive teaching concerning the lords of the lamps and so forth."
Śrī Śiva said:
Having assumed the bound lotus posture (baddhapadmāsana), one should worship Dīpanātha at the crown of the head.
One should draw the eight groups of consonants in the eight directions, accompanied by pairs of vowels; within those groups, the syllable of the Great Sound (Mahānāda) should be placed.
First is Satyabinduka, then Śrīkaṇṭha and the others;
thereafter is their Lord of the Letters, Nandanātha, as the fourth immediately following.
At the end of the word *atirikta*, one should extract the word *varṇāya*;
then one should utter the word *raktadvādaśaśaktyārdhayuktāya*. (6.4)
"O Field, accept this offering, whether it be a pair or even a single one!
Svāhā!"—this mantra, ending with *svāhā*, is proclaimed for the Lord of Dīpa.
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship Dīpanātha in the northeast;
having brought earth from the two banks of a river, [one should perform the rite] while remaining in the state of Ucchiṣṭa.
Having made the form the size of a palm tree, one should write the letters of its name upon its heart;
having written the name, the *māyā*, the weapon, and the *dhatura* [mantras], it is completed upon the ground.
By reciting it twenty-one times, one may bring even Urvaśī under control.
Now, O Goddess of Gods, another secret is told; listen.
Holding [the rosary] in the left hand, one should perform the oblation with the right hand;
having given the rosary into the hand of the Śakti, O Śivā, one should have the counting performed.
O Goddess Śivā, one should have the rosary strung after two or three months have passed;
a rosary that has snapped by itself serves as an occasion for expiation.
O Śivā, having recognized that the thread has worn out, one should string a new garland;
O Goddess, after six months, the garland of a worn-out thread [must be replaced].
O Maheśānī, for one who would place [the rosary] down, destruction will occur;
if the garland should break by itself, one must perform an expiation.

One should perform a thousand recitations and burnt offerings (japa-homa) for Gajāntaka; then, having performed the re-knotting [of the rosary], preceded by the installation of the vital breath (prāṇasthāpana). (6.13)
Then the rosary shall grant success; otherwise, it is not so—this is the word of Śaṅkara.
If the rosary should fall from the hand during the preparatory rite, the recitation, or the fire-oblation, [the result is lost].
Having recited the expiation (prāyaścitta) one hundred times, one should increase it by a tenth part;
then, according to the sequence of the expiation, one should abandon the recitation by a tenth part.
Some here maintain that there must be a preliminary rite (*puraścaryā*);
having recited [the mantra] one hundred times as an atonement (*prāyaścitta*), one should perform the preliminary rite once again. (6.16)
O Goddess, one should perform ten thousand oblations with milk-rice and coconut preparations;
one shall bring the three worlds under control—of this there is no doubt. (6.17)
"O beloved, one may generate affection through an oblation of sesame seeds and rice.
The Goddess Śrī said:
'A handful is declared to be the measure for rice, while exactly one hundred sesame seeds are prescribed.'"
O Great Goddess, tell me how that equality [is achieved], O Śaṅkara;
or [how it is achieved] by means of just half a handful of rice grains, O Maheśvara. (6.19)
"Or fifty sesame seeds should be taken; O Lord, remove my doubt.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Goddess, one should offer a handful (prasṛti) or a hundred [seeds] by means of their combination."
O Supreme Goddess, it is proclaimed as the preferred offering for the deity Dakṣiṇāmūrti,
consisting of rice grains measuring exactly half a handful.
Fifty sesame seeds should be taken as approved by the sage Akṣobhya;
and the oblation of barley and sesame seeds should be performed according to the proper method.
In that same manner, the combination of sesame seeds should be performed as prescribed for the time;
one should offer oblations into a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) of equal weight according to the Kālikā-mata.
The deity will grant him boons; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He shall become the sovereign of the three worlds; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.

Having placed the sixteen vessels and worshipped the Supreme Deity, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) at the end of that [worship] during the night; at the conclusion of that, there should be the libation (tarpaṇa).
One should perform the "conch-mouth" (śaṅkhamukha) for the eyes of the deity; this has been declared in the system known as Kerala. Now hear the system known as Kashmir. (6.27)
Just as with the Goddess, so too is the one called Devīviśeṣa proclaimed;
O Queen of the Gods, one should establish the heap of vessels facing oneself.
O Goddess, according to the view of Caitanya, one should establish [the deity] with the horizontal wheel (tiryak-cakra) facing oneself as well as facing the deity. (6.29)
It has been stated that there are nine, six, and five directions; how then is the arrangement of the limbs (aṅga) and so forth conceived?
O Goddess, does this direction belong to oneself, or to the deity?
Śrī Śiva said:
This most secret of secrets is now being told; listen with reverence.
When a worthy recipient stands before you, one should perform the ritual assignment of the limbs (*aṅgakalpana*) as if he were a god.
O Pārvatī, the doctrine of Nirañjana has been proclaimed; even in its presence, the doctrine of Pārvatī has been declared. Now listen to the Rudravīra doctrine.
The vessel for the Goddess is like the primary limb of the God; its limbs and so forth should be understood as being like one's own limbs.
Having understood the sequence of the eastern direction therein, one shall certainly accomplish everything. (6.33)

O Śivā, that which begins with the seat (āsana) and ends with the purification of the elements (bhūtaśuddhi) is declared to be the "established east" (siddhaprācī); thereafter, the "imagined east" (kalpitā) occurs.

O Maheśānī, the direction established for worship— beginning with the location and ending with the ritual vessels— is proclaimed as the "Ancient Accomplished" (Siddhaprācī), which bestows auspiciousness.
O Goddess, in the ritual manual of Śambara, the direction intended for the placement of the worship concludes with the *arghya* offering;
however, in the procedure for one's own eastward orientation, the *mahābhūtabali* offering shall take place.
The offering for the goddesses is to the left of oneself, while that for Mṛḍa is on one's right;
the worship of the limbs is performed in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, in the center, and in the cardinal directions.
The doctrine of Kerala has been declared; now hear the doctrine of Cidghana.
[It is established] in the southeast, southwest, northwest, and northeast corners, as well as in the center. (6.38)
O Great Goddess, in the four directions according to the path of the circular mandala,
[one should worship] the six limbs in the southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest, the center, and the back.
O Goddess, according to the tradition of Kālarudra, the six-limbed worship (ṣaḍaṅgapūjana) should be performed upon the filaments, the corners, and the bodies.
The worship of the limbs has been described according to the sequence of the ancients,
by way of fourfold repetition and by the process known as withdrawal.
The six-limbed worship has been declared; listen with reverence to the specific detail:
in the rite of the offering of *argha*, the "Siddha-prācī" is said to be located upon the pedestal (*pīṭhaka*). (6.42)
O Supreme Goddess, it may be fashioned by Mṛḍa in some cases;
O Great Goddess, it may be perfected in some cases, and it may be fashioned in others. (6.43)
One should worship the lineage of gurus extending as far as the northwest direction;
O Great Goddess, the gurus are always present behind the Vidyā.
At dawn, by way of the triple row and following the sequence behind the Goddess,
according to the order beginning with the divine [gurus], one should place one's own three gurus below that.
One should draw three lines from Dakṣoda to the west;
the Divyaugha [line] is behind the deity, while the other two are in those two locations.
But when there is no distinction regarding the Vidyā, O Śivā, one should worship one’s own guru;
for it is proclaimed, O Maheśānī, that the position of the guru is above all.
O Goddess, just as you are in the Siddha, Prācī, Viloka, Kerala, and Gauḍa systems— wherever the directions are conceived— so too are you.
"O Goddess, they do not possess primacy; rather, the deity itself must be primary.
The Śrī Devī said: "In this matter I have a doubt; dispel my doubt. (6.49)
O Śiva, if the worship were performed according to the path of the imagined sequence, O Lord,
there would be a displacement of the deities' positions and the site itself in the event of a reversal of the directions.
Śrī Śiva said:
Wherever the Lord arrives, there alone do the deities of the limbs and so forth reside.
O Goddess, the limbs do not possess primacy; rather, it is in His worship that primacy resides.
One should perform the recitation and worship of the limb-mantras (aṅgamantras) with a tenth part [of the main mantra];
by that, O Goddess, they grant success, otherwise they act as an obstacle to success.
When, who, or what is Mahādeva? Or what is the Prācī (the East) that remains established?
O Maheśvarī, the sun goes toward the Vāruṇī (the West) eternally and non-eternally.
The reversal of day and night is held in the hand of the practitioner;
he is capable of effecting the exchange of the moon and the sun.
The moon would be in the place of the sun, and the sun would be in the place of the moon;
in this sequence, O Goddess of Gods, is the succession of the cosmic eggs (brahmāṇḍas).
(64) When and how did the eastern direction remain fixed? How many Purandaras have been born?
O Goddess of the gods, even a mere insect becomes a Purandara [Indra] once in a lifetime. (6–56)
O Goddess, where and who are situated— all this is within the range of the practitioner’s perception— when, facing the desired direction, one should extract the King of Mandalas (cakrarāja).
That very same [direction] has been previously specified; one should apply this sequence everywhere.
When, having turned to face the east, one worships the Mistress of the Wheel (Cakreśī), || 6.58 ||
Then, O Maheśvarī, the west would become the east for the deity;
when one should extract the cakra while facing the west.
The first [method] has already been described as being in the east; now listen, O Pārvatī, regarding the one in the south:
when one faces the south and raises up the wheel. (6.60)
Then what was north becomes east, and what was west becomes south;
when one worships the Goddess while facing north, [these directions are thus established].
O Supreme Goddess, in brief, the south itself becomes the east;
likewise, O Goddess, in the rite for specific desires, if [the deity] is situated in the intermediate directions.
O Goddess, the eastern direction within my own abode has been proclaimed in brief;
in whatever manner Śivā proceeds, so too do her attendants.
O Maheśvarī, those by whom this place was previously obtained through her compassionate glance come here for the purpose of serving the Goddess.

O Goddess, in the ritual of offering the sacrificial oblation (balidāna), whether the deity is already established or merely imagined, one should perform it according to the sequence of facing oneself, known as the "hand of the deity" (devatāhastadakṣa). || 6-65 ||
In Kerala and Gauḍa, the east is declared to be from the front petal of the Goddess,
proceeding in a clockwise direction according to the positions of the right hand.
The worship according to that sequence has been declared in the doctrine known as Kāśmīra;
[one should worship] one's own body, one's own goddess, and one's own guru, O Supreme Goddess. (6.67)

O Dear One, O Great Goddess, one should worship one's own essential nature by way of its abiding within one's own body; during the ritual of worship, O Maheśānī, one should worship after visualizing it before oneself.
