In this regard also, O Goddess of the gods, there is self-nature by way of one's own nature;
and in that form, there is one's own form as well as that of the Guru.
Thus, O Goddess of gods, the triad [of each] within the three [paths] is, in brief, considered to be everything according to the sequence of the three paths. (6–70)
O Goddess, one should present the substance for the *balidāna* offering before the deity;
O Beloved, either facing oneself or facing the deity. (6-71)
Everything is considered here in brief, according to the Kerala tradition, the Kashmir tradition, and indeed the Gauḍa path. (6–72)

Thus ends the sixth chapter, titled "The Determination of Dīpeśa and Others," in the third section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā. || 6 ||
The Seventh Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Śrī Śiva said: O Maheśvarī, do not fear, do not fear; [the rite] begins from Bhinnāñjana.
O Goddess of the gods, O Śivā, having meditated upon Vṛttānanda, who grants all desires,
one should remember the fire situated at the crest-lock (śikhā), appearing in the form of the practitioner of the crest-lock (śikhā-sādhaka).
O Maheśvarī, having meditated with the intellect upon the sword as the tongue of the Goddess, [one should contemplate] the state of dullness of the target in the crest-lock, O Supreme Goddess. (7-3)

O Goddess, the Goddess always resides within the heart of the one to be perfected (sādhya). O Mistress of the Gods, it is there that the tongue experiences the consumption of the nectar, which removes all dullness.
Having meditated thus, O Hero, one should recite the mantra; one shall obtain the knowledge of the three times.
O Maheśānī, O Maheśvarī, this is the visualization for specific desires in the ritual of Tārā.
Beginning with the *pratyālīḍha* stance and adorned with the five mudrās—
having meditated thus with effort, one should place the *jāḍya* (stupidity) upon the skull.
The act of severing [the bonds] by the agent must be contemplated; the wise one is the sovereign of the three worlds.
In the Kali age, there is no capacity to bestow sovereignty without Tārā. (7-7)
The auspicious right foot was placed upon the heart of the corpse.
Having placed the pair of feet of the corpse in the order of their natural sequence upon the left foot, that is called *pratyālīḍha*.
In the practice of sādhana, the head [of the corpse] should always face either east or west;
its nature as a corpse has been described, with the left hand placed upon the heart.
Kālikā shall have four arms and hold a bow as her weapon;
if there is a fifth [hand], it is a skull held in the hand that bestows boons.
In the Mahākālamata, the skull in the form of a shaven head is considered [the symbol];
in the Kali age, Tārā; in the Kali age, Kālī; and in the Kali age, both Tārā and Kālikā.
Through the differentiation of Śiva and Śakti, Śakti is present within the body;
Tārā is Śiva, and likewise Kālī is proclaimed to be the form of Śakti. (7.13)
Kālī and likewise Śiva, as well as Tārā, are proclaimed to be the forms of Śakti.
Oh, how wonderful is the knowledge of those who possess wisdom—the wise one is solely devoted to Kālī and Tārā! (7.14)
O Goddess, the secret and the most profound secret have been declared before you;
O Mistress of the Gods, the arrangement of the regions is now being told—listen with care. (7–15)
O Śivā, beginning from Vaidyanātha and extending as far as Bhuvaneśā,
the region known as Aṅga is not at all defiled during pilgrimage.
O Śivā, beginning from Ratnākara and extending as far as the Brahmaputra,
the land of Vaṅga has been described by me as the bestower of all spiritual accomplishments.
O Śivā, the region of Kaliṅga is said to extend from the eastern part of Jagannātha to the banks of the Kṛṣṇā river; it is devoted to the Vāmamārga.
O Śivā, O Maheśānī, starting from the Kaliṅga country and extending fifty-eight yojanas to the south, it is celebrated as Kāliṅda.
Starting from Subrahmaṇya up to the god Janārdana, that shall be the Kerala country; in its center is Siddhikerala.
Rāmeśvara, Veṅkaṭeśa, Haṃsa, Keralabodhaka, and extending from Anaṃtaśaila as far as the city of Uḍupa; (7.21)
All that region is proclaimed as Kerala, extending from the monastery of Śāradā to the slopes of Mount Kunkuma. (7.22)
At that time, the land of Kaśmīra shall extend for fifty yojanas;
[it shall contain] Kāleśvara, Śvetagiri, Tripurā, and Nīlaparvata.
O Goddess, the one called Kāmarūpa is on the summit of Gaṇeśagiri;
O Śivā, beginning from Sāmā, there are fifteen [sites], with Ujjayinī in the center.
O Indra among kings, as far as the Mārjāratīrtha inhabited by those dwelling in Kolāpura,
so far extends the Mahārāṣṭra country within the range of Karṇāṭa.
The region above Jagannātha is Śrī Bhramarāmbikā, and below it is the land called Andhra; now listen with respect to Saurāṣṭra.

O Goddess, having crossed the western [shore] from Koṅkaṇa, one whose range extends to the edge of the ocean—beings as numerous as a mere fraction of people exist as far as the end of Hiṅgulāja. (7.27)
O Goddess of gods, the region of Saurāṣṭra is indeed called by the name Gurjara;
it extends from Śrīśaila up to the middle portion of the land of the Colas.
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, the Tailaṅga country, extending from Mūkāmbikā to the Malaya mountain, is devoted to meditation and study. (7.29)
O Goddess of the Hill, the land known as Malayāla, which promotes the attainment of mantras,
extends from Rāmanātha to Śrīraṅga.
O Goddess, the Karṇāṭa country bestows the enjoyment of sovereignty;
it extends from the Tāmraparṇī river to the front half of the mountain’s slope.
The region known as Avantī is there, where Kālikā resides;
she is Bhadrakālī, situated to the west of Rāmadurga.
There lies the country named Śrīvidarbha, where the Vaidarbhas reside;
it is situated to the east of Gurjara and to the south of Dvārakā.
O Maheśānī, Marudeśa is the land primarily inhabited by camels;
it lies below Śrī Koṅkaṇa and to the northwest of the Tāpī river.
O Goddess of gods, the Ābhīra country is situated on the Vindhya mountain,
to the east of Avanti and likewise to the north of the Godāvarī.
The great country known as Mālava is devoted to wealth and grain;
between Draviḍa and Tailaṅga lies the celebrated region of Cola.
And they are said to have long ears; for there may indeed be internal subdivisions [among them]. To the west of Kurukṣetra and likewise in its northern part— || 7.37 ||
O Maheśānī, ten and three yojanas to the north of Indraprastha is the land of Pāñcāla, O Deveśī, adorned with the pride of its own beauty. (7.38)
O Goddess of gods, beginning from the Pāñcāla country and extending southeast from the Mlecchas lies the land of Kāmboja, which is devoted to horses and wealth.
The Vairāṭa country is proclaimed to lie to the south of the Vaidarbha country and Indraprastha, and to the east of the Maru country. (7.40)
O Maheśānī, to the south of Kāmboja and to the west of Indraprastha lies the Pāṇḍya country, which produces great heroism. (7.41)
O Śivā, beginning from the banks of the Gaṇḍakī and extending to the edge of the Campā forest, the land of Videha is well-known; that, however, is called Taira-bhukti. (7.42)
O Goddess of the Gods, beginning from the land of Kāmboja and extending eastward from the great Mlecchas lies the Vālhīka country, which is preeminent for the production of horses.
O Śivā, O Goddess of gods, beginning from Taptakuṇḍa and extending to the end of Rāmakṣetra,
the Kirāta country is situated upon the Vindhya mountain.
O Śivā, O Goddess of the gods, the region of Baktrāna, which extends from the Karatoyā river to the end of Hiṅgulāja, is devoted to the great Mlecchas.
O Maheśvarī, beginning from Hiṅgupīṭha and ending at Markeśa,
the region known as Khurāsāna is devoted to the path of the Mlecchas.
And in the midst of that, O Goddess, in the north, Airāka is proclaimed;
it begins from Kāśmīra and lies to the west of Kāmarūpa.
O Goddess of the gods, the land of Bhota is to the south of Mānaseśa;
the land of Cīna is proclaimed to be to the southeast of Mānaseśa.
O Maheśānī, extending from Mount Kailāsa to the source of the Sarayū river, and reaching as far as the Amogha, it is known by the name Mahācīna.
O Maheśvarī, O Queen of the Gods, the land of Nepal extends from Jaṭeśvara to Yoginī; O beloved, listen now to [the description of] Śilahaṭṭa.
O Śivā, O beloved, beginning from Gaṇeśvara and extending as far as the great ocean, there is a region named Śilahaṭṭā situated upon the mountain.
O Śivā, beginning from the land of Vaṅga and extending as far as Bhuvaneśa,
the Gauḍa country is renowned as being proficient in all branches of knowledge.
To the east of Gokarṇeśa, to the north of Āryāvarta, to the west of Tairamūka, and to the east of Mahāpurī. (7.53)
O Śivā, the great kingdom of Kośala shall have the Solar dynasty as its refuge,
extending from Vyāseśvara to the end of Taptakuṇḍa.
The great region called Magadha is indeed not detrimental during a pilgrimage;
in the sequence from Dakṣa to Uttara, Kīkaṭa and Magadha follow in due order. (7-55)
O Śivā, beginning from the mountain Caraṇa and ending at Gṛdhrakūṭa, that region shall be Kīkaṭa; the land north of that is considered Māgadha.
The region surrounding Jagannātha is proclaimed as Oṭkala, O Maheśvarī, extending from Kāmagiri to Dvārakā. (7.57)
O Maheśvarī, hear now of the land named Śrīkuntala belonging to the Hūṇas;
it lies to the south of Kāmagiri and likewise to the north of the Maru desert.
The land of the Hūṇas is well known, for heroes indeed dwell there;
then, starting from Ghaṭṭa and situated between it and Koṭīśa— || 7.59 ||
Indeed, the coastal region of the ocean is celebrated as Koṅkaṇa;
while Kaikeya is situated in the middle portion between the Brahmaputra and Kāmarūpa.
O Śivā, to the south of Magadha and to the west of the Vindhya mountains lies the region named Śaurasena, which illuminates the Solar dynasty.
Starting from Hastināpura and extending south of Kurukṣetra, as well as to the east of Pāñcāla, the land of the Kurus is proclaimed. (7.62)
O Śivā, to the east of Marudeśa and to the south of Kāmādri lies the great land called Siṃhala, the most excellent among all lands.
To the east of Śilahaṭṭa and likewise to the north of Kāmarūpa,
O Goddess of Gods, is the Pulinda country, beyond which lies Naranārāyaṇa.
To the east of Gaṇeśvara and to the north of the ocean, O Śivā, the region of Kaccha is well-known; listen with reverence to its ritual service.
To the north of Pulinda and to the west of Kaccha, O Auspicious One,
is the region known as Matsyadeśa, which abounds in fish.
Between Vairāṭa and Pāḍya, in the order from east to south, the Madra country is well-known; Mādrīśa resides there.
O Goddess of gods, to the east of Śūrasena and to the west of Kaṇṭhaka lies the excellent Sauvīra country, the lowest of all low countries. (7.68)
To the west of Avantī and to the south and north of Vaidarbha, the Lāṭa country is well known; now hear about Barbara, O Pārvatī. (7-69)
Starting from Māyāpura and extending northward from Saptaśṛṅga lies the great country called Barbaraka; now listen with respect to Saindhava.
O Supreme Goddess, O Beloved, beginning from the region of Laṅkā and extending as far as Makkā, there lies the great land known as Saindhava upon the mountain.
These fifty-six regions have been proclaimed by me to you, O beloved;
even within these, O Goddess of gods, there are numerous sub-divisions of regions.
O Goddess of the gods, there are millions of such [mantras], yet these have been proclaimed as the principal ones.
This is a secret, a most profound secret, which must be guarded against the presence of the uninitiated (paśus).
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the seventh chapter, titled "The Regulation of the Arrangement of Countries," in the third section of the northern part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 7 ||
The Eighth Chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I now wish to hear about the five systems."
Śrī Śiva said:
Indraprastha, Yamaprastha, and Varuṇaprastha.
O Great Goddess, Kūrmaprastha, Devaprastha as the fifth, and Indraprastha, O Maheśānī—listen, for I shall describe them in their proper order. (8-2)
O Great Goddess, Indraprastha, joined by ten million Yoginīs, is proclaimed to be in its eastern part, along with Mathurā and Gokula. (8.3)
Vṛndāvana is in the north-eastern corner, Hastināpura is in the north,
Dvārakā is in the west, and Gadāvarta is in the south.
The region within the mouth of Kālikā in the central part of Indraprastha is designated as Vārāhī-kṣetra; that is called Indraprastha.
And that very place is proclaimed as Siṃhāsana, O Maheśānī;
Yamaprastha is situated in the south.
Someśvara is in the west, while Saptaśṛṅgī is in the east;
Māyāpura is on the left side, and Vyaṅkaṭeśa is on the right.
In the center, Yamaprastha would be within the range of Kamalā’s face;
there would be Śaṅkhāvarta, and that field would be named Māyā.
The lion-throne of the king is proclaimed to be to its right;
then, when the Lord of the World is reached to the east, there shall be the Lord of Poets.
Likewise, O Goddess, that which is called Vāruṇa is now being described; listen.
Makkeśvara is in the west, and Hiṅgulā is indeed in the north.
The goddess Trailokyavijayā is proclaimed to be on the right side;
there should be rājāvarta stone, and that is located at the cool-faced [mouth].
At its end are the seven oceans, and at the very edge of those,
I have described to you that plateau known as Śrīvāruṇa.
O Maheśānī, O Pārvatī, listen as I describe Kūrmaprastha:
it is located to the south of Gokarṇeśa and within the range to the east of Kāmākhyā. (8.13)
To the north shall be Mānaseśa, and to the west Sāradā;
this is indeed the Triple-Circled (Triguṇāvarta), declared to be the face of Vajreśī. (8.14)
O Maheśānī, that Devaprastha shall be pervaded by hosts of fifty-six crores of Cāmuṇḍās; listen now as it is described. (8.15)
Śrīraṅga is said to be in the south, Gāyatrī is in the west;
Jagannātha is in the east, and Amarakaṇṭaka is in the north.
Kāñcīpura is in the middle portion, as is Mohanāvarta;
that is the face of Lalitā, adorned by the hosts of Vidyās.
The sacred field of Kāmākhyā has been described as adorned with great mantras,
and further embellished by the hosts of the nine hundred thousand Mahāvidyās.
O Goddess of gods, these five manifestations have been described by me to you:
Kṛṣṇa, Mudraṇa, Rāma, Śrī Viṣṇu, and Varadeśvara.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva revolve in a cycle through the three states, from the supreme (parā) up to that which transcends the beyond (tadatītānta).
For these are remembered as manifestations of Viṣṇu; indeed, no lord of the earth is without Viṣṇu.
May he become the lord of Pañcaprastha, devoted to Kālī and Tārā.
O Supreme Goddess, the secret and the most profound secret has been told.
It must be concealed, concealed, concealed like one's own private parts.
Thus it has been declared in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (8.22)

Thus ends the eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Five Prasthas," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Tārā.
The Ninth Chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the secret doctrine previously mentioned."
The illustrious Śiva said:
Out of devotion for you, that which is a secret and even a greater secret is now being told.
Listen to [the description of] the great forest of yoga named Ānandabhuvana; O Goddess of the Gods, having brought forth the Śakti, one should perform her initiation.
She was consecrated, virtuous, devoted to mantras and yantras, the wife of a king, like a goddess, and the very form of a guru. || 9.3 ||
O beloved, [one may worship] the royal courtesan, the brahmin courtesan, the divine courtesan who is supreme in the arts,
the sacred-site courtesan, the secret courtesan, and the dance courtesan.
Having brought [it] together day and night as appropriate, O Pārvatī,
one should diligently initiate [the disciple], O Goddess, into the digit that delights the three worlds.
Having placed [the deity] upon a bed of flowers and having offered water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), and water for sipping,
one should worship with diligence through the sixty-four modes of service (catuḥṣaṣṭyupacāra).
O Maheśvarī, having meditated upon one’s own chosen deity, one should worship Trijaṭeśvarī with various divine ornaments of jewels and erotic adornments. (9.7)
When there is a division of mantras and the repetition is more frequent in a short mantra,
one should worship that deity in the corner surrounding the *bindu*.
Having worshipped her along with her limbs and her retinue— she who grants boons according to one's desire—
one should gaze upon her and recite [the mantra], O Goddess, at all times without indolence.

In that [image], O Pārvatī, Goddess of the Gods, one should meditate upon the Goddess with the thought that she is a deity; then, contemplating her two feet, one should recite [the mantra] with effort amidst great festivities.
One shall become the lord of all accomplishments; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having worshipped the deity therein, one should be intent upon beholding the Śakti.

O Supreme Goddess, the wise one who conquers the three worlds should worship her; O Śivā, having contemplated her face with the thought that she is the Goddess herself, he should do so during the day.

If one recites [the mantra] three thousand times over meat, that person shall become a knower of the three periods of time. O Śivā, having understood this secret code (kūṭa) of it, one should recite it one hundred thousand times during the day.
Having seen her smile, one should recite [the mantra] fifty thousand times during the day;
one will then become equal to the five objects of desire—of this there is no doubt. (9.14)
Having gazed upon her bodice, one should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times during the day;
one shall become a master of all supernatural powers—of this there is no doubt. (9.15)
Having seen the creeper startled during the day, one should mutter the Divākara mantra;
O Śivā, seeing Tārā during the day, one should mutter it while free from all agitation.
A man shall become a lord of all accomplishments and become equal to Kālī;
by beholding women intent on laughter during the day, he shall obtain a gathering of Yoginīs.
Having made the creeper his support during the day, the Lord of the Triple-Lakṣa becomes threefold;
indeed, having gazed upon the deity during the day, he remains intent on meditation upon that god.
By practicing for three months, one certainly beholds the deity;
having approached [the deity] during the day and embraced [her], O Maheśvarī. (9.19)
One should recite it one hundred and fifty thousand times, and one shall become equal to Śiva and Śakti;
by performing it for a hundred thousand times during the day, one becomes a lord of the earth.

Having observed a moist creeper by day, one who upholds the three powers should recite [the mantra] ten million times, equal to ten million moons; and having observed a solar [object] by day, he should recite it three hundred thousand times.
Having observed the knots at the tips of the creepers, the king should mutter [the mantra] during the day;
having observed [the deity] established in the state of *sthāyībhāva*, he should mutter it one hundred thousand times with undistracted mind.
By reciting [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one will surely become equal to the king of kings;
having seen a flowering creeper by day, the beautiful woman recites [it].
Beholding the creeper that had moved at will, Śaṅkara muttered prayers during the day,
having entered the circle of the creeper and become intent on meditation upon the deity.
O Goddess, by reciting [the mantra] day and night, one becomes equal to Bhuvaneśī;
upon seeing a creeper devoted to singing, one should offer it betel.
Beholding the red tint of betel, one should constantly recite the mantra a hundred thousand times;
by reciting for Kālī daily during the day, one becomes Śiva himself—of this there is no doubt.
Having taken a betel-roll with a sprig of *latā*, one should consume it while reciting the mantra;
O Goddess, one who is thus engaged with the *svara* [mantra] shall obtain the boon of the deity. (9.27)
Having assumed the guise of a Gandharva by day, having taken from the hand of a creeper-like woman who was breaking her bed, he attains all supernatural powers (*siddhi*).
O Maheśvarī, at the junction of the eighth lunar day, one should go to the house of the one hundred and eight creepers and perform recitation daily for the duration of the day. (9.29)
Practicing in this manner on every eighth day, one shall become a lord of all accomplishments;
at the junction of the new moon and the fourteenth day, one should be accompanied by three hundred creepers.
Having offered a flower for each [recitation], devoted to the attire of China,
one should recite the mantra during the day, O Great Goddess, until the next fourteenth day.
One should recite [the mantra] until free from fear and endowed with all accomplishments; having approached Nīlaveśa, one should perform worship.
He who practices the *surateśī* for three months shall indeed obtain that creeper, having beheld it fully equipped with all the requisites for enjoyment.
By reciting [the mantra] day and night for three days, one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi),
provided that while observing her engaged in dance, one remains intent on meditation upon the deity.
One should recite the mantra of the Goddess day and night; one shall obtain poetic skill over the three worlds.
Having beheld that Goddess intent upon playing the lute, one should recite the mantra during the day.
"One shall become equal to Rājarāja; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
Upon seeing a creeper intent on playing the mṛdaṅga drum during the day, one should recite [the mantra]. (9.36)
One certainly beholds the boon-granting deity within five months;
having seen the creeper situated in the foam, one should recite the mantra for the duration of a day.
Having become the lord of all siddhis, Hara, the conqueror of the three worlds,
beheld the creeper engaged in dance and chanted for a day and night, O Śivā.
A man shall become like a star; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Having seen a creeper with loose hair during the day, one should recite [the mantra] two hundred thousand times. (9.39)
Becoming equal to Kālītārā, he attains the siddhi of Chinnamastā;
this most secret of secrets has been proclaimed out of affection for you. (9.40)
"O Goddess of gods, this Ānandayoga has been described by me out of affection for you.
Thus it has been briefly explained; specifically, it is auspicious on the day [of its occurrence]. (9.41)

Thus ends the ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sadhana of the Creeper," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 9 ||
The Tenth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive explanation of that which was briefly indicated."
Śrī Śiva said:
This was indicated in the *Śaktisaṃgama-tantra* and other scriptures at the location of Meru.
That very [teaching] is now being told with effort; be attentive in mind.
What has been stated in general terms, listen to its specific details with reverence. (10.2)
O Supreme Goddess, [it may be performed] in the months of Pauṣa, Māgha, Bhādrapada, or Jyeṣṭha;
O Goddess, whether in the dark or the bright fortnight, but especially during the dark fortnight. || 10-3 ||
O Goddess of the Gods, on the seventh, the thirteenth, the ninth,
as well as the sixth and the new moon day, Dhūmra rises into the expanse of the sky.
O beloved, whether it be on a Pāta, Bhadra, or Ādina yoga, or during Gaṇḍa or Śūla; or under the asterisms of Bharaṇī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, or Raudra (Āśleṣā).
O Maheśvarī, when Dhūmra is situated in the asterisms of Hasta or Citrā, he becomes very powerful;
whatever is performed or caused to be performed by one who is devoid of authority [is rendered ineffective]. (10.6)
Or, O Goddess, by that yoga, Dhūmraketu shall arise under the influence of great sin for the purpose of destroying the burden of the earth. (10.7)
O Goddess of the gods, for three years, five months, and sixty nāḍīs and palas— measured by the number of the principles (tattvas)— the central [channel] will become smoke-colored.
O Goddess, after four months, there will be the banner of Śakra;
thereafter, O Maheśvarī, there will be the banner of Ahi, which has the form of a serpent.
Śakraketu, who resembles a clod of earth; likewise another, Ghaṭaketu;
another, Pādukāketu; and then the one known as Hasantī.
Resembling the tail of a tiger and then resembling the tail of a serpent— O Goddess of gods, these marks appear at every step.
One should construct a Śrīvidyā-maṇḍapa; then peace will prevail.
Therefore, O Great Goddess, this must be kept secret in the Kali age. (10–12)
The multiplicity of divisions is said to arise from the distinctions of half, middle, and full;
thus, O Mistress of the Gods, through such division, there are three hundred and five Merus.
O Maheśānī, Agni, Meru, and Vidhi are the bestowers of accomplishment;
the practice of Meru must be performed according to the sequence of the oral tradition. (10.14)
If that lowest of men should perform [this act] out of greed, delusion, fear, or hypocrisy, I shall seize all his possessions and cast him into hell. (10.15)
When Ghaṭaketu appears, O Maheśānī, the family perishes;
Dhūmraketu, however, brings about the destruction of the king. (10.16)
When Dhūmraketu appears, that family shall enter the abode of Yama within a year; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O Goddess, just as one who is outside the Vedas is excluded from all rites, so too shall this man be excluded from the twice-born; there is no need for deliberation on this point. (10.18)
He indeed becomes a destroyer of his family and is purified only through penance;
by mere association with him, even a sovereign lord may be deprived of his kingdom. (10.19)
Therefore, O Goddess of the Gods, one should diligently perform an expiation;
by that, O Goddess, he shall become pure, and not otherwise—he will certainly go to hell. (10.20)
Through the knowledge of the rays of the glorious Meru, one becomes a conqueror of the three worlds;
O Supreme Goddess, that lowest of men who performs [this] out of ignorance— 10.21.
That most wicked person of evil conduct will certainly become a partaker of suffering;
yet, by performing a hundred Prājāpatya penances and twenty gifts of cows, he shall be purified. || 10-22 ||
One should feed a thousand Brahmins; thus one becomes pure, and not otherwise.
Otherwise, O Goddess of the lords of gods, the Supreme Lord would be the destroyer. (10.23)
Pratyaṅgirā herself is the Teacher; indeed, she is the primordial heroine who effortlessly wields even the Brahmāstra, O Goddess of gods, for the sake of its destruction. (10.24)
With seven years or nine years, one with hair on the body certainly perishes;
with three months or five years, the protector of the earth perishes.
By means of rain one obtains a wife; by five years, a daughter;
and by a year of menses, a sister—through contact with them, according to the sequence of the sages.
O Śivā, how could one who is not joined with initiation (dīkṣā) obtain that fruit, even with thousands of millions of mouths or hundreds of millions of tongues? (10.27)
How can there be the power to describe his greatness here in this Kali age?
In the Kali age, which is filled with sin, the attainment of Mount Meru is not considered possible.
O Dear One, the Meru of Nyāsa and the Meru of Yantra should be performed somewhere;
however, this is indeed a *tāmasa* rite and should not be performed by one who desires their own welfare. (10.29)
Through conversation with a cowherd, one may attain the state of Goloka;
however, through conversation with an unknown twice-born man, he becomes the lowest of Brahmins.
It must be kept secret, kept secret, kept secret at all times. Through secrecy one attains perfection; through secrecy one goes to the state of Śiva.
"O beautiful one, it should not be given to the disciples of others, nor to a miser;
one should not give it to one who lacks initiation, but should guard it like a mother's lover.
Thus has the secret been briefly declared; now hear another. (10.32)

Thus ends the tenth chapter, titled "Unknown Inauspicious Omens," in the third section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 10 ||
The eleventh chapter.
The Goddess said:
"Now, please explain that which has been indicated by these portents, such as earthquakes and the like."
The illustrious Śiva said:
"Knowing it to be a secret, O Goddess, I did not speak of it to you."
O Great Goddess, this very point was stated by Koṭivināyaka:
"The number of comets is proclaimed to be eighteen thousand. (11.2)
In the midst of that, O Maheśānī, the number is proclaimed to be one hundred and eighteen;
within this, O Śivā, there are fifty banners.
Some have the appearance of brooms, and likewise the appearance of trees; some possess the form of crests, and others resemble hand-gestures (mudrās). || 11-4 ||
O Auspicious One, they may have the appearance of grass, or resemble conch shells, or be curved;
O Dear One, they may also have the shape of a tree trunk or the form of a jar. (11-5)
O Maheśvarī, it may last for twenty-one days, or for two such periods;
likewise, O Devī, it may last for one month, or for two such periods, O Parameśvarī. (11.6)
Wandering indeed through the four directions during the day, there may be a rising;
and by means of the conjunction of the four watches, there is likewise a rising at night.
O Great Goddess, the Banner of the Sequence (Kramaketu) arises continuously one, two, three, four, or five times.
O Goddess, O beloved, whether in a single form or in diverse forms,
it exists in every form until the end of the Brahma-kalpa.
In the first [period], there will be the destruction of the region; in the second, the destruction of the kingdom;
in the third, there will be the collapse of the royal umbrella (the throne); and in the fourth, there is universal suffering.
O Goddess of the lords of gods, in the fifth [year], there is a gathering of all beings everywhere,
occurring through the sequence of three and three months, by means of the conjunction of five and six years.
When the smoke-bannered comet (Dhūmraketu) appears, then the royal umbrella perishes;
having reflected thus with diligence, one should perform propitiatory rites.
Thus has been briefly declared the determination regarding Dhūmraketu, as well as the falling of stars during the day and the appearance of such stars. (11–13)
Likewise, O Goddess, the appearance of a serpent-bannered comet during the day, or the disappearance of the moon on the full-moon day—especially on the full moon of Kārttika—is a portent. (11–14)

(On page 81: During the conjunction of the twenty-seven lunar mansions, as well as the circle of the directions and the mandala of the five elements, at the assembly of the Seven Sages (Saptarṣis). (11–15)
The appearance of the moon on the new moon day (amāvāsyā) is a cause of dissolution;
likewise, an earthquake, the loud laughter of an image, and its breaking are also such causes. || 11-16 ||
O Maheśvarī, the falling of meteors during the day or night are evil omens;
having seen these signs, one should perform the recitation for well-being (svastivācana).
Great portents and the like shall occur; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
There will be the collapse of the royal umbrella, the ruin of the kingdom, and likewise the fear of a great pestilence. (11.18)
In every respect, it is indeed possible for which reason the characteristic is stated; having obtained a peacock feather, O Śivā, [one should worship] the great destroyer of barbarians.
O Goddess, Aśvapati has been described; now hear about Gajanāyaka.
O Maheśvarī, having reached the end of Koṅkaṇa, it extends as far as the southeast.
O Goddess, the Lord of Elephants has been described; now listen to the Leader of Men (Naranāyaka).
O Beloved, he who extends from the east to the west is called the Lord of Men (Narapati). 11-21.
O Goddess, the characteristics of all [these] have been described in the *Śambhutāṇḍava*;
now I shall briefly explain the wheel known as the Day and the Hour (*dinahorā*).
O Śivā, this is a secret, a supreme secret, more hidden than the hidden;
by the mere knowledge of which one may perceive the three periods of time.
O Great Goddess, you are my devotee; therefore, I shall tell it to you—the wheel of Viṣṇu’s skill and the skill of Time as well.
The wheel of skill in the Buddhas and likewise the skill in Rudras do not equal even a sixteenth part of the wheel of skill in the days.
Indeed, Śiva alone is the knower of the wheel of the skill of the day;
having struck five lines, they are likewise struck by the staff.
The movement through the directions has been described, O Goddess, as well as the sequence for the paths of the intermediate directions.
In this manner, one should practice the eight-fold wheel, beginning with the eastern face. (11.27)
In the west, there should be a pair of feet, and then the part called the four arms;
by revolving like a ball, each [direction] becomes a face according to its respective name. (11.28)
O Goddess of gods, the sixteen eternal ones follow the sequence of the counter-lines;
if the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā are firmly established within all the limbs, [then success is attained]. (11.29)
The sixty-four Yoginīs are arranged according to the sequence of lines;
likewise, the fifty-six Gaṇeśas are situated upon the lines of the lamps. (11.30)
The Vaiṣṇavas, beginning with Keśava, are established in the grammatical case-endings (kāraka);
and the enumeration of these case-endings is indeed proclaimed as the "World" (bhuvana).
In the domain of sovereignty, the Mahādevas and Śrīkaṇṭhas are proclaimed;
therein reside the fourteen grahas, distinguished by their movement through the mobile and immobile worlds. || 11-32 ||
The moon and the sun are fourfold through the distinction between the moving and the non-moving,
as well as by the sequence of revolution through the twenty-eight lunar mansions.
There, one should perform the accumulation according to the division of moving and non-moving beings;
thus, in the third pair, the pair of eyes is proclaimed.
At the position of the feet, however, the Omniscient One has proclaimed a threefold division;
the front, the left, and the right are proclaimed as the three parts. || 11-35 ||
O Goddess of gods, O Śivā, the movement of the planets and constellations occurs within a single day and night,
pervading two nāḍīs each through the processes of emanation and withdrawal.
By way of emanation, it is the sun; by way of withdrawal, it is the moon.
In the gross sequence, O All-knowing One, the sun begins at dawn.
Beginning from the twilight (sandhyā), the moon [phase] occurs during the night, and the reverse likewise;
thirty-six thousand seven hundred verses are thus declared.
O Śivā, O Sovereign of the Universe, those who always obey my command bestow their fruit upon you by pervading Dinakauśalaka through the sequence of their rotation. (11.39)
But in the opinion of others, O Goddess, movement by way of the left path is proclaimed as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) in the eighteen Siddhāntas. (11.40)
They meet at some time or another through the conjunction of fortune; of this there is no doubt.
For whichever weekday the sun rises upon, that is the planetary influence for that very morning.
In Kerala, at the place named Vyaṅkaṭeśa, my doctrine has been proclaimed for the virtuous.
Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the secret that was previously indicated. (11.42)
Śrī Śiva said:
A protector of the earth would become a servant, and a poet would likewise become mute;
a lord of wealth would fall into a state of wretchedness, and fire would attain the state of coldness.
Even Maheśvara may become deformed; such is the fruit born from the performance of the Medhā sacrifice.
The fruit of the consecration for the Sāmrājya-medha is said to extend to the very end of one's life. (11.44)

Human birth is difficult to attain in this world, and knowledge of the Tantra is even more difficult to obtain; O Śivā, through the placement of the mantra (vidyānyāsa) and through contemplation, the state of a Brāhmaṇa is attained.
Indeed, for a thousand yugas he performed ascetic penance by means of the sequence of the Great Vidyā and the sequence of the fivefold and sixteenfold [rites].
By means of the sequence of the deposition of power (śaktinyāsa) and the sequence of daily worship,
one who is thus engaged in ascetic practice shall attain the status of a lord of the earth.
It was accompanied by fifty crores of Cāmuṇḍās and fifty Gaṇapas,
traversed by Gadāvarta, and adorned by Vārāhī as well.
O Goddess, this station is crowded with more than a hundred hosts of Vārāhīs and is adorned by the sixty-four families of Yoginīs.
The place named Indraprastha, situated in the center of Kāli’s heart,
is adorned in age after age with imperial sovereignty, sacrificial sessions, initiations, and other such rites.
O Goddess, the state [of liberation] comes into his hand; it is not otherwise.
O Maheśānī, during the Tārkṣya-graha, one may travel ten thousand yojanas with sovereign power.
He in whose hand shines the accomplishment consisting of the fulfillment of desires, and who likewise ever possesses the radiant Tārā, the accomplishment of will; (52)
Whether she be Kālī or Sundarī, whoever possesses her favor through the *aṅka-mantras*, banners, and so forth, as well as the *pada* mantras and the like, should recognize her as Kālī.
O Goddess, if the previously mentioned protectors of that [mantra] are diminished, it will certainly perish;
formerly, in the Kṛta Yuga, O Goddess, they were the foremost among gods and Daityas.
Having established two preceptors, they exercised the enjoyment of sovereignty;
Bhauma was declared the preceptor of the gods (gurus), and Śukra is remembered as the preceptor of the Daityas.
The *mṛtasaṃjīvinī* spell, entry into another’s body,
the summoning of others’ spells, and likewise a hundred types of missiles.
O Śivā, since thirty-three crores of Māyās are under your control,
O Maheśānī, he was entreated for a single moment out of affection for you.
"O Maheśānī, knowing that all who are born at this moment become perfected beings (siddhas), I then granted that moment. (11.58)
At that time, those who were born indeed became Siddhas, bestowers of success;
eighty-four Siddhas were born, whose sphere of activity was that very time. (11.59)
Thus, O auspicious goddess, nine lords were born at the moment of Śukra’s birth;
those who were born at the time of his birth, O goddess, became perfected beings (siddhas).
O Supreme Goddess, what need is there to speak of him who is manifest before our very eyes?
Who on earth, or even in the abode of the gods, is capable of restraining him? (11.61)
Whether in the abode of the Nāgas or in the sovereignty of the gods, he is indeed the conqueror of the three worlds;
yet there is no one on earth who can subdue him.
And the weapon that conquers the three worlds shines in his hand;
O Goddess, [he possesses] the recitation of names as well as the recitation of mantras.
For he who is joined with Khecarī is the paralyzer of the moon and the sun;
being equipped with the weapon of the fire of time, he is the bringer of restraint.
Thus ends the Śukra [section].
O Maheśvarī, in the past, for thirty yugas, he was devoted to the worship of Śiva,
performing daily worship with karavīra flowers.
Then Mahādeva, being pleased, spoke these words:
"A group of nine treasures has been granted; Indra and the others shall be your worshippers."
"O Kubera, lord of the gods, dwell forever in my heart;
O Śivā, the status of the Lord of Treasures was then granted by me."
Dhanadā, Kamalā, and Lakṣmī shall always dwell there, bestowing happiness;
likewise, human rulers, yakṣas, yakṣiṇīs, and hosts of kinnarīs [shall reside there].
"They shall perform service for you; O beloved, may you become the Lord of Wealth.
Thus was the boon granted to him by me previously, O Maheśvarī.
Who among those dwelling in the midst of the world could possibly be his adversary, O Goddess, in whose hand the glorious Krodhamaṇḍala shines? (11.70)
O Goddess, there is the Maṇḍala of Mantras, as well as the Great Maṇḍala;
also the Maṇḍala of Vidyās, and likewise the Maṇḍala of the Retinue.
O Śivā, for one who is indeed endowed with the six Śāmbhava [powers], he who would inflict restraint upon him should strike Dhanada with the Mahākrodhāṅkuśa [the Great Wrath Hook].
But Dhanadā will bring about the destruction of Kubera.
Thus ends the section on Dhaneśa.
O Maheśānī, he who has been established in the third [position] by Mahākālī— || 11-73 ||
The fire, which has the form of the third eye, is designated as Vīrabhadra, Rudra, Krodha, and Kālāntaka. (11.74)
I have described dissolution as a synonym for the withdrawal of entities;
whatever effect arises exists in that very form. (11.75)
Impelled by Śrī Kālī, he exists in various forms;
born from the wrath of Kālī, he is the proclaimer of the faces of the deities. (11.76)
Whatever is offered in sacrifice or given as a gift to him will all turn to ashes;
he alone is the submarine fire (vāḍavāgni), appearing in various forms according to the requirements of each specific task.
O Maheśānī, O Goddess, there is no Maheśvara without Agni;
from a mere insect up to the limits of the universe, fire exists everywhere. (11.78)
Born from the cremation ground, Kālī was appointed to the eyes of Kālī; when the time for universal dissolution arrived, he was impelled by Kālī, O Śivā.
Having reduced the cosmic egg to ashes, she who is the primordial Great Illusion (Mahāmāyā) in the form of the beginningless creation— namely, the fierce Caṇḍikā— is filled with garlands of flames.
She who is the illustrious Siddhikarālī, she who is the supreme Guhyakālī, she who is declared to be Kālakālī, and she who is the digit of Mahākāma; || 11-81 ||
O Goddess of gods, by her the entire universe was established upon the root tusk;
the infinite millions of universes shine as the ornament of that root tusk. (11.82)
"Since they shine among the teeth, they are known as the 'royal teeth' (rājadanta); these two teeth of mine, which devour the three worlds, are both effective in their task. (11.83)
O Goddess, by that power of will, creation was produced once again.
Then, O Maheśānī, the fire was placed within his own eyes;
[the number of oblations] for the fire is one hundred and eight, and for the sun it is one hundred and sixteen.
One hundred and thirty-six belong to Soma, and the triad of eyes belongs to Śiva;
O Goddess, these very kalās are employed in the Śāmbhava and other [empowerments].
O Great Goddess, such is the fire described by me to you;
O beloved, who indeed in the universe is its subduer?
Whether he be a worshiper of the nine wheels or even a worshiper of the six wheels,
he is one who has attained the sovereignty of Śambhu and is devoted to the practice of the five weapons.
He who is intent upon the worship of that [deity] consisting of the ten sciences, and who is capable of reversing day and night, [attains success]. (11.89)
He is indeed capable of suppressing the fire, and not otherwise.
Thus ends the section on fire.
He who is proclaimed as the lord of thirty-six crores of gods; || 11-90 ||
Known as Devendra, he was the bestower of great sovereignty; O Goddess of the gods, he was devoted to the worship of Śrīvidyā for a period of ten million billion years.
Then, endowed with the Śāmbhava state and possessed of the initiation of wisdom (medhādīkṣā),
he is joined with the circle of rays and invested with the circle of sovereignty.
Devoted to the recitation of the *Cakra* and endowed with the recitation of the *Yantra*,
[he performs it] by means of the sequence of the letters beginning with *ka* and *ha*, and those beginning with *kā* and *hā*, numbering two thousand times the number of *kalās*.
O Goddess Śivā, by whoever this pair of restraints (yamayuga) has been performed through disciplined austerity, that person attains this station known as Indra.
O Goddess, having obtained the five jewels and being intent upon the heroic practice (vīrasādhana),
the state known as Indra shall come into his hands.
O Śivā, the station is presided over by nine hundred million great mantras;
its protectors, O Maheśānī, are fifty million Bhairavas.
O Śivā, that place is protected by millions upon millions of mantras, including the King of Wrath (Krodharāja), Śarabha, and likewise Pratyamgirā. || 11-97 ||
The attainment of Indra’s station is not the fruit of meager austerity;
who indeed exists anywhere in this world of moving and unmoving beings who can restrain him? (11.98)
And because they perform cruel deeds, they are proclaimed as Rākṣasas;
whatever [beings] there may be within the cosmic egg or upon the surface of the earth— || 11.99 ||
O Goddess, he in whose hands all the siddhis are always held is alone capable of exercising restraint; it cannot be otherwise.
The practitioner who likewise accomplishes the collyrium, the sky-walker, the sword, the vetāla, and the pill, as well as thousands of moons and suns; || 11-101 ||
He in whose house Sundarī, Kālikā, and Tārā are always present certainly possesses the power to subdue even the Lord of the Gods.
It should not be revealed to unworthy men; what more need be said?
Thus has the characteristic of the accomplishment of Kālikā been briefly explained. (11.103)
(87) This has been taught by me to you according to the systems beginning with *ka* and *ha*;
it must be kept secret, kept secret, like one's own womb or another woman. (11.104)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive teaching on the play of the individual soul.
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall explain the determination of the deposition of the living soul (jīvanyāsa).
The *jīvanyāsa* is fivefold: the Seed, the Flow, the Right, the Ocean, and the Kālānala;
thus it is declared to be fivefold in Śivā, according to this sequence.
O Pārvatī, according to the divisions of Gauḍa, Kerala, and Kāśmīra, the determination of the sixteenth digit (candravinirṇaya) occurs within the body of the God and in the effigy (puttalī). (11.107)
O Pārvatī, one should join [the mantra] according to its specific characteristic (liṅga) with a Gaṇapa, a doll, a Śivaliṅga, or with the Durgā known as pārthivā.
O Goddess, in the sequence known as Kāśmīra, the sixth [letter] is adorned with fire (the letter *ra*);
O Goddess, this sequence is proclaimed according to the order beginning with plurality (*bahutva*). || 11-109 ||
In the Gauḍa [tradition], however, there would be equality between the two; this has been kept secret in the Āgamas.
O Goddess, in the sequence known as Kerala, one should join the sixth with the Moon. (11.110)

If one worships for twenty days at the end of two or three hundred repetitions of the Rudra-mantra for the purpose of warding off the afflictions of the planets, it will indeed ward off all planetary afflictions.
By worshipping twenty-one [times], one is liberated from all sins;
by worshipping a hundred daily, O Śivā, one obtains all desires.
O Goddess, by worshipping [the deity] a thousand times, an unfortunate man becomes fortunate;
by worshipping three thousand times, he becomes capable of accomplishing all undertakings. || 11-113 ||

Having thus worshipped one hundred thousand [times] and so forth, one becomes the lord of all siddhis; O Goddess, [the mantra] may consist of one, two, or three syllables, or it may assume infinite forms by the millions.
O Pārvatī, Śiva remains forever pervading everything;
having stated that these are the vital breaths of Śiva, one should perform the union of the breaths within the earthen [liṅga]. (11.115)
O Maheśānī, Śiva is one, but the vital breaths (prāṇas) are many, O Śivā;
O Pārvatī, the breaths of Śiva exist pervading everywhere.
O Goddess, among the earthly [deities], Śiva is the vital breaths; on the sixth [digit] marked by the moon, the sequence known as Kāśmīra has been told to you by me.
Śiva is the giver, Śiva is the enjoyer, Śiva is the doer, and he is stainless;
his entire body is smeared with ashes, and his limbs are adorned with rudrākṣa beads. (11.118)
Twenty-seven rudrākṣas are proclaimed to be like the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā);
O Maheśānī, those of the stated number are proclaimed to be like the ritual bath (snāna).
O Goddess, O Auspicious One, one thousand beads are prescribed for the rite of divination;
O Beloved, one should wear two, three, or four thousand rudrākṣa beads.
Having fashioned a circle of rudrākṣas, whether superior, inferior, or middling,
one who becomes adorned with rudrākṣas shall in an instant become equal to Rudra.
Three lines should be worn on the head, two on the circle of the arms, and as many as one desires on all other limbs; such is the number prescribed for the ear and for Śivā.
O Goddess, regarding the wearing of rudrākṣas, there are two specific rules:
one should not associate with those who are hated by women or those who have been cursed by their gurus. (11–123)
In the Kali age, three kinds of rudrākṣas have emerged from the three eyes:
the dhanaśrī originates from the right eye, while the other two are the moraṅga and the uttara.
The third, however, is the *malākī*; fire does not burn its body.
These are proclaimed as the Rudrākṣas, known as the eyes of Rudra. (11–125)
O Śivā, whatever mantra one recites while staying in the pavilion of rudrākṣas, that very mantra shall become perfected; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
When the thread has worn out, O Goddess, one should make a new thread, place it [there], and recite the mantra;
one should worship in the Rudrākṣa pavilion for the sake of attaining success.
O Goddess, by worshipping the Śrīcakra in two ways within the pavilion of Rudrākṣa beads, one attains the very form of Śrīvidyā; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. (11–128)
I shall explain the twofold nature by which one may become composed of the divine (maya):
there are four Śiva-cakras and five Śakti-cakras. || 11-129 ||
The city of the earth (bhūpura), the line of qualities (guṇarekhā), the pairs of serpent-petals, then the serpent-petal, O Goddess, and the wheels of Śiva, O Pārvatī. (11–130)

Phaṭkārabhairava, and likewise Bibhakṣabhairava. || 11-253 ||
Vīreśa Bhairava, Śrīmanteśvara Bhairava, Haṃsagarbha Bhairava, and Caṇḍikeśvara Bhairava. || 11-254 ||
The wise one should worship [the deity] on the crown of the head, the forehead, the throat, the heart, the region of the navel, the linga, the mūlādhāra, and all the limbs. (11.255)
One should recite the vidyā according to one's ability and offer the bali oblation according to the prescribed rule:
"Oṃ kṣe/ ca kṣetrapāla, [one] should utter the word 'imaṃ baliṃ'. (11-256)
"Joined with *gṛhṇyuk* and *svāhā*, this is considered the offering to the Kṣetrapāla;
such, O Goddess, is the procedure for worship according to the tradition of Śrī Kālī and Kāla. (11.257)
O Goddess, the method for invisibility is considered [to be thus];
even the secret has been revealed in connection with Mahākāla. (11.258)
"O auspicious lady, you must keep this secret, a most profound mystery;
it must be guarded, guarded like one's own womb and no other.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the eleventh chapter, titled "The Ritual Procedure for the Mantra of Mahākāla," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and the Great Fierce Tārā. 11.
The Twelfth Chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
The illustrious Śiva said:
The method for invisibility and the entry into another's body have been declared.
O Goddess of the gods, it is said: listen and be attentive;
one should worship the bliss of nectar arising from the Kula and Akula.

Having offered the nectar of the family (*kulāmṛta*) that arises from [the union of] the two, one should recite the mantra, which is equal to ten million suns, while standing in the midst of the disputants. (12.3)

Likewise, in the family [of the lineage], due to the firm binding of Kuṇḍalinī, she resides in the support (ādhāra), in the middle of the petals, in the two-petaled [lotus], the abode of the two-footed one. || 12-4 ||
In the sixteen-spoked [cakra], in the yuta-liṅga, in the twelve-spoked maṇipūraka,
in the ten-petalled [cakra] at the heart, and in the six-petalled and four-petalled [cakras].
A man observing the vow of celibacy should worship the goddesses in his throat and forehead, amidst the flickering movements of his tongue, within the interior of a woman's body.
Enveloped in white garments and with pure intentions, he proceeds by way of Brahma through the sequence of piercing the *liṅgas*.
Having drunk the divine nectar situated at the point of emission, flowing like a stream of milk,
one should then enter the *kula* once again after having consumed that *kulāmṛta*.
One should again go to the Ākula and offer [the offering] at the Dvādaśānta;
in the great thousand-spoked wheel (sahasrāra) is the Vāgbhava [bīja], which is like the full moon.
Then, having pierced the Brahma-knot and drunk [the nectar] with seven or eight streams,
one should cause it to enter from the uvula through the path of Brahma at the root of the palate.
Having filled the tongue with that Vidyā, which consists of the forms of the Mātṛkā letters—
having gone outside in the form of letters and appearing like a lamp upon the tip of the tongue.

One should contemplate the Great Vidyā, beginning with the syllable *Vāgbhava*, as having the form of a lamp, extending from the base up to the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*) and reaching the tip of the tongue.
Having raised the Vidyā from the Ādhāra through the hands, the feet, and likewise through the three channels,
one should lead Vāgīśī to the twelfth [center].
Taking hold of the twelve supports, one should break through that knot;
then, taking hold of the tip of the tongue, one should visualize it in the form of a lamp-flame.
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred thousand times there, one shall utterly burn away all evil;
then, having known all that is moving and stationary, one shall attain omniscience. (12–15)
By the power of breath control (prāṇāyāma), the perfection of recitation (japa) arises;
specifically, twenty-one thousand and six hundred [times].
Every day the living being conquers the supreme state consisting of the bliss of Brahman;
its birth is the commencement of recitation (japa), and its death is the offering thereof.
Even without formal recitation, there is constant recitation at all times.
Having understood recitation in this way, one should offer it to Gaṇeśa and the other deities. (12–18)
In this manner, for both the individual soul (jīvātman) and likewise for the supreme soul (paramātman), there are six hundred and six thousand [breaths] respectively. (12–19)
Then he should offer six thousand, then another thousand,
and again a thousand to the Guru in due order.
Upon this golden-colored foundation (ādhāra), one should contemplate the letters from 'va' to 'sa';
one should visualize them as possessing the brilliance of a mass of lightning within the maṇipūraka.
One should contemplate the letters from *ḍa* to *pha*, radiant with the luster of great sapphire;
one should contemplate the great fire of tawny color as being like the pericarp.
One should contemplate the letters from *ka* to *ṭha* struck by the fourth vowel;
then, upon the pure [element] of smoky color, one should place the vowels of red color.
Within the command, which has the luster of lightning, one should contemplate the two radiant syllables *ha* and *kṣa* upon a thousand-petaled lotus shining with the brilliance of camphor. (12.24)
Thereafter, one should contemplate that which is blue in nature at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
I shall now declare its fruit, as well as [the fruits] for the six cakras, in their proper order.
Through the practice of meditation on the *ādhāra*, the accomplishment of mantra arises.
Thereafter, for the sake of the knowledge of the *vidyā*, one should meditate upon the *nābhicakra*; within six months, the practitioner of mantra shall attain the knowledge of the body. (12.27)
Through the practice of meditation on the heart-lotus, a person becomes a knower of the three periods of time;
and through the practice of meditation on the throat, the perfection of the body arises. (12.28)

The great yogin, through the essence of the Sun, knows whatever occurs in the three worlds day after day; there is no doubt that the practitioner of mantra knows it throughout the three worlds. (12.29)
Through the union of Śiva and Candra, one becomes possessed of the power of speech like Śukra and Jña;
one should constantly practice the udāna breath for the purpose of paralyzing water. (12.30)
Through the practice of equanimity, the yogi is not burned even by fire;
thence, as a subtle great element, he can even rescue the subtle.
Through the practice of meditation on Kālikā, the practitioner shall possess the speed of thought;
by the power of knowledge of the body, he shall attain invisibility.
By the power of invisibility, one may enter the body of another;
becoming a master of the eightfold powers beginning with atomization (aṇimā), one shall become a lord of ten million siddhis.

"Through the power of the great mantra, the yogi obtains that which is unobtainable. If such detachment arises toward these states of supernatural accomplishment (siddhi), [then one has truly understood]. (12.34)
The yogi attains liberation (kaivalya) and reaches the state of pervading Kālī.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (12.35)
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the definitive teaching on Kālīnityā.
Śrī Śiva said:
Kālī, Kapālinī, Kullā, Kurukullā, and Virodhinī. || 12-36 ||
Vipracittā, as well as Ugrograprabhā, Dīptā, or likewise Nīlā, Ghanā, Balākā, Mātrā, Mudrā, and Mitā. || 12-37 ||
O Śāmbhavī, listen now to this eternal maṇḍala and its sequence;
Kālīnityā and her mantra are now being described—listen.
Then one should utter the pair "Viṣabīja" and "Māyā Kālī";
having pronounced the word "Mahākālī," one should then utter the word "Kaumārī. (12.39)
"O Goddess, grant me the state; *ṭhaṭha*—this mantra is considered joined [with these syllables].
This nineteen-syllable vidyā is proclaimed as the Nityā Kālī. (12.40)
Parśurāma is declared to be the seer (ṛṣi), the Anuṣṭubh meter is proclaimed;
Kālikā is declared to be the deity, and Māyā is proclaimed as the seed-syllable (bīja). || 12-41 ||
The power (śakti) shall be Kālikā, and the pair of Ṭha-s shall be the pin (kīlaka);
this is proclaimed as the application for the purpose of pleasing Kālikā and so forth. (12.42)
O Goddess, one should perform the six-limbed practice through Māyā conjoined with the [appropriate] caste;
thereafter, O Maheśānī, one should meditate within the mandala of the extinction of the funeral pyre.
Dark-complexioned, most terrifying, with a dreadful roar and formidable, she is richly adorned with a garland of severed heads and brandishes a sword in her right hand. (12.44)
Holding a threatening gesture (tarjanī) in her left hand, she dances in the realms of the pretas;
having meditated thus, O Maheśānī, hear now that yantra, O Pārvatī. (12.45)
O Goddess of gods, [one should construct] two triangles, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and a square;
having worshipped Kālī in the *bindu*, one should then [worship her] again in the pair of triangles.
The three qualities (guṇas), those Puruṣas, and their powers (śaktis) are considered to follow in sequence;
likewise, the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī, and the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons. (12.47)
O Goddess, one should worship [the deities] within the Bhūpura with offerings of incense, lamps,
and various kinds of food, especially the five types of edible sweets.
One should offer [the oblation] to Kālikā; then she will become pleased.
Having performed the rites up to the waving of lights (nīrājanā), one should then recite the mantra for the measure of one hundred thousand times.
One should perform the fire oblation (homa) according to the prescribed rite with milk-rice (pāyasa) ten times [the number of recitations],
or alternatively, one may offer oblations with karavīra flowers for the sake of attaining all accomplishments.
O Goddess, he certainly becomes the lord of all accomplishments; of this there is no doubt.
I shall now declare the various types of mantras; listen attentively as they truly are.
O Great Goddess, the three names are each preceded by the syllable Om;
O Great Goddess, they constitute three mantras through the application of the three seed-syllables.
Furthermore, O Goddess, through the application of Dhruva and Māyā, there is a triad of Vidyās;
O Maheśānī, each of these three Vidyās consists of nine mantras.
One should not disclose this mantra to those who are unfortunate, the wretched, the cruel, or those who perform evil deeds; [only then] will one possess all sovereign powers.
One becomes possessed of fortune, renown, and merit; of this there is no doubt.
Upon seeing a beautiful woman, one should speak to her as follows: [12-55]
She indeed becomes agitated and will seek enjoyment according to her own will.
One should contemplate the Vidyā on the forehead, the heart, and the center of the womb, in due order, preceded by the recollection of its name. (12.57)
"He attracts her swiftly; what is the use of further talk?
He himself is Kālīputra manifest—there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Thus it has been spoken in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (12.59)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter, named Kālīnityā, in the third section of the Uttarabhāga of the Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja, in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā.
Chapter Thirteen.
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the supreme ritual of Kapālinī.
O Lord of Gods, the second eternal goddess (nityā) is declared to be the supreme Kapālinī. (13.1)
"O Maheśāna, tell me now her mantra.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O Queen of the Gods, that which is being told is secret, never before proclaimed anywhere."
Listen now to that second *mauṃ* of the *Kapālinī Mahāvidyā*:
first, having uttered the seven *kulas*, place the *kāma* (the syllable *klīṃ*) in the position of fire (*ra*). (13-3)
One should utter the seed-syllable (bīja) that has the form of Kālī, enriched with the ornament of the *indirā* dot, [addressing her] as "O Kapālinī, whose mind is fond of the great skull. (13.4)
"Give me the accomplishment of the skull, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this is the mantra ending in *svāhā*.
This king of mantras, consisting of thirty syllables augmented by half a syllable, is most excellent. (13.5)
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Triṣṭubh is cited as the meter (chandas), Kapālinī is the deity here, and Kālikā is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja). || 13-6 ||
Svāhā is declared to be Śakti; Hūṃ Phaṭ is said to be the Kīlaka. The application (viniyoga) here is proclaimed for the sake of attaining Kapālinī. || 13-7 ||
One should perform the six limbs in sequence using the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels;
one should meditate on her who has the luster of a mass of collyrium and possesses a pair of full, swelling breasts.
She has a face like the moon, lips like the bimba fruit, loose hair, and is naked;
she is surrounded by four severed heads and adorned with conch-shell bracelets.
Holding a sword, a trident, the gesture of granting boons, and the gesture of fearlessness in her four hands respectively, the goddess is devoted to song and laughter.
O Goddess, one should thus meditate upon the supreme Nityā Kapālinī:
[a mandala consisting of] three triangles, a circle, and adorned with eight petals. (13.11)
This Yantra of the goddess Kapālinī, adorned with a Bhūpura and graced by four gates, bestows universal sovereignty. (13-12)
Likewise, one should worship Mahākālī, Mahālakṣmī, and Mahāsarasvatī,
as well as Rati, Prīti, and Kānti, in the second triangle.

In the third triangle, one should worship Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā); in the center, having worshipped Kapālinī, one performs the worship of the Mātṛkās upon the eight petals. (13–14)
Then, devoted to the Kula tradition, one should worship the eight Bhairavas, the lords of the directions, and their weapons with the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra).
The practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with *hayāri* flowers;
for the sake of attaining his desired goal, he should also offer oblations of meat and honey.
Then the goddess Kapālinī certainly becomes perfected;
O Goddess, how could Kapālinī be perfected without the preliminary rite (puraścaryā)? (13–17)
A man, remaining on a seat made of matted hair with his mind always fixed upon that [deity],
[should worship] the great garland, the great vessel, the great yantra, the seat, and so forth.
Having performed this according to the rules, O Goddess, one then becomes a practitioner (sādhaka).
Now I shall speak further of the prowess of Kapālinī.
O Maheśānī, having collected five skulls from battle heroes on a Tuesday at the beginning of the night, one should be provided with all five.

Having become accompanied by the practitioner, marked with a vermilion tilaka, and having performed the binding of the directions, the purification of the elements, and so forth, along with offerings to the skull-bearers and others; || 13-21 ||
With sword in hand, clothed in the directions, with disheveled hair and filled with joy—such is that practitioner, endowed with a sense of self-conceit. || 13-22 ||
Having placed the practitioners at a great distance, O Goddess, one should kindle a lamp with a wick soaked in ghee and recite the mantra of Kapālinī there.
By good fortune, the siddhi of Kapālinī may perhaps prevail; nevertheless, it will surely come to pass for one who is a devotee of Kālikā. (13-24)
If, by the turn of fortune, a skull is ever obtained, then the accomplishment of the Skull-Bearer (Kapālinī) is achieved; for one should indeed collect that which is blazing. (13.25)
Having placed that glowing substance upon the skull, one should indeed recite the mantra;
this is proclaimed as the great ointment known as *saṃmohanāñjana*. (13.26)
O Maheśānī, what is there that is not held in her hand within that skull?
This eternal Kapālinī is the second Kālikā. (13.27)
Thus has it been briefly explained; now hear of Kullā, the third.
She who is known by three names—Kālikā, Kullukā, and Kullā—is considered to be threefold. (13–28)
Therefore, she is known by the name Kullā because she has attained the state of being honored by the family;
and because she is honored by the family of the sciences (vidyās), she is celebrated as Kullukā. || 13-29 ||
(104) Because she is worthy of worship by the *kula*, the Mistress of the *kula* is named Kullā;
I shall proclaim her mantra—listen attentively to it as it truly is. (13.30)
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable of Kālikā;
"Kullāyai" is the heart-mantra, O Goddess, this seven-syllabled mantra has been proclaimed. (13.31)
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is said to be its meter (chandas), Kullākālī is the deity here, and Kālikā is said to be the seed-syllable (bīja). || 13-32 ||
The one known as Kullāśakti is declared to be the *kīlaka* (the pinning nail);
its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the accomplishment of all aims. || 13.33 ||
One should worship the Kummārī-yanttra itself on the seat (pīṭha) as spoken by Kālikā;
O Goddess, by worshipping the Kumārī, Kullā will certainly become perfected (siddhā). || 13-34 ||

One who desires the vision of Śrī Kullā should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times, eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) during the day while remaining pure, and likewise at night while remaining impure. (13.35)
Sometimes resembling a cloud, sometimes like a celestial light,
she has four arms and three eyes, and is adorned with an elaborate crown.
One should visualize Kullā seated upon a corpse, positioned above ten mandalas;
her left hands display the gestures of boon-granting and fearlessness, while her right hands hold a book and a rosary.
One should contemplate Kullāmbā, who is skilled in various amorous graces;
for him who contemplates thus, there arises the digit consisting of the ten vidyās.
O Maheśānī, by the power of Kullāmbā, this indeed comes to pass;
one should perform the oblation with oleanders and hibiscus flowers in the tenth part of the number of recitations.
One should satisfy it with fragrant waters in the tenth part of that amount, and likewise perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana).
O Goddess, at the conclusion of that, one should feed Brāhmaṇas and a young maiden.
One should worship [her], O Supreme Goddess; the Kullā-vidyā becomes perfected.
O Great Goddess, the Kullā-vidyā is the illuminator of all vidyās. (13.41)
O Goddess of the Gods, for this [rite], there is a yantra for occasional or optional rites:
having drawn two triangles, it is adorned with a circle and eight petals. (13.42)
Equipped with four gates and joined with a single enclosure of earth (bhūpura),
one should place in the center the most excellent seed-syllable of Kālī, conjoined with her seed-mantra.
One should worship Dhṛti, Puṣṭi, Medhā, Tuṣṭi, Prajñā, and Jayā within the two triangles; then, on the petals, the eight Mātṛkās and Bhairavas.
One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) equipped with weapons in the Kullukā enclosure;
or else, O Goddess of the gods, [one may worship] everything as in the case of Kālikā.
On the two Navarātras, during the two eclipses of the moon and the sun, at the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti), and on other excellent occasions, one should worship the extraordinary yantra. (13.46)
At the very moment the ritual task arises, one must perform the worship of Kullukā;
without the worship of Kullukā, the Vidyā does not attain success.
That vidyā which is joined with the first and the last shall attain success;
for a guru who does not know the first and the last is indeed a destroyer of his disciples.
Indeed, a mantra is perfected when it is endowed with its beginning and end;
for one who is devoid of the beginning and end, there shall be no vision of the deity.
The world is pervaded by these two: pleasure and fear. This application is to be understood from the context; it has not been stated by me anywhere else. (13.50)
In the case of the Kullādevī and Ādinityā mantras, the recitation (japa) is indeed limited to two [repetitions].
If that mantra is not mastered through these two, it is not fit for recitation.

Kullā is declared to be eternal as the third [power], in whom this entire essence of the world is established; thus has the abbreviated worship of Kullā been briefly explained. What else do you wish to hear? (13.52)

Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Kullānityā," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 13 ||
The Fourteenth Chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear another great secret."
And now, tell me the ritual procedure for Kurukullā.
Who is Kurukullā by name, what is her nature, and what is her mantra?
O Lord of Gods, tell me all this, if I am dear to you. (14.2)
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which is the most secret of secrets;
because it is the object of worship for the Kula among all sciences (*vidyās*), Kullukā is superior to Kullukā. (14–3)
Because Kullā is also worthy of worship, Kurukullā brings great prosperity;
O Great Goddess, her mantra is the most excellent among all mantras. (14.4)
Having extracted the *kālikārcam*, one should utter the word *kurukulle*;
then [the words] *kālīm*, *māyām*, *mama*, and *sarvajana*. (14.5)
Having uttered "vaśamānaya," and then "Kālī" and "Kurukullā," O Goddess of Gods, the mantra ends with "māyā svāhā" after lifting up the word "pada. (14.6)
This mantra, consisting of twenty-seven syllables, is the celestial wish-fulfilling tree;
O Goddess, its heart-mantra is the nine-syllabled Kurukullā.
O Maheśvarī, O Queen of the Gods, Kurukullā is distinct from the Śrīvidyā;
O Goddess, Kālī is a limb of the Vidyā, while Śrīvidyā is Kurukullikā. (14.8)
This is the divided Mahāvidyā, Kālīnityā, the fourth;
O Goddess, without the heart-mantra, Kurukullā is not accomplished. (14.9)
O Pārvatī, having learned the heart-mantra of Kurukullā with diligence, one should utter the syllable *praṇava*, extract the *kūrca* mantra, and then speak the word "Kurukulle. (14.10)
O Goddess, the mantra of Kurukullā Kumārikā ends with *hrīḥ* and *svāhā*;
it is declared as the heart-mantra (*hṛnmanu*), the most excellent among all mantras. (14.11)
Kālabhairava is its seer (ṛṣi), Bṛhatī is declared to be its meter (chandas), and the deity is Kurukullā, the supreme one who consists of all vidyās. (14.12)
*Krī* is the seed-syllable, *hrīḥ* is likewise the power (*śakti*), and *svāhā* is declared to be the pin (*kīlaka*). Bhairava is declared to be the seer (*ṛṣi*) of Kurukullā Kumārī. (14.13)

The Virāṭ meter is declared [for this mantra], the syllable *kūrca* (hum) is proclaimed as the seed-syllable (*bīja*), and *svāhā* is specified as the power (*śakti*); the application (*viniyoga*) is according to one's desire. || 14-14 ||
Kullakullā, Mitrakullā, Kurukullā, and Hṛdaṅgamā; Kālī, Dhruva, Kurukullā, Krīṃ, and Hrīṃ—[protect] me from all sides. (14–15)
*Janavaśaṃ krī*, *kuruyuk*, *kurukulle*, *triviṣṭape*—this [mantra] is taught as ending with *svāhā*; for it is indeed the Virāṭ Bhairava. (14–16)
The seed-syllable is *hrīṃ*, and likewise *svāhā* is the power (*śakti*); *krīṃ* is considered the peg (*kīlaka*).
Its application (*viniyoga*) for all purposes is proclaimed to be as before. (14–17)
The application (viniyoga) shall be as before; listen now to the arrangement of the limbs and so forth.
One should perform the six limbs in sequence by means of the six long vowels combined with the seed-syllable (Kālī-bīja). 14–18.
Then one should meditate upon the Great Wisdom Goddess Kurukullā, the Mistress of the Family,
seated upon a corpse and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a skull and a chopper in her hands, bearing a sword and a shield,
resembling a mountain of collyrium, divine, with loose hair, and possessing four arms.
She possesses a pair of full and elevated breasts, a broad chest, and shapely hips;
she is intent on bestowing bliss upon her devotees and grants the desires of spiritual practitioners.
One should thus meditate upon the goddess Kurukullā, who brings great prosperity, a passionate woman who intoxicates people, her eyes rolling from the influence of the *āsava* liquor. (14-22)
Having meditated thus, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while offering the three sweets;
O Dear One, one should also perform the fire-oblation with bilva leaves and bilva flowers.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part [of the recitations], and the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with a tenth part of that;
the feeding of Brahmins should be a tenth part of that, by which the mantra becomes perfected.
One should worship in the seat of Kālikā, which is radiant with three triangles,
enriched with the ornaments of a circle and an eight-petaled lotus, and beautified by two enclosures of squares.
One should write the seed-syllable (*bīja*) within the *bindu* and worship the triad of the three powers of Kālī:
Kālī, Tārā, Chinnamastā, Bālāmbā, Bagalā, and Ramā.
The worship of Ugragarbhā, Ugrabījā, and Ugravīryā—the third—is proclaimed to be performed in sequence within the three triangles. (14.27)
O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the eight Bhairavas, beginning with Brahmā, within the eight petals;
then one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas), ending with their weapons.
One should worship Kurukullā in a cemetery, a cremation ground, a forest, or a wilderness teeming with spirits; he attains all accomplishments.
Whatever the practitioner desires in his heart, that he shall obtain;
O Goddess, he should honor all the Brahmins and the married women.
By the mere propitiation of Brahmins, what is there that does not come into one's hand?
Through rice, victory is attained; through wheat, the arrival of wealth. (14-31)
By means of black gram (māṣa), the enemy meets his death; by means of mung beans (mudga), one obtains the fruit of liberation;
and by the oblation of sesame seeds and rice, he attains great joy.
By means of an oblation of *rājī* and salt, one will certainly attract a woman of desire;
O Goddess, with mustard seeds and salt, there is the shattering of a woman's pride. (14.33)
By an oblation of ghee and salt, one pleases the hearts of women;
by means of turmeric, poverty is surely destroyed—of this there is no doubt. (14.34)
Thus has the definitive teaching on Kurukullā been briefly proclaimed;
it is a most profound secret. What more do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
"Tell me the ritual for Virodhinī, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
Indeed, the Nityā Virodhinī is said to be more strictly secret than even the most profound secrets.
Understand correctly that the one designated as the fifth is eternal;
having first extracted the *praṇava*, one should then extract the *kālī-praṇava*.
Then, having uttered *māyā*, *kāma*, and *kūrca*, one should state the word *virodhinī*;
then the word *śatrūnuccāṭaya*, and one should speak the pair *virodhaya*. (14.38)
The mantra ending with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, proclaimed as the destroyer of enemies, consists of thirty-two syllables; it is the supreme king of mantras. (14.39)
This is declared to be the great mantra; the seer is said to be Bhairava.
Gāyatrī is prescribed as the meter, and Virodhinī is the deity. (14.40)
The seed-syllable of Kālī is her seed; Māyā is proclaimed as her power (śakti).
The seed-syllable of Kāma shall be the pin (kīlaka); the application (viniyoga) is according to one's desire. (14.41)
One should perform the pair of six-limbed rites with the seed-syllables of Kālī and the six long vowels;
one should meditate upon her, resembling Mount Añjana, appearing as a young woman of sixteen years.
She has a pair of full and elevated breasts, is adorned with garlands of snakes and bones,
possesses four arms and three eyes, and stands upon a corpse-lotus.
The Great Goddess holds a three-pronged trident, a serpent-noose, a bell, and likewise a hand-drum, in her four arms respectively.
"Clad in smoky-colored garments, with a yellow body and a slightly smiling face, [he said]:
'Do not fear, O hero! Choose a boon; I shall grant you everything.'"
