"Whatever task has presented itself, that very task I shall perform.
To the goddess, who was speaking thus, with her beautiful smile and captivating form, [he spoke].
One should worship her, who is intent on creating opposition and brings about the destruction of enemies,
upon the pedestal described for Kālikā, which is adorned with three triangles.

In [the maṇḍala] enriched with the ornament of a circular eight-petaled lotus, beautified by a single outer city-wall (bhūpura), adorned with four gates, and possessing a pericarp radiant with the seed-syllable Śrī; 14.48.
In the pericarp, within the three triangles, one should place in sequence the goddesses Virodhinī,
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvālinī, Jvālinī, and Visphuliṅginī.
Then one should worship Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and Havyavahā;
thereafter, one should indeed worship the tenth [deity], Virodhinī, upon her head.
On the eight petals are the eight Bhairavīs accompanied by Bhairava;
on the outer square (bhūpura) are the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons outside of that.
Then, having performed the *nīrājana* rite, one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations into the fire with *nimba* wood ten times the number of recitations, according to the prescribed rule.
Having fashioned a garland of *ariṣṭa* fruits, a man seated upon a great skull-throne should diligently offer *ariṣṭa* fruit as an oblation for the destruction of his enemies.
One should offer oblations with *vibhītaka* seeds for the destruction of all enemies;
by offering oblations with *dhattūra* flowers, a person causes enmity among his enemies. (14.54)
With the flesh of a crow and an owl, one kills an enemy in an instant;
the wise man should perform the oblation with the flowers of the rājavṛkṣa tree in a fire of its wood.
When conjoined with Dhūmāvatī and others, she becomes an accomplished one who creates opposition;
when joined with Arkā and others, she causes hatred toward enemies. (14.56)
Facing the northwest, O Maheśānī, one should drink slightly warm water prepared from pungent cumin; the enemy shall become afflicted with fever.

For the purpose of destroying the malevolent magic of others and for one's own protection, according to the prescribed rule, [one should perform it] in a solitary place, in the house of a mother, at a cemetery, or in a temple of Śiva. (14.58)
One should recite the hostile vidyā ten thousand times according to the prescribed method;
one should offer oblations of *vibhītaka* wood for the warding off of enemies.
Having gone into water reaching up to the navel, through the union of the rays and the water,
one should satisfy the deities with water and perform the Trailokyadveṣaṇa rite.
Then, desiring to perform the rite of attraction (ākarṣaṇa), one should bring earth from an anthill;
having taken earth from a cremation ground, along with wheat, asafoetida, and cumin.
O Supreme Goddess, one should have an effigy fashioned in the form of the person to be acted upon (sādhya),
and having placed a cord upon its nose, preceded by the rite of installing the vital breaths (prāṇapratiṣṭhā).
One should mutter the hostile mantra there and worship with *karavīra* flowers;
having fashioned an effigy (*puttalī*) from milk, one should heat it in a fire of *khadira* wood.
By this sequential method for fourteen days,
the excellent man who performs it becomes a bringer of all things into his power.
Through yoga, he draws toward himself a woman full of intoxicating pride;
having reflected upon this drawing-in, one must consider whether it will come to pass or not. (14.65)
Having meditated on a noose at the throat of the target and a blazing goad upon his head—by contemplating in this way, O Goddess of Gods, one becomes an attractor of the three worlds.
Thus has it been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual for Virodhinī," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 14.
The Fifteenth Chapter.
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the ritual procedure for Vipracitta."
Speak, O Mahādeva, if I am dear to you.
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess of gods, even this secret is being told out of affection for you;
formerly, I was intent upon the slaying of the extremely wicked Vipracitti.
Known as Vipracitti, she is the destroyer of Vaipracitta;
she is the sixth eternal Great Vidyā. O Pārvatī, hear now her mantra. (15.3)
One should utter the Praṇava, the word Kamalā, and Kāma; then one should utter the word Cāmuṇḍe, and having pronounced the word Vipracitte, one should utter Duṣṭaghātini. (15.4)
Having uttered "Destroy my enemies" until this day, O Beloved, and having uttered "Grant me success," the mantra ends with *huṃ phaṭ svāhā*. (15.5)
The great mantra of Vipracitta consists of thirty-four syllables;
its seer is Īśvara, O Goddess, and its meter is declared to be Jagatī.
Vipracittā is indeed the deity, Cāmuṇḍā is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja), Kamalā is called the power (śakti), and the Kāma-bīja is the pin (kīlaka). || 15-7 ||
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) with the desire enriched by the six long vowels. [She is] mounted upon a lion, situated in the midst of a corpse-skeleton.
Four-armed, with three eyes, possessing full and elevated breasts, naked, with disheveled hair, with a lolling tongue, and terrifying. || 15-9 ||
She has fearsome fangs and a gaping mouth, with blood flowing from the corners of her lips;
she holds a sword, a severed head, a skull-cup, and a trident in her hands, and possesses a massive belly.
She resembles a blue lotus, is dark-complexioned, bestows grace upon her devotees,
is intent on the destruction of the Daityas, and grants fearlessness to practitioners.

Having reflected thus, O Goddess of the gods, one should recite the mantra of Vipracitti, the beloved of Śiva, one hundred thousand times; one should then perform the oblation with white water-lilies (kumuda) ten times the number of recitations.
p. 112) Then, one should perform libation with water scented by eight fragrances in a tenth part [of the number of recitations];
sprinkling in a tenth part of that; and consecration in a tenth part of that. (15.13)
One-tenth of that [number] should be used for feeding Brahmins for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of the mental resolve;
[the mandala] should be triangular, circular, hexagonal, and adorned with a circle and eight petals.
[The mandala] is joined with a square and a circle, adorned with the seed-syllable and the *bindu*.
One should worship Vipracittā in the *bindu*, and one should worship Triguṇā in the triangle.
In the hexagon are the six limbs; on its petals are the Mothers and Bhairava;
in the outer square are the world-protectors and their weapons beyond that.
Then, having performed the lustration rite (nīrājana), one should offer the recitation (japa) to the Goddess.
One who is engaged in the preliminary service (puraścaryā) is fit for the ritual application (prayoga), and not otherwise.
O Goddess, the practitioner should offer oblations with *sākalya* flowers in rites for pacification;
he should offer with *mālatī* for subjugation, or with *ketakī* for the attainment of eloquence. (15–18)

With *karavīra* flowers, subjugation (*vaśīkāra*) is achieved; with *kiṃśuka* flowers, immobilization (*staṃbhanam*) occurs; enchantment (*mohanam*) is brought about by *uḍra* flowers; and with *dhattūra* flowers, one should prescribe killing (*māraṇam*). (15–19)
With *bṛhatī* there is the eradication of enemies; with *girikarṇī*, the acquisition of wealth;
with *kāśa* flowers, the eradication of enemies; and with those born from *karṇikāra*, the inciting of enmity.
O Goddess, one should indeed offer oblations with wild rice (nīvāra) for the sake of attaining success in grain;
thereafter, one should offer oblations with pea-flowers (kalāya), and from that all prosperities shall arise.
O Goddess, by offering kusumbha flowers one shall obtain a desired woman;
and by offering madhūka flowers, one will certainly achieve one's desired goal. (15–22)
O Goddess, by offering oblations with *dhātakī*, one becomes a lord of wealth and grain;
whatever medicine exists for a particular disease, that [oblation] effects the destruction of that disease. (15.23)
Thus, the definitive exposition concerning Vipracitta has been briefly proclaimed.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the definitive exposition concerning the Ugrānityās. (15–24)
Śrī Śiva said:
Although it is a most profound secret, it shall nevertheless be told; listen.
[The mantra consists of] the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of the bride (Vadhū-bīja), the seed-syllable HŪṂ, and then Bhuvanā. (15–25)
Again, preceded by *pūrvaṃ*, then *hūṃ phaṭ*—this is the seven-syllable mantra of Ugrā.
Bhairava is declared its seer (*ṛṣi*), and the Bṛhatī meter is proclaimed for it. (15–26)
The seventh [mantra] is proclaimed as the eternal deity Ugrā;
the seed-syllable *kūrca* (*hum*), *phaṭ* is the power (*śakti*), and *vadhū* is said to be the pin (*kīlaka*). (15.27)

The application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the sake of attaining all desired objects and so forth; the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) is performed with the seed-syllable known as Māyā, enriched by the six long vowels.
Then one should meditate upon the supreme and fierce goddess, standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture,
four-armed, three-eyed, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Naked, with a terrifying mouth and fearsome fangs, she was formidable;
sporting upon the lap of a corpse, she dwelt in her abode within the cremation ground.
Dark-complexioned, with loose hair, holding a sword and a blue lotus,
with a skull-cup and a flaying knife in her hands, she is intent upon the granting of boons.
One should meditate upon the fierce Mahāvidyā and perform the recitation of it two hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations with lotuses mixed with ghee in the tenth part of that number.

One-tenth of that is the libation (tarpaṇa), one-tenth of that is the sprinkling (mārjana), and one-tenth of that is the feeding of Brahmins; by this, the fierce [mantra] will certainly grant success.

One who is performing the preparatory rite (puraścaraṇa) should reside on a mountain, in a desolate wilderness, in a formidable forest, on the bank of a river, at a solitary linga, or in a cremation ground. || 15-34 ||
Now, listen as the worship diagram (pūjāyantra) for her is duly described:
it consists of a triangle, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and is adorned with a circle and a square enclosure.
One should draw the most excellent *kūrca* seed-syllable in the center of a triangle, which is either adorned with eight tridents or embellished with vajras. (15.36)
One should worship Tārā, who is blue and has a single tuft of hair, within that triangle;
thereafter, O Goddess, one should worship the eight Ugrāghoras upon the eight petals.
Having worshipped the eight Vairocanas, one should then worship the Padmāntakas;
one should worship the world-protectors and their weapons according to the prescribed ritual rule.

Then, having performed the lustration rite (nīrājana) and offered the recitation (japa) to the Goddess, one should always perform the recitation while remaining seated upon a corpse or [another seat]. || 15-39 ||
Always bearing a tilaka of vermilion, intoxicated by the bliss of consciousness (saṃvit),
with disheveled hair and the quarters as his garment, he is devoted to his devotees and has conquered his senses.
O Supreme Goddess, having prepared a great Chinese tree and creeper,
and having gazed upon that triangle, one should always keep the mind fixed upon it.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times; Ugrā will certainly be accomplished.
O Sovereign of the World, everything else is proclaimed to be like that of Tārā. (15.42)

The rites of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), worship, meditation, and the performance of the preliminary service (*puraścaryā*) should be understood to be the same as those for Mahogratārā. What more do you wish to hear?
The Śrī Devī said: O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear about the eighth Nityā named Ugraprabhā, who is auspicious, eternal, the bestower of constant bliss, and most excellent. (15.44)
Śrī Śiva said:

Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should extract the seed-syllable of Śiva, mounted upon fire (the letter *ra*), adorned with the nasal sound (*nāda*), the dot (*bindu*), and the sixth vowel (*ū*). (15.45)
Having uttered the two seed-syllables, [one says]: "O Goddess Kālī, Great Goddess, show your true form, O Ugraprabheśvarūpaka! (15.46)
The mantra of Ugraprabhā is said to be joined with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*;
the mantra of Ugrābhā is said to be enriched with twenty-five *tattvas*. (15.47)
The sage is declared to be Mahākāla; the meter is proclaimed to be Triṣṭubh;
and the deity is celebrated as Ugraprabhā-Mahākālī. (15.48)
HŪM is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja), OṂ likewise the power (śakti), and PHAṬ the pin (kīlaka).
Its application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the purpose of beholding Kālikā and other such goals. || 15-49 ||
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) with the seed-syllable named Ugraprabhā and its six long vowels;
one should meditate upon the divine Ugraprabhā, who possesses the luster of a celestial blue lotus.
Four-armed, with three eyes, seated upon a corpse-lotus, naked, with disheveled hair, and possessing full, elevated breasts. (15.51)
Her lotus-face was exceedingly serene; she fed upon the flesh of corpses;
she wore a girdle fashioned from the gathered hands of dead bodies; and her face was smiling.
Holding a sword and a severed head in her left hands, and a skull-cup and a chopper in her right,
she generates supreme bliss and deceives Death.
Having meditated thus upon the Great Vidyā, O Śivā, one should recite it two hundred thousand times;
one should worship her on the pedestal described by Kālī, which is radiant with two triangles.
In [a maṇḍala] richly adorned with a circle and eight petals, embellished by two outer enclosures of earth,
and containing a lunar disc of fierce radiance, one should worship Kālī, Tārā, and Rocanī.
In the first [triangle] one should worship the Goddess; in the second, the hosts of Tāriṇīs—namely Tārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlā—in the second triangle. (15.56)

On the eight petals are the eight Mātṛkās, and at the tips of the petals is the group of eight Bhairavas; in the outer enclosure (bhūpura) are the world-protectors (lokapālas), and outside of that, their weapons.
The teachers should perform the worship three times for each [deity];
thus, one should perform the recitation of the beloved Ugraprabhā two hundred thousand times.
One should offer as a fire-oblation (homa) one-tenth of that amount of *vajra* flowers soaked in *maireya* wine;
then, one should satisfy [the deity] with one-tenth of that amount of milk or honey.
Furthermore, one may perform the sprinkling with curd, sugarcane juice, or even water from the footstool;
the cleansing (mārjana) is one-tenth of that [number], and the feeding of Brahmins is one-tenth of that.
Thereafter, one should worship the maiden and also worship the Śakti;
having fashioned an image upon the banner of Ugraprabhā, one should maintain it. (15.61)
Having conquered the gods and asuras in battle, one shall become a conqueror of the three worlds;
for by reciting the mantra of the fierce and radiant Śivā over a drum, a shield, or a sword, [these same results are attained]. 15.62
Having attained all accomplishments, a man shall become the very form of Kālī;
having beheld the Maṇḍala of Māninī, he should recite the mantra of Ugraprabhā.
Kālikā shall become the bestower of success; there is no need for deliberation on this point. O Goddess of the Gods, what may the practitioner not accomplish by contemplating her there?
O Śivā, having partaken of meat, one should recite the mantra of Kālī known as Ugraprabhā.
By practicing for only one month, Kālikā becomes a bestower of boons.
Thus it has been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Ugraprabhā Nityā," in the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā, within the third section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*. 15.
The sixteenth chapter. The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Tell me that, O Lord of Gods: the ritual procedure for Dīptānityā.
Śīśiva said: In the ancient tantras, the radiant Nityā of great exaltation is well-guarded; she is the ninth in number, the essence of essences, and of great exaltation. (16–2)
I shall proclaim the mantra for that [practice]; listen attentively as it is correctly explained:
the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālīkā, and likewise the seed-syllable of Kaulinī. (16.3)

Having extracted the seed-syllable of the *kūrca* mantra, immediately thereafter, one should utter the word "dāya" after pronouncing "to Dīptā," followed by the phrase "bestower of the fruit of all mantras. (16.4)
The supreme mantra ending in *huṃ phaṭ svāhā* consists of nineteen syllables;
by subtracting half that number, it is proclaimed to have ten syllables. (16.5)
Mahādeva is proclaimed as its seer (ṛṣi), Uṣṇik is celebrated as its meter (chanda), and the ninth eternal goddess (nityā) named Dīptā is proclaimed as its deity. || 16-6 ||
The seed-syllable of Kālī is her seed; indeed, she is the power (śakti) Kaulinī herself.
"Svāhā" is said to be the *kīlaka*, for its application is for the sake of Kālī. (16–7)
At dawn, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) joined with the six long vowels;
one should meditate upon the goddess Mahodarī, blazing like a great sapphire gem.
Four-armed, three-eyed, adorned with a garland of severed heads, naked, with disheveled hair, possessing terrible fangs, and formidable in appearance. || 16-9 ||
Seated upon a corpse-lotus, with full and elevated breasts, she is adorned with bracelets and conch-shell bangles fashioned from the bones of corpses. || 16.10 ||
Licking a corpse somewhere, laughing, and intoxicated with passion;
the eternal bestower of boons to her devotees, who causes the darkness of the Kali age to shine away.
Adorned with a girdle of human entrails, she follows the path of yoga;
holding a sword and a severed head in her left hands, she bestows fearlessness and the boon of grace with her right hands.

Having thus meditated upon the Mother who is brilliantly radiant, with beautiful teeth, most fierce, and dwelling in the cremation ground, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, O Śivā.
One should perform the fire-oblation with *karavīra* flowers ten times the [number of] portions;
the oblation should be performed with *kadalī* for the sake of attaining all splendor. (16.14)
One should perform the oblation (havana) with the water from the pedestal using a tenth part [of the previous amount];
and the sprinkling (mārjana) with the water of the eightfold scents (gandhāṣṭaka) using a tenth part of that.
One should feed Brahmins and indeed feed a young maiden with a tenth part of that;
then the practitioner, having mastered the mantra, becomes fit for its application, and not otherwise.

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and preceded by the remembrance of the Guru, one should meditate upon the Guru in the *sahasrāra* according to the previously described method of meditation. (16–17)
One should meditate upon the supreme Root-Vidyā from the Mūlādhāra to the tip of one’s own tongue—
Sarasvatī in the form of a lamp, whose nature is that of the Root-Syllable.
Having recited the complete Mātṛkā, one should utter the root-mantra (mūlavidyā); having again recited the Mātṛkā, one should once more utter the mantra. || 16–19 ||
O beautiful one, having consecrated the water three times with this sequence,
one should then meditate upon the root-mantra as being in the form of a lamp upon the tongue.
O Śivā, O Mistress of the Gods, one should drink that water which has taken the form of radiant energy and is accompanied by weapons;
by this yoga, a man shall become a knower of the three periods of time. (16–21)
O Śivā, even without ritual placements (nyāsa), without meditations (dhyāna), and without recitation and the like,
the fourfold scholarship is established in his hand.
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of the *jātī* flower, poetic skill becomes submissive;
O Goddess of the Gods, by means of the *kunda* flower, there is mastery over all scriptures. (16–23)
A *śāntika* (pacifying) homa is performed with *dūrvā* grass; the warding off of death is accomplished with *guḍūcī*.
Intoxication is said to be produced with wine, and immobilization is declared to be achieved with the *jambū* fruit. (16–24)
Through mango one attains the power of subjugation; through lotus, great prosperity;
through dried cow dung, eradication; and through the fruits of the karkkaṭī, inciting enmity. (16–25)
One who has mastered the mantra should perform all such rites as killing with a blue flower, or attracting with *marīca*. (16–26)
Collyrium, pills, the sword, alchemy, elixirs, the sacrificial pap, the forehead mark, the garment, the drum, and the skull-cup. (16–27)
In this way, the accomplishment of such rites will indeed occur through the blazing mantra.
Thus has it been taught in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (16–28)
The Śrī Devī said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the ritual procedure for the Nīlā-vidyā;
for Nīlā is indeed blue in nature, the Great Nīla-Sarasvatī. (16–29)
"If I am dear to you, tell me the ritual procedure for it.
Śrī Śiva said:
"O wise one, listen to the extraction of the mantra, by which one attains perfection. (16–30)
O Great Goddess, having extracted the pair of *kūrca* mantras, likewise the two *kālī* seed-syllables, and the two *māyā* syllables, [one obtains] the essential form *hasabalamarī*. (16-31)
Now, O Maheśvarī, the mantra Nīlapatākā begins with "Nīla" and ends with "huṃ phaṭ.
This supreme Nīlapatākā bestows all supernatural accomplishments (siddhis).
Ugracaṇḍā, Lalajjihvā, and she who is Siddhikarālikā—these are declared to be the five blue ones, along with Mahānīlapatākikā. (16.33)
Bhairava is declared to be its seer (ṛṣi), the Bṛhatī meter is said to be its meter (chandas), and the deity is the tenth Nityā, Mahānīlapatākikā. || 16-34 ||
Indeed, the nature of the *kūrca* seed-syllable is designated as *śakti*;
and *hūṃ phaṭ*, O auspicious lady, is the *kīlaka*, which is to be employed for the purpose of Kālī. (16.35)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) using the seed-syllables of Kālī and the six long vowels.
Then, one should meditate upon Mahānīlā, who has the luster of a mountain of black collyrium.
She has four arms and three eyes, is adorned with a garland of severed heads,
sits upon a corpse, and her eyes are rolling from intoxication.
She has eyes like those of a young fawn, a serene lotus-like face,
is adorned with a girdle of small bells, and wears human ears as her ear-ornaments.
With a lolling tongue, a gaping mouth, and terrifying fangs, she was fearsome;
she was always dark-blue to sinners, cruel, yet most excellent to those possessing merit.
She is intent on destroying the wicked, bestowing boons upon the practitioner,
and making the four quarters resound with the cries of packs of jackals and flocks of vultures.

O Goddess, one who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should mutter three hundred thousand times this mantra, which begins with such a form and possesses the luster of a grove of blue lotuses.
According to the sequence of family tradition and by means of the application of the prescribed order,
[one should offer] karavīra, javā, bilva, mallikā, and other flowers, combined with ghee.
One should perform the oblation in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) on a well-prepared ground;
a libation (tarpaṇa) consisting of ten parts should be performed with milk and also with wine. (16.43)
One should cleanse [the area] with red water and then feed the Brāhmaṇas,
as well as a married woman, a young girl, or three auspicious women according to one's capacity.
A mantra perfected through *puraścaraṇa* bestows all desired objects;
however, the *puraścaryā* for practitioners (*mantriṇām*) depends upon the available materials, such as those of kings and others. (16.45)
One who has completed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) is fit for the practical application (prayoga), and not otherwise.
I shall now describe her yantra, by means of which one becomes a master of supernatural powers (siddhi).
One should draw the *kūrca* mantra in the center of the *bindu*, and above that, a triangle;
then a circle, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, another circle, and a square enclosure (*bhūpura*).
The auspicious Yantra of Nīlāmbara is richly adorned with four gates;
at the four gates are Baṭuka and the other door-deities surrounding it.
And outside of that, on the eight petals, O Dear One, are the Bhairavas; on the filaments are the eight Mātṛkās, and in the circle, the eight Siddhis in sequence.
In the hexagon are the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), and in the triangle are the three deities;
in the triad [of the triangle], they are Kālarātri, Mahārātri, and Moharātri, in due order.
Having worshipped the Blue Goddess (Nīlā) in the center, one should then offer the food offering (naivedya);
then, having performed the lustration ceremony (nīrājana), and having praised and bowed, one should dismiss her. || 16-51 ||
Having diligently accomplished the blue [deity] and the host of thirty-six yakṣiṇīs— namely Kālī, Kūrcā, Vadhū, Māyā, and the yakṣiṇī named So-and-so— [one attains success].
O Dear One, these thirty-six yakṣiṇīs, preceded by the syllables *ante pīmāni* and followed by *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*, have been extracted in their proper sequence. (16.53)
In the same way, the powerful Yakṣas [are invoked] with "hūṃ krīṃ hūṃ prīṃ" and the *puṭa* mantra; all eighty-four Yakṣas are proclaimed to end with "huṃ phaṭ. || 16-54 ||
Having attained the siddhi of the yakṣiṇīs, the practitioner shall obtain happiness;
O Pārvatī, he becomes a king in this world even without a kingdom. (16.55)
He who treats one who is little-knowing as a scholar, and likewise a fool as a learned man, [treats] even the jewels and wealth of the kingdom in such a manner. (16.56)
He who indeed gives to a Sādhya is a Yakṣa; there is no doubt in this matter.
The womb of birth is proclaimed to be twofold: divine and human. || 16-57 ||
Having assumed each respective form, one attains that specific accomplishment (*siddhi*).
The Śrī Devī said: "What, however, is the fruit of the accomplishment of a Yakṣiṇī, and what is the fruit of the accomplishment of a Yakṣa? (16.58)
"Tell that to me, O Supreme One who has crossed over compassion; salutations be unto you!
Śrī Śiva said:
"The gold coin, the pill, the sword, the vampire, the sandals, and the collyrium. (16.59)
Elixir, rejuvenation, concealment, the tilaka-mark, invisibility, as well as the skull-cup, the cloth, the conch, the trident, and likewise the hand-drum (ḍamaru). || 16-60 ||
Attraction and subjugation, as well as delusion and expulsion, and likewise the great magic of Indra and the construction of illusions such as those of Indra and others. (16.61)
The supernatural powers such as Khecarī and others, including the practice of ascending upward and so forth—these must be kept secret, kept secret! What else do you wish to hear? (16.62)
The eternal one named Nīlā is proclaimed as the banner at the beginning of the Śrīvidyā and other [practices];
likewise, she effects the destruction of the confusion regarding the arrays of yantras, mantras, and other such conventions.

One should perform the practice according to the method stated for the *lopāmudrā* beginning with *ka*; that same method applies to the one beginning with *ha*. Both of these [methods] also apply to the *kāmarāja* [mantra]. (16.64)
At that time, Kādikālī and Hādikalpadruma [arose];
O Goddess, the circle of Yakṣiṇīs and Yakṣas was proclaimed at the beginning of the letter *ka*.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Dīptānityā," in the third section of the northern part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 16.
The seventeenth chapter.
The Holy Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear the worship according to the sequence of the Eternal Cloud (Ghanānityā)."
Rising like a dense cloud, having the form of a cloud, perpetually dense, and constantly arising. || 17-1 ||
O ocean of compassion, please tell me the daily mantra-worship of her who has the dense abode, who is resonant with sound, and whose form is the rising of the hour-glass (ghaṭikā). (17-2)
Śrī Śiva said:
Having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), and likewise the three syllables of Kālikā, followed by *ghanālaye ghanāghane*, the mantra is considered to be *hrīṃ hūṃ phaṭ*. (17.3)
This mantra, "bhuvanākṣaro ghanāyāḥ," is the celestial wish-fulfilling tree;
Aghorabhairava is its seer (ṛṣi), and Virāṭ is proclaimed as its meter (chandaḥ). || 17-4 ||
The seed-syllable of Kālī, as well as Māyā, Śakti, Huṃ, and Phaṭ, are the Kīlaka;
O Goddess, this is proclaimed as the application for the propitiation of Kālikā. (17.5)
One should perform the six-limbed ritual with camphor using the seed-syllable possessing the six long vowels;
[one should meditate on] Ghanānityā, the Great Vidyā, who resembles a dark blue cloud.
Her eyes possessed the luster of an intoxicated cuckoo and the radiance of a ripe jambu fruit;
her mass of hair hung down long over her extended forefeet, adorned with hanging strings of pearls.
Four-armed, three-eyed, delighting in nakedness, with a gaping mouth and terrible fangs, and full, elevated breasts. (17.8)
Her face was suffused with streams of blood trickling from the corners of her lips;
she possessed a terrifying form, adorned by the bracelets on the hands of heroes.
She should be constantly meditated upon by heroes as holding, in sequence, a sword, a shield, a battle-axe, and a mallet; she whose abode is the dense clouds of great heroes.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice with lotuses smeared with ghee;
O Dear One, the libation (tarpaṇa) should then be performed with scents, milk, and other substances for one-tenth of that number.
One-tenth of that amount should be performed as sprinkling with cool water,
and one-tenth of that should be offered as a meal for Brāhmaṇas.
Thus, joined with the ritual action, he attains the accomplishment of the mantra.
I shall now explain the dense machine (ghana-yantra) and what its mode of worship should be.
It consists of a hexagon, a circle, and an eight-petaled lotus, adorned with a square enclosure (bhūpura).
Within the hexagon are the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) and likewise the six deities.
On the eight petals are the eight Mātṛkās; thereafter follows the worship of Bhairava.
The world-protectors (lokapālas) are in the *bhūpura*, and their weapons are outside of that. (17.15)
Having recited the mantra according to one's capacity, one should then perform the lustration (nīrājana) of the Lord.
At the conclusion of the lustration, O Goddess of the Gods, having offered praise, bowed down, and performed the ritual dismissal (visarjana), [one should proceed].
Thus, in brief, has been described Ghanānityā, whose abode is dense and who is pervaded by the eight supernatural powers (siddhis). What more do you wish to hear?
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess of the gods, listen; I shall describe the procedure for the worship of Balākā.
Balākā-Dvādaśī is eternal and brings under her control all other eternal [observances].
O Maheśānī, listen now as the mantra of that [goddess] is being told—the knowledge of which causes all branches of learning to reach their respective proper places. (17–19)
One should extract the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, the Kūrca, and the Māyā; then Balākā, followed by the word "Kālī," O you of most wonderful prowess! (17–20)
"Grant me the fulfillment of my desired goal, hūṃ phaṭ svāhā"—this is considered the mantra.
Kālikā is its seed-syllable (bīja), and the "kūrca" sound is proclaimed as its power (śakti). (17–21)
Māyā is designated as the *kīlaka*; by means of the *kīlaka*, the six-limbed [mantra] is formed.
Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*), one should perform meditation, O Maheśvarī. (17–22)
Resembling collyrium and the infinite, with the radiance of ten million fires at the end of time,
four-armed, three-eyed, and dwelling in the fortress of the skull.
She is naked, with a terrifying face and full, elevated breasts;
she has fashioned a girdle from a collection of corpses and sits upon a corpse.
With disheveled hair, reeling with intoxication, her lotus-like face serene,
possessing a radiance equal to ten million suns, and adorned with a garland of severed heads.
Holding a sword and a severed head in her left hands, and bearing a skull-cup and a raised index finger in her right hands, she is Mahākālī, who assumes the form of a crane.
The goddess who dwells in the cremation ground, accompanied by bhūtas and pretas,
surrounded by jackals of terrible form, and uttering fearsome cries.
"Do not fear! Speak, O best of heroes, what is in your heart; I shall accomplish it for you.
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; the mantra will certainly become perfected. (17–28)
The wise one should offer oblations with ten parts of *bilva* leaves smeared with ghee;
he should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with a tenth part of that, and the sprinkling (*mārjana*) with a tenth part of that.
Feeding one-tenth of that number of Brahmins is prescribed;
by the mere propitiation of the Brahmins, the rite attains completeness in all its parts.
O Maheśānī, even if the foot-part is deficient, that [rite] becomes complete with limbs through the feeding of twice-born brahmins; all else one should perform just as in the Kālikā ritual. (17.31)
"Thus it has been briefly proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the secret beyond secrets."
"Now tell me the rule for the Mātrā-nityā.
Śrī Śiva said:
"The Mātrā-nityā which has been proclaimed is the most excellent among all the eternal [practices]. (17–33)
O Maheśānī, listen correctly to her mantra:
the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, Māyā, Kūrca, and the Mātṛkā.
The letters of the Mātṛkā with the bindu, then indeed the four seed-syllables; again the letters of the Mātṛkā, the four seed-syllables, and once more that same sequence.
Thus, O Maheśānī, the Mahāmātras are proclaimed as those who possess forbearance.
Grant me quickly the accomplishment of the four seeds within the Mahāmātra. (17.36)
"Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," O Goddess of the Gods, is considered the supreme mantra of the Mothers;
then, O Śivā, [follow] the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, the Kūrca, and Māyā. (17.37)
In the middle, one should give the name "Nityā" in the vocative case alone;
thus, O Pārvatī, the various forms of the Nityā-mantras are produced.
Furthermore, the seed-syllables are proclaimed to end with *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*;
they may be employed through initial conjunction, as encapsulated mantras (*saṃpuṭa*), or by placing *hūṃ phaṭ* at the end. || 17.39 ||
(124) Thus, there are ninety varieties of mantras for the Nityās. Bhairava is declared to be their seer (ṛṣi), and the Uṣṇih meter is proclaimed as their meter (chandas). || 17-40 ||
The deity is proclaimed as the one renowned as Mātrādevī;
*krīṃ* is the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *hūṃ* is likewise the power (*śakti*), and *hrīṃ* is declared to be the pin (*kīlaka*). (17.41)
The application (viniyoga) is proclaimed for the sake of the great goal and for the sake of Kālikā;
one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa) joined with Māyā and the six long vowels. (17.42)

In this manner, one should meditate upon the Great Wisdom (Mahāvidyā), who has the luster of a mountain of blue collyrium, possesses four arms and three eyes, and is seated upon a lotus atop a severed head. (17.43)
Holding a skull and a chopper in her hands, bearing a sword and a severed head, she is supreme, possessing prominent teeth, exceedingly fierce, with a violent roar, and most terrifying. (17.44)
Mounted upon the chest of a corpse, licking a corpse,
such was my mother Ambā, who uttered most terrible cries.
Having reflected thus, O Goddess of the gods, one should perform a recitation (japa) of exactly one hundred thousand times;
one should then offer oblations (homa) ten times that number with bilva fruits or plantain fruits.
One should perform the fire-oblation (havana) ten times the number [of recitations] using grapes or milk-rice (pāyasa);
one should diligently carry out the libation (tarpaṇa), the ritual sprinkling (mārjana), and the feeding of Brahmins. || 17-47 ||
If any limb [of the mantra] is omitted, the recitation (japa) must be performed twice that number of times;
the procedures for recitation, worship, and so forth are like those of Kālī, Vallī, and Mātṛ.
"Thus has it been briefly proclaimed; what else do you wish to hear?
The Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear that which is the most secret of secrets."
Śrī Śiva said:
O Goddess, even this secret is being told to you; listen now to the ritual procedure for the Mudrā Nityās, which is the most excellent among all essences.
The eternal one named Mudraṇī is indeed the Sealer (Mudriṇī) within Śrīvidyā;
the goddess named Daṇḍinī is the Sealer (Mudriṇī), whose form is beauty itself. (17.51)
She who effects the mental sealing of Mahāvidyā and the others is therefore called the Mudrā Nityā, the Supreme Mother of all accomplishments.
Having uttered the Praṇava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, Māyā, and Kūrca in sequence, and having pronounced the pair of seed-syllables Prīṃ and Phreṃ, one should extract the word "Mudrāmbā. (17.53)
"O you whose nature is the *bhojaga* mudrā, grant me the accomplishment of the mudrā!
HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ—this auspicious mantra consists of fifteen syllables. (17.54)
Mahādeva is its seer (ṛṣi), and Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chaṃdas);
the goddess Mudrānityā Mahādevī is proclaimed as the deity (devatā). || 17-55 ||
The seed-syllable of Kālī is her seed-mantra; Māyā is proclaimed as her power (śakti).
The "Kūrca" mantra is said to be the pin (kīlaka) of Kālī when joined with the six long vowels.

O Maheśvarī, having performed the six-limbed ritual placement (ṣaḍaṅganyāsa), one should meditate upon the Mudrā, who resembles a mountain of collyrium and is adorned with a garland of severed heads. (17.57)
She is naked, with terrible fangs, possessing a fierce roar and being exceedingly terrifying;
she has disheveled hair and delights in being unclothed.
She has tawny eyes and a blazing tongue; her fierce movements are terrifying;
she wears a girdle made from a multitude of corpses, and her face is laughing. (17.59)
Her face is made radiant by streams of blood trickling from her two corners of the mouth;
she holds a skull and a flaying knife in her hands, and carries a sword and a shield.
She was passionately attached to Mahākāla, and being afflicted by hunger, she cried out, "Grant me a boon! Grant me a boon! Grant me a boon! (17.61)
Having reflected thus, O Goddess of the Gods, one should worship the yantra with devotion:
a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, a circle, an eight-petaled lotus, and an outer enclosure.
It is enriched with the beauty of four gates; at those gates are Gaṇapa, the Yoginīs, the Kṣetrapālas, and Baṭuka as the fourth.

One should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and the lords of the worlds (lokeśas) in the earth-fortress (bhūpura) in due order; having worshipped the eight Mātṛkās on the petals, one should worship the eight Bhairavas on the filaments (kesara).
On the tips of the eight petals are the eight siddhis; in the six corners are the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
She is the giver of sovereignty, the giver of enjoyment, the giver of liberation and victory, and likewise the giver of fearlessness.
The sixth [syllable] is said to bestow success; one should worship it in sequence within the six corners.
One should fully worship Will (icchā), Knowledge (jñāna), and Action (kriyā) within the triangle.
Having worshipped the mudrā in the center with all five types of offerings,
and having thus completed the worship, one should then perform the lustration ceremony (nīrājana).

O Goddess of the Gods, at the conclusion of the *nīrājana* rite, preceded by breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), one should recite the mantra two hundred thousand times while offering very white *karavīra* flowers. (17.68)
Having performed the fire-oblation (havana) ten times [the number of recitations], one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) ten times that amount;
then one should carry out the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) and the feeding of Brahmins.
Thus, when the mantra has been mastered, the practitioner is fit for its application and not otherwise;
for whatever he fixes his mind upon in his heart, that very task he indeed accomplishes. (17.70)
Everything has been declared as in the Kālī system; I have explained the specific distinction.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?

Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of the Mudrā-Nityās," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrī-Śaktisaṅgama-Mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 17 ||
The eighteenth chapter.
The Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear the sequence of the ritual procedure for Mitānityā."
Tell me respectfully that measured [mantra] which is the most excellent among all vidyās.
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess of gods, I shall declare the most secret of secrets:
the Great Queen of all vidyās, known by the name Mitā, who brings great prosperity. (18–2)
I shall proclaim her mantra, the wonderful mantra of Kālī for all her limbs:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Oṃ), one should extract the seed-syllable of Kālikā. (18.3)
One should extract the seed-syllable of the *kūrca*, as well as *māyā* and the *vāgbhava* seed-syllable;
having uttered the word *mite*, one should likewise utter the word *parimite*.
Furthermore, one should extract the syllable for valor (*parākrama*) and the seed-syllables:
*sohaṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, followed by *svāhā*; this mantra consists of twenty-seven syllables. (18.5)
O Goddess, this mantra has been declared; now hear its seer, meter, and other details.
Mahākāla is its seer, and Triṣṭubh is proclaimed as its meter. (18.6)
Mitānityā is the deity, Kālikā is declared to be the seed-syllable (bīja),
Kūrca is the power (śakti), O Great Goddess, and Māyā is declared to be the pin (kīlaka).
One should perform the six-limbed ritual with the *kīlaka* mantra enriched by the six long vowels;
one should meditate [upon her] resembling a dark mountain, like a dark rain-cloud.
Clad in red garments, seated upon a corpse, adorned with a garland of severed heads,
she possesses a pair of full and elevated breasts, a broad chest, and shapely hips.
She has her hair loosened and flowing, she delights in being naked,
she dwells in the center of the lotus-heart of Mahādeva, and she wears a conch-shell bracelet.
Resembling the fire at the end of an aeon, dwelling in the cremation ground,
holding a sword and a severed head in her left hands, and bestowing fearlessness and the boon of grace with her right hands.
Her heart yearning for the practitioner, she bestows boons upon the practitioner;
she delights in the intense fragrance residing in his mouth, and is herself overwhelmed with passion.
One should meditate upon the divine Dakṣiṇā, the protector of the distressed, who is radiant with eyes and other features that are slightly reddened and full, and who is smiling. (18–13)
Having meditated thus upon the goddess Mitā, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) three hundred thousand times.
O Dear One, the fire-oblation (*havana*) should be performed with *kiṃśuka* flowers or with *jyotiṣmatī*. (18.14)
The fruit is considered to be like that of the *kiṃśuka* tree when offered with *jyotiṣmatī* flowers; one should offer with the reddish *karavīra* flower for the sake of mantra-siddhi. (18.15)
One should offer oblations in a consecrated triangular pit into a fire of khadira wood;
by offering betel leaves as an oblation, one shall bring Kālikā under one's control.
And by means of the *puṣpāktā* and *nāgavalī*, one shall attain the siddhi of the *nāginīs*; O Maheśvarī, one should offer oblations with *vajrapuṣpa* for the sake of the *ḍākinīs*. (18.17)

By means of *dhattūra* one brings about the destruction of enemies; with *kunda* flowers one attains poetic skill; through *jātī* flowers there is the attainment of victory; and with *tila* flowers there is an increase in strength. (18–18)

With *punnāga* flowers one attains the goals of human endeavor (*puruṣārtha*); with *ketakī*, one obtains a beloved woman; with *āsuryā*, there is the destruction of enemies; and with *candana*, one is always victorious. (18–19)
In the same way, O Goddess, by means of agallochum (agaru), one shall obtain the status of a king of kings;
by means of an oblation of red sandalwood, one should perform the enchantment of all beings.
Through *girikarṇī* there is the attainment of a maiden; through *sevya* one attains the form of Śiva;
through *guḍūcī* there is the destruction of enemies; and through *marīca* there is supreme attraction. (18–21)

Through betel nuts (pūgīphala) one gains great fortune; likewise, through nutmegs (jātiphala), wealth; through campaka flowers, the power of paralyzing (staṃbhana); and through rose-apple (jaṃbvā), the destruction of the suffering of rebirth.
Thus, one should accomplish [the rite] directed toward desire by means of various methods;
thereafter, one should perform a libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of the oblations (homa) upon the surface of the sacred seat (pīṭha).
One should likewise perform the sprinkling (mārjana) with water scented by the eight fragrances and with saffron-water, using a tenth part of the quantity used for the libation (tarpaṇa).
One-tenth of that [number] should be fed to Brahmins, as well as capable young maidens;
O Goddess, he who worships and feeds them attains all accomplishments (siddhis). || 18-25 ||
Now, listen as the yantra for the ritual of worship is described:
having drawn three triangles, one should draw a circle joined with six corners.
It is richly adorned with the beauty of a circular eight-petaled lotus, endowed with a surrounding city-walls (bhūpura),
beautified by four gates, and decorated with a central bindu.
In the first triangle, one should worship Kālī, Karālinī, and Ghorā;
and in the second triangle, Vāmā, Jyeṣṭhā, and Raudrikā. (18–28)
In the third triangle, however, one should likewise worship Will, Knowledge, and Action;
then, O Goddess, in the circle, one should first worship Vārtālī.
O Goddess of the gods, in the second part one should worship the Laghu-vārāhikā;
O Goddess of the gods, in the third part one should worship the Svapna-vārāhikā. (18–30)
Having worshipped the *tiraskaraṇikā* (the curtain) in the fourth part, O Goddess Śivā,
one should worship the four doors on the left of the hexagon, O Queen of the Gods.
In the hexagon, one should worship the six limbs; likewise, the eight siddhis in the circle;
on the petals, the eight Mātṛkās are to be worshipped, and at their end, the eight Bhairavas.
Outside of that, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) and their weapons within the Bhūpura;
thus having worshipped the limited, eternal Vidyā Mitrā Nirañjanī.
A person thus engaged in propitiation shall attain the accomplishment of mantras;
or else, listen to the method of meditation in the perpetual sequence in another manner. (18-34)
All of them resemble mountains of collyrium and are adorned with garlands of severed heads;
in their right hands the goddesses hold swords, and in their left hands they display the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*).

Holding auspicious and beautiful lotuses, with their excellent hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness—this is the general visualization prescribed for the ritual of the Name-mantras. (18.36)
The secret has been told here: the eightfold accomplishments (siddhis) are in one's hand—the collyrium, the pill, the sword, the vetāla, and the host of yakṣiṇīs.
The *caruka*, the forehead mark (*tilaka*), the garment, the skull-bowl, the sandals, as well as the staff,
the *kinnarī*-attainment, the *ḍāmara*, and so forth, constitute the great arts (*mahākalā*).
The movement of both the mobile and the immobile, as well as minuteness, levity and so forth, entry into another's body, and then the elixir of immortality (rasāyana). || 18-39 ||
Touching, the removal of anxiety, the movement among living beings, and likewise the raising of the dead—these divine accomplishments reside in his hand. (18.40)
Having extracted the great seat (mahāpīṭha), the Nityās should be established in their proper order;
or else, one should worship one's own deity in the center with the root mantra.

p. 130) For the sake of attaining success in the mantra as described, one should meditate by means of the objects belonging to one's own family (kula), and one should worship and satiate the Śakti with food, clothing, and other such offerings. (18.42)
One should fumigate with the ten-fold incense (daśagandha), and then the deity will descend;
her eyes will be red, her limbs motionless, and her lotus-like face serene.
One may become a single Śakti, while the others remain stationed at her side;
at that moment, having fashioned an auspicious image made of black gram (māṣa) as her material form (prakṛti).
One should provide enjoyments consisting of meat cooked in ghee;
at every morsel, one should offer wine as well as pieces of fish and shellfish.
Having first uttered the seed-syllable, [one says]: "O Eternal One, O Fierce-faced One, O Fierce-tusked One, O Lolling-tongued One, this [person] has been assigned to you. (18.46)
Having recited the first seed-syllable, one should utter "ĀHĀRA BHAKṢAYA YUGAṂ SVĀHĀ" followed by two ṬHA letters; then one should meditate upon the enemy as dead. (18.47)
O Goddess of the Suras, at that very moment she carries away the life-breaths of the measured one;
hearing that he has died, one should then feed the measured one.
Afterwards, one should fumigate that bestower of boons with incense made from the five ingredients;
then, having caused her to laugh and granted the boon, she shall depart from the body of the Śakti.

Or else, in a cremation ground, she who possesses a radiance equal to the submarine fire (vaḍavāgni) should be worshipped with human flesh and the ritual substances of the lineage for the destruction of the king along with his army.
For subjugation, one should use a garden; for eradication, a riverbank. There is no knowledge superior to this, which produces immediate conviction. (18.51)
Renowned in the Northern Tradition (Uttarāmnāya) and worshipped by me in a hundred ways, this [mantra], though more secret than the secret, has been revealed by me to you. (18.52)
"Beyond this, O Great Goddess, what else do you wish to hear?
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear about that incense which was mentioned by you. (18.53)
"What substances are used therein for that which is beloved of the ten scents?
Śrī Śiva said:
"One should take three parts of saffron (kāśmīra) and likewise three parts of agallochum (aguru). (18.54)
There are five parts of moonstone (*candrakānta*), two of musk (*mṛganābhi*), eight of black sandalwood (*kṛṣṇacandana*), and six of white sandalwood (*śvetacandana*). (18.55)
Having divided seven parts of mahiṣākṣa, twelve of sarjaka,
and eight of māṃsī, one should take one part from the clarified butter (ājya).

This is the ten-fold incense; now listen, O beloved, to the five-fold incense: take one part each of the root of black aloe-wood, leaf, and bark, along with *svarṇapuṣpa* and nutmeg; one should burn this incense in equal proportions. (18–57)

Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, titled "The Ritual of Mitānityā," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 18.
The nineteenth chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said: "O Lord of Gods, by your grace, the ritual procedure for Mitā has been heard by me."
Speak the Tiraskaraṇī [mantra], which causes great delusion.
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen, O Goddess, I shall proclaim that which causes great enchantment—the well-guarded [mantra] which constitutes a limb of both Śrīvidyā and Bālā. (19–2)
The seed-syllable of Vāgbhava, the seed-syllable of Kālikā, Bhuvaneśī, and Haripriyā;
after the word "tiraskaraṇī," one should then utter "sakalajanam. (19-3)
One should say "Vāgvādini sakalapadam" for the minds of ordinary people;
one should say "Cakṣuḥ śrotraṃ tathā jihvāṃ ghrāṇaṃ tiraskaraṇam" [for the senses]. (19-4)
This mantra is traditionally remembered as ending with "svāhā," consisting of two *kuru*s, two *ṭha*s, and the syllable *klīṃ*.
One should then utter the Vāgbhava-bīja, Bhuvanā, Lakṣmī, and the word "bhagavataḥ. (19–5)
This second supreme mantra, joined with Svāhā,
is Māheśvarī, who obscures the vision of all living beings.
This supreme mantra is joined with "namah kuruyuk svāhā";
then follows the word "trailokyamohini" and the word "mahāmāye. (19.7)
Then one should speak of the concealment of the eyes of all people;
joined with *kuruyuk* and *svāhā*, this is the fourth mantra in sequence.
One should extract the syllable of the illusion of speech (vāṅmāyā), which is the seed-syllable of Kamalā (the lotus), namely the pair of syllables *hsau*.
Then one should extract the words *oṃ namo bhagavati śrīmaheśvari*. (19-9)
Then one should utter the word "sarvajanamanaścakṣuḥ," followed by the word "tiraskaraṇa," joined with "kuru" and ending with "svāhā. (19.10)
The five mantras, which are the protectors consisting of the five *makāras*, have been taught in sequence;
one should recite these five mantras for the sake of protecting the five *makāras*.
Hrīṃ Klīṃ! One should utter the word "Bhagavati Māheśvari," and then the words "Sarvajana" and "Manacakṣu. (19.12)
Having uttered *tiraskaraṇam*, followed by *kuru yuk* and joined with *svāhā*, this is proclaimed as the sixth yoga for the purpose of complete protection and other such aims. (19.13)
The seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra is Śakti; Gāyatrī is declared to be its meter (chandas).
It eclipses the minds and eyes of all cattle and people. (19.14)
O Goddess, the deity is declared [to be Tārā]; the seed-syllable (bīja) is proclaimed as *klīṃ*;
*hrīṃ* is the power (*śakti*); *krīṃ* shall be the peg (*kīlaka*); and the application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of subduing (*tiraskṛti*). || 19-15 ||
One should say "namas" with the two thumbs for *vāṅ-māyā-kamalā-kāma*; the wise one should then place the seed-syllable for "O Blessed One" (*bhagavati*) there on the two index fingers. (19–16)
The Māheśvarī [mudrā] is formed with the two middle fingers; then the Sarvātiraskaraṇī is formed with the two ring fingers; and the two Kurus are formed with the two little fingers.
Furthermore, one should place the seed-syllables on the pair of palms and backs of the hands;
having thus performed the placement upon the heart, one should carry out the ritual placement of the letters (varṇanyāsa).

One should likewise place [the mantras] on the right arm, the right back, the right thigh, the right knee, the right foot, and the right hand; and in the same manner, one should place them on the left side as well.
Having placed the mantra on the base of the arms, the back, the knees, and the head,
O Goddess, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpakanyāsa) with the complete vidyā.
Then one should meditate upon the Great Vidyā, whose form is that of Tiraskaraṇī—her hair disheveled, naked, yet adorned with all ornaments. (19–21)
I bow to her who, by her very sight, bewilders the multitude of deluded beings;
now, attend properly to the great meditation for the purpose of their restraint.
Śivā is dark-complexioned, with three eyes red and rolling from intoxication;
she wears black garments and holds a sword in two of her arms.
With her two enchanting arms, she carries a date-palm and a water-jar;
she is mounted upon a dark-blue horse, proceeds ahead, and is adorned with blue ornaments.
Clad in blue garlands and garments, anointed with blue perfumes, and enchanting to the mind,
she was concealing the world under the guise of sleep.
The Blessed Lady, who holds a sword as her weapon, is intent on protecting her devotees;
she is engaged in uprooting the fettered souls (paśus) and bears the gesture of threatening the fettered.
O Goddess, one should write the mantra—prescribed for the veil—upon birch bark using saffron and other pigments; then, one should place it before the water-pot.

One should recite the great mantra one hundred thousand times in a single auspicious sacred site; then, a fire sacrifice (havana) consisting of ten parts of that number should be performed with bilva fruits soaked in honey and ghee.
One should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with a tenth part of that, the sprinkling (mārjana) with a tenth part of that, and the feeding of Brahmins with a tenth part of that. (19–29)
Thus, once the mantra has been mastered, the practitioner of the mantra should perform the rite of piercing;
this vidyā accomplishes all goals and causes blindness among those who are bound. (19.30)
"O Goddess, like the Svapnavārāha [tantra], these two are distinguished by their specific preliminary rites (puraścaryā).
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear? (19-31)
The Goddess said:
O Lord of Gods, I wish to hear of the great wonders as well;
tell me those, O you who are beyond compassion, if I am dear to you. (19-32)
Śrī Śiva said:
Listen now as I speak that which is more secret than secrets;
the Svapnavārāhikā Vidyā is proclaimed here to be threefold.
First is the fifteen-syllable Vidyā, then that consisting of eighteen syllables;
enriched with twenty-four principles, it is proclaimed as the Great One (Mahatī). || 19-34 ||
In the center of that [maṇḍala], which is enriched with all the most excellent auspicious symbols, is the eighteen-syllable mantra;
its ritual procedure is now being told—listen! (19–35)
One should utter the Vāgbhava [bīja], then Bhuvanāhṛd, and then Vārāhī;
having extracted "Aghore," one should add the four *ṭha* syllables in the dream state.
The mantra ending with the wife of Vahni (svāhā) is the revealer of the future and other matters;
it is declared to consist of eighteen syllables, and its seer (ṛṣi) is said to be Īśvara.
The meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh, and Svapneśī is considered the presiding deity.
Aiṃ is the seed-syllable (bīja), Hrīṃ is the power (śakti), and the six-syllabled mantra ends with Ṭhaṭha Svāhā. (19-38)
In the heart, *aiṃ* and likewise *māyā*; "Salutation to Vārāhī" is indeed the head (*śiras*). "O Aghorā" is the crest-lock (*śikhā*), and "in a dream" (*svapne*) shall be the armor (*kavaca*).
The four *ṭha*s should be at the eyes; *svāhā* becomes the weapon (*astra*), O Dear One.
One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) on the hips, throat, cheeks, ears, eyes, and head. (19–40)
Dark as a mountain of blue collyrium, adorned with jewels and gems, mounted upon a horse, holding a discus in her hand, and others bearing a plough as their weapon. (19.41)
In her two lower hands she holds a scissor and a skull-cup filled with blood;
beneath her feet is Hiraṇyākṣa, and she is intoxicated with passion and pride.
Having thus meditated upon the power of Viṣṇu, which is filled with various energies and adorned by various hosts, one should then begin the worship.
One should propitiate the Goddess in the center of the *bindu*; then one should draw a triangle.
Therein, one should worship Nidrā, who is exceedingly gracious and has the limbs of a child. (19–44)
Then, in the center of the hexagon, [one should worship] Mahogrā, Pretayakṣikā,
Śvāsakālā, Bhīmavatī, Nakhajvālā, and Mahodarī.
Then, in the center of the eight petals, one should [worship] Girīśa, Caturānana, Phaṭkāra, Baddhamātaṅga, Kulīra, Vāyara, and Bali.
And having fully worshipped Caṇḍīśvara, one should then [worship] Mātaṅgī, Vṛddhamātaṅgī, Asitāṅgī, and Kaphotkaṭā at the twelve-syllable [mantra].
The greatly exalted one, the bearer of the departed, the power of gnosis endowed with action,
Vagalikā, the radiant Bhānumatī, Somadevī, the ancient one.
Then, having performed worship in the sixteen-spoked [cakra] by means of the process of withdrawal (saṃhāra) starting from the east,
one should worship Indrī, Saurī, Maheśānī, Tārā, Yakṣaprasū, and Dharā.
Vāmā, Virodhinī, Śyāmā, Mātaṅgī, Surarākṣasī, Padmāvatī, Kālarātri, Tāmasī, Madanā, and Madā. (19.50)
She should be worshipped with yellow perfumes, unbroken rice grains (akṣata), and likewise with the articles belonging to her family;
then, joined by the Śaktis, one should recite the mantra one hundred and fifty thousand times.

The practitioner of mantra should offer oblations ten times the portion [of the main rite] using flowers of *hayamāra* and the flesh of the enemy of horses (*hayāri*) into a triangular or *yonikuṇḍa* fire-pit.
One should perform libation, purification, and the worship of the Yoginīs;
thus, the practitioner whose mantra has been perfected shall accomplish auspicious applications.
An oblation with honey, clarified butter, and wine reveals Hari;
by performing it one thousand and eight times, it shall declare the desired object of the practitioner. (19.54)
An oblation of *kadamba* flowers at night will reveal a treasure;
an oblation made with blue lotuses will forcibly attract a woman. (19.55)
A fire sacrifice performed with *javā* flowers and pieces of black meat brings a king under one's control;
a sacrifice made with the entrails of a cat terrifies the seeker who practices the rite.
An oblation performed with seeds of *putrājīvaka* becomes a bestower of sons;
having fashioned an auspicious image of the person [desiring a son] out of mung-bean flour... (19.57)
If one performs the oblation for him, death occurs immediately; of this there is no doubt.
Having recited [the mantra] three thousand times, [the deity] declares in a dream what is auspicious or inauspicious. (19.58)
What task would not be accomplished by an oblation of wild meat and minced flesh?
[The mantra is: Tāre namo bhagavati vārāhi, [repeated] twice, followed by ṭhaṭhaḥ. (19.59)
The fifteen-syllable mantra produces immediate conviction;
it is declared to be Akṣobhya Bhairava, and its meter is considered to be Śakvarī. (19.60)
The deity is Svapnavārāhī; the six limbs [are assigned] to the words in sequence as before.
O Goddess, the worship and so forth, as well as the ritual application, are also as previously described. (19–61)
At the end of the seed-syllable, one should extract the goad-seed of Bhuvaneśvarī;
likewise, the pair of words "Vārtālī" and the pair of "Vārāhī. (19–62)
From that [comes] Svapnaśvarī; then the pair [Sa and Ha], followed by the letter of the Moon (I) adorned with a bindu, and then Vāyu (Ya) joined with a bindu—this is the twenty-four-syllable mantra.
Janārdana is its seer (ṛṣi), the Saṃskṛti is declared to be its meter (chandas), and the deity is Svapnavārāhī, whose eyes are red and rolling. (19.64)
[She is] pierced by the God of Love, three-eyed, with the crescent moon as her crest-jewel,
her face formidable with fangs, and adorned with a garland of heads.
One should worship on the seat previously described, which bestows the fruit of all times.
In this very context, O Pārvatī, hear the account of Kṛṣṇa and Mātaṅgikā.
Having first extracted the Praṇava, one should indeed utter "namo bhagavati," and then extract "kṛṣṇamātaṅgini" and "śirovalkaladhāriṇī."

Then, for one who identifies with all people, the *māyā* (hrīṃ) followed by the six long vowels, having extracted the word "so-and-so," one should utter "vaśyākṛṣṭiṃ me" (subjugation and attraction for me). 19-68.
The mantra ending with "kuru svāhā" is the celestial wish-granting tree for all.
Its seer (ṛṣi) is known as Kṛṣṇa, the most excellent among all the best of gods. (19-69)
It is known as the Virāṭ metre, and by means of Māyā it possesses six limbs:

*Oṃ* is said to be the seed-syllable (*bīja*), *Bhuvanā* the power (*śakti*), and *Svāhā* the pin (*kīlaka*). Furthermore, its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the purpose of bringing the three worlds under control. || 19-70 ||
Skilled in playing the lute, like a mass of clouds, possessing the grace of beauty, with lips like the *bimba* fruit, lotus-eyed, with a graceful body and a garland of scattered hair,
wearing playful and swaying golden earrings, she was the source of the arising of dharma, artha, and kāma.
May Caṇḍī, of fierce prowess, be the accomplisher of all our aims. || 19-71 ||
Having meditated thus, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; then the mantra becomes perfected.
One should recite with hands soiled by food remnants and offer the bali-oblation with such remnants. (19.72)
O Goddess of the gods, as he recites thus, the supernatural powers (siddhis) and the subjugation of people arise; what more do you wish to hear? || 19-73 ||

Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Tiraskaraṇikā," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Indrakṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 19 ||
The Twentieth Chapter.
Śrī Śiva said:
[One should meditate upon] Kāma, mounted on the station of Śakra and endowed with the *ratibindu*.
Having extracted the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, one should extract the Parā-prāsāda.
Spoken in both forward and reverse order, this six-syllabled great vidyā, Sampatsarasvatī, is the most excellent among all vidyās. (20.2)
For the distressed, the poor, and likewise for those who have lost their status,
the Sarasvatī of prosperity bestows great wealth and knowledge.
O Maheśānī, Kṛṣṇa is the seer (ṛṣi), Gāyatrī is declared to be the meter (chandas), and the goddess Sampatsarasvatī is proclaimed as the deity (devatā). (20.4)
The seed-syllable is *klīṃ*, and likewise the power is *hasauḥ*; this is declared to be the *kīlaka*.
O Great Goddess, its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the sake of attaining prosperity. (20.5)
O Goddess of the gods, one should perform the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with the six-syllabled mantra;
having performed the pervasive placement ninefold, one should meditate upon the captivating Goddess.
I bow to the Sarasvatī of prosperity, who has the form of the dawn and is attended by many millions of elephants, horses, chariots, and foot-soldiers.
Having meditated thus, O Maheśānī, one should draw a triangular wheel;
then a hexagon should be drawn, adorned with a circle and eight petals. (20.8)
The yantra, when joined with the bhūpura (earth-fortress), is considered to fulfill all desires;
one should worship the goddess Sampatsarasvatī within the triangle.
The eight desired Mothers, accompanied by Bhairava, are to be worshipped;
the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the square, and their weapons outside of that.
O Śivā, having thus worshipped the obstructions, one should recite the mantra three hundred thousand times;
O Maheśānī, one should perform the fire-oblation with palāśa flowers using a tenth part [of that number].
One who has completed the preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa) is fit for the ritual application (prayoga), and not otherwise.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform oblations with milk-rice (pāyasa) ten thousand times.
The king on earth becomes endowed with a thousand horses;
he should recite the mantra six thousand times daily and perform the fire-oblation with lotuses ten times that number.
139) Endowed with a multitude of chariots, horses, wealth, and grain, his fortune shall certainly become unshakable within a year. (20.14)
One should constantly offer a thousand oblations into the fire with rice grains;
from the mandala, there is no doubt that one shall attain the status of a king. (20.15)
The mantra-practitioner should recite the mantra ten thousand times daily at the root of a Bilva tree;
within half a month, the adept attains complete prosperity. (20.16)
Whoever offers one hundred and eight oblations at its root with *hunedbilva* fuel-sticks will attain great prosperity in that house within even three months. (20.17)
If a man eats his food after touching it ten times while reciting [the mantra], there will be an inexhaustible abundance of food in his house; of this there is no doubt. (20.18)
Pure and with a one-pointed mind, one should recite the mantra on the bank of a river;
having offered oblations of cow’s ghee ten times the number of recitations, one shall bring the three worlds under one's control.
One should constantly offer oblations with ghee four thousand times with devotion;
within a month, the practitioner attains the sovereignty of the supernatural powers, such as atomization (aṇimā) and the rest.
Thus it has been briefly declared; now hear, O Śivā, the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Om), one should take the syllable *kāṣṭha* (ṭha) conjoined with the sixth vowel (ū). (20–21)
O Maheśānī, [the letter] 'ka' joined with the bindu and endowed with the moon-bindu;
thereafter, O Maheśvarī, the twenty-fifth [letter] joined with the bindu.
One should utter the seed-syllable of Śakra joined with a long *nāda*, then the wind (*māruta*) joined with a long [vowel], and then the earth and the wind. (20–23)
This ten-syllable great mantra (mahāvidyā) is the destroyer of untimely death;
Vāmadeva is its seer (ṛṣi), and the Paṅkti meter is proclaimed for it. (20–24)
The deity is proclaimed to be Mahārudra, the Conqueror of Death;
the seed-syllable (bīja) is said to be the Praṇava (Om), and Jūṃ is proclaimed as the power (śakti). || 20-25 ||
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) with the mantra syllables "candracandra" and "candravahni," followed again by "vahnivahni" in sequence, one should meditate upon Supreme Śiva.
He stands upon a crystal-clear lotus, holding a full water-pot in the crooks of both arms;
with two other lotus-hands he holds two jars that are eternally full,
while from those two [jars] he causes a beautiful crescent moon to flow down, drenching his head.
Thus maintaining the Lord, may the net of our ritual procedures enter into the pure state for a long time. || 20-27 ||
Having thus established the elements, O Śivā, one should draw a hexagon on the external seat;
there one should draw eight petals, and then a circle should be drawn there. (20–28)
O Goddess of the gods, one should worship Śiva Mṛtyuñjaya in the center of the hexagon,
and in the six corners, the five mantras beginning with Satya and Sadāśiva.
Then, O Supreme Goddess, one should worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) together with their weapons;
one should perform the preparatory rite (puraścaryā) by reciting [the mantra] one hundred thousand times, and the fire-oblation (homa) with sesame seeds should be ten parts of that.
Immediately thereafter, O Supreme Goddess, one should recite [the mantra] three hundred thousand times;
the destruction of untimely death will surely occur, and not otherwise. (20–31)
O Goddess Śivā, by reciting [the mantra] twelve hundred thousand times on a mountain peak, one certainly attains a lifespan of a kalpa and lives for a hundred years; it is not otherwise.
O Goddess, one should perform ten thousand oblations with *dūrvā* grass for the destruction of death;
thus has it been briefly declared. Now hear the *pathiṣadrudraka*.
Having uttered the *praṇava* (Om) and the word of salutation (*namaḥ*), one should pronounce the word "Rudrāya," followed by the word "pathiṣat" endowed with the dative case-ending.
Having said "Svasti," protect me and preserve my station;
this Rudra-vidyā, heard on the path, removes fear upon the way. (20-35)
Vāmadeva is said by the wise to be the seer (ṛṣi) of this mantra;
they declare the metre (chandas) to be Paṅkti, or else Gāyatrī, O Śivā. (20.36)
Rudra, the remover of all fears, is the deity on the path;
the seed-syllable is said to be *praṇava* (Om), and *namaḥ* is declared to be the power (*śakti*). (20.37)
"O Śivā, this six-limbed [ritual] has been described by me as consisting of one syllable, two, three, and four syllables, [and again] three and four. (20.38)
Resembling pure crystal, endowed with four arms,
equipped with the Pināka and Kārmuka bows, and provided with an arrow and a chisel.
Endowed with three mantras, he beheld the Lord whose crest is the deer-marked moon,
who resembles Mount Kailāsa and is mounted upon his bull.
One should meditate upon the god Sadāśiva, joined with Annapūrṇeśvarī, who bears the name Pathiṣad Rudra; he is the destroyer of fear from thieves and other dangers on the road. (20.41)
(141) This meditation has been proclaimed by me; hereafter I shall describe the yantra.
First, one should draw a hexagon, and then one should draw eight petals. (20.42)
Thereafter, one should draw an underground chamber (bhūgṛha) provided with a door and possessing auspicious characteristics;
in its center, within a hexagon, one should worship the god Paśupatirudra.
In the six corners, one should worship the six limbs there with their respective mantras:
Nandikeśa, Nandi, Bhṛṅgin, and indeed Bhṛṅgirīṭi.
Mṛḍa, Vīrabhadra, Kumāra, and likewise Gaṇapa—one should worship these on the eight petals; O beloved of mine, one should thus offer prayers. (20–45)
In the eight directions within the house of the earth, one should worship the eight guardians of the quarters (dikpālas).
Thus, one should worship the Lord Rudra, who is accompanied by these enclosures (āvaraṇas).
Having performed worship, one should recite the mantra four hundred thousand times without sloth;
then, having offered oblations with sesame seeds ten times that number, the mantra will become perfected.
Once this mantra has been mastered, the wise practitioner should employ it;
when the fear of thieves arises on a journey, one should recite it one hundred and eight times.
Then, on a lonely path beset by thirst, this best of practitioners will undoubtedly become invisible to thieves. (20.49)
One should recite this great mantra three hundred and eight times;
right there, one immediately obtains water resembling nectar.
A man who is deprived of food on the road and oppressed by hunger should recite this great mantra one thousand and eight times.
One immediately obtains sweet food from a hundred Brahmins;
this is a secret, a most secret, and a supreme-most secret. (20.52)
"O Pārvatī, this secret wonder is indeed to be guarded like one's own womb.
Thus it has been told in brief; what else do you wish to hear?"

Thus ends the twentieth chapter, titled "The Ritual for the Sixteen Rudras on the Path," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgamamahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. 20.
The Twenty-first Chapter.
The Illustrious Goddess said:
"O Lord of Gods, I desire to hear about the wonderful method for the subjugation of enemies."
The illustrious Śiva said: Listen as I relate this curiosity, which is a secret even among secrets. 21-1.
The Ārdrapaṭeśvarī Vidyā is now described for the subjugation of enemies:
having first extracted the Praṇava (Om), followed by "namo bhagavati" (salutation to the Blessed One). || 21-2 ||
Having uttered "Ārdrapaṭeśvari," one should say the word "Harinīla"; then, having pronounced the word "Kālī," one should utter the word "Ārdrajihve. (21-3)
One should utter Caṇḍalohinī, then Rudrāṇī, Kapālinī, Jvālāmukhī, Saptajihvā, and Sahasranayanā. (21.4)
One should say, "Come, I give this animal to you";
having extracted the life of such-and-such [a person], one should utter the word "cut. (21.5)
Then, one should utter "hūṃ" against that which seizes the abode of the vital breath;
and the words "phaṭ bhūrbhuvaḥ svaḥ phaṭ svāhā," [saying] "Drink the blood! (21.6).
In the Māravādinī [mantra], one should extract the word for "enemy" (*śatru*) and utter it;
having spoken the two instances of "cutting" (*chedaya*), one should extract the pair of "drinking" (*piba*). (21.7)
And the mantra-king beginning with *śoṇitaṃ ca padaṃ hūṃ phaṭ* and ending with *svāhā*, pervaded by the three consonants, consists of one hundred and twenty-three syllables. (21.8)
The sage is declared to be Durvāsas; Gāyatrī is said to be the meter;
"Nikṛnta" is the seed-syllable (bīja), and "Svāhā" is proclaimed as the power (śakti). || 21-9 ||
The application for the purpose of subduing enemies has been proclaimed.
With the six *hrīṃ*s, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*) and then meditate upon the Supreme Mother (*Parāmbikā*).
She has extremely cold and fierce fangs, three eyes, and hair bristling upward;
she is marked by a skull-bowl, a fruit, a hand-drum, a curved knife, and a trident;
she resembles a thick rain-cloud, and her garland of tinkling bells is reddened by the glow of the dawn.
May Bhadrakālī be with me for a long time for the sake of the perfect accomplishment of worldly existence.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times in a desert region or a cremation ground;
having performed ablutions while still wearing wet clothes, one should direct [the rite] toward the enemy. (21.12)
If the recitation is performed, the death of the enemy occurs within half a moment;
by mere recitation alone, the killing of the enemy takes place at the end of a month.
Starting from the eighth day of the dark fortnight until the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight,
one should recite the mantra for that duration, incorporating the name of the enemy.

O Goddess, even if an enemy resembles Mukunda himself, he shall go to the abode of Yama from the very day of the commencement [of the rite]; so too shall the gods, beginning with Brahmā and Rudra. (21.15)
They will not be able to protect him;
death shall come to him from the first lunar day (pratipad) of the dark fortnight until it reaches the tenth lunar day (daśamī).
Having recited the mantra, O Goddess of gods, one should sprinkle water in the direction of the enemy;
taking water in the hollow of the palms, one should cast that water toward the enemy's location.
One should slay the host of enemies; there is no need for hesitation here.
Having uttered the name of the enemy, O Supreme Deity, by means of this mantra. (21.18)
Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and eight times with *bṛhatī* flowers for the gods while maintaining the root vow, the destruction of enemies will certainly occur. (21.19)
One should offer an oblation of black gram with the sixteen types of ritual services;
having made the request for the task to be accomplished, one should recite the mantra, [thinking] "the destruction of the enemy will come to pass. (21–20)
Thus has it been briefly proclaimed; now hear, O beloved, about Vārtāyakṣī:
the Praṇava, the Vāgbhava, Māyā, the Śrībīja, and the Jyotirbījaka.
One should extract the goad (A), the seed-syllable of Bhṛgu (M), the circle of the mouth (U) with a bindu (Ṃ), and the third letter (I) joined with a bindu (Ī); thus one should draw forth Vīramodana.
