Having extracted the word *āgneyī*, one should utter the word *mahāvīre*;
having pronounced the word *sarvabhāvapada*, one should utter the word *darśanī*. (21–23)
Having uttered the word "Nandanavana," one should utter the word "Vāsinī.
Having pronounced the word "Mahāsupta," one should utter the word "Jāgariṇī. (21–24)
"Show me your ear, svāhā"—this is the king of mantras ending in svāhā.
On a Sunday or during a festival, one should perform an oil massage.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice (*homa*) with sesame flowers;
in the afternoon, one should likewise offer one thousand or one hundred and eight oblations. (21–26)
"O beloved, having recited [the mantra] while a man sleeps at night, it reveals everything;
for the sake of attaining the knowledge of the three times, I shall perform the recitation for you. (21–27)
Having formed this resolve, one should obtain the fruit of recitation at the three times of day:
the fruit of this world, the fruit of the next world, and the supreme fruit, which is the fruit beyond all fruits.
Having declared "I know it," a man becomes one whose mantra is perfected;
O Priyaṃvadā, for this [mantra], there is no requirement for the seer, the meter, and so forth, nor for meditation. (21–29)

Thus has been briefly declared [the mantra of] Piśuna; now hear the mantra of Śatamanyu. Having uttered the seed-syllable *Śrīṃ* and the other [syllables], one should recite the word *Śatarudra*. (21–30)
Having uttered "sau prastāṅgīpadaṃ," then the word "saphala," then the word "vārtā kahapadaṃ," and thereafter one should utter the word "karṇa. (21–31)
Having uttered the word "piśuna," the mantra is joined with "māyā" and "svāhā";
this is declared to be the King of Mantras, for which the preliminary rite (puraskriyā) consists of one thousand recitations.
The sage of this [mantra] is Sahadeva, the meter is said to be Anuṣṭubh, and the deity is Mahālakṣmī, the informer known as Śrīmatkarṇa. (21-33)
The seed-syllable Vāgbhava is declared [to be the deity], the Kāmabīja is the Śakti, and the Parā-bīja is the Kīlaka; one should utter the word "mama" [as the application].
Having uttered the word "sakala," one should extract the secret word;
the application (viniyoga) is proclaimed as being for the purpose of the knowledge of speech. || 21-35 ||
With *hrīṃ* and the six [syllables], one performs the six-limbed ritual (*ṣaḍaṅga*), and with the *vyāhṛtis*, the binding of the directions.
By this sequential application, Piśuna bestows all supernatural accomplishments (*siddhi*).
Thus has been briefly declared [the mantra] preceded by the word *kirāta*.
O Goddess of gods, listen now to the *vārāhī* [mantra]; be attentive in mind. (21-37)
Having extracted the Vāgbhava seed-syllable, one should extract the Vārāhī seed-syllable;
then the Śrī seed-syllable, followed by the Tāra (Oṃ), and "namo bhagavati. (21-38)
Having extracted the word *vārāhī*, one should extract *varāhamukhi*;
having uttered *kirātarūpiṇi*, one should speak the word *ekarātri*. (21.39)
Having extracted the word *prasanna*, one should utter the word *varade*.
Having pronounced the word *mama kārya*, one should say the pair *siddhiṃ kuru*. (21.40)
Having procured a *vibhītaka* fruit, one should take its marrow—the seed-syllable of Śrī, the seed-syllable of Stambhana, and the seed-syllable of Vāc, joined with *svāhā*. (21–41)
Having obtained that ash-powder, one should apply collyrium to the eyes;
then, O Supreme Goddess, having offered incense at night, one should perform the recitation.
She becomes gracious quickly; there is no need for deliberation here.
Listen to Kālavādinī, who tells everything just like the Dream-Vārāhī. (21.43)
One should extract the Praṇava, the syllable Bhuvana, Lakṣmī, the seed-syllable of Speech, and the seed-syllable of Desire,
joined with Saṃvarta-rati and endowed with the Bindu.
Having uttered the Praṇava and the word "Hṛdaya," and then the word "Bhagavati," one should extract the past (bhūta) and then extract the future (bhaviṣya), O Goddess of the Gods.
Having uttered the word "present" (vartamāna), at its end, one should address the speaker of time;
then, having extracted the word "phenomenal world" (prapañca), one should utter the word "embodied being" (śarīrin).
Having extracted the word "saha," he should then say "amukaṃ me vada" (tell me such-and-such);
having said "kathaya kāryam" (tell the matter), he should again extract the seed-syllables.
One should recite the mantra ten thousand times and perform a fire sacrifice consisting of one-tenth that number,
O Goddess of Gods, on a Sunday according to the prescribed rite for the purpose of attraction.
O Śivā, at night, before going to bed, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times, or even one hundred and eight times; thereafter, one should lie down to sleep.
Whatever matter one contemplates in a dream, the deity will certainly reveal it;
therein, the vision of the name and so forth should be observed according to the prescribed rules.
"Whatever power is conceived by anyone shall become sevenfold.
Thus has it been briefly declared; now hear the ritual procedure for Dhūmāvatī.
Having uttered the triad of *dhū* seed-syllables, one should recite the pair of *dhūru*s;
then, having uttered the word *Dhūmāvatī*, it is joined with *kroṃ svāhā phaṭ*. || 21-52 ||
The first mantra has been declared; now listen respectfully to the second.
One should utter the Praṇava, the Dhūmra seed-syllable, and the word "Dhūmāvatī. (21.53)
"Devadatto dhāvati svāhā"—this is the king of mantras;
its seer is known as Kṣapaṇaka, and the meter is said to be Gāyatrī. (21.54)
The deity is Dhūmāvatī, and the seed-syllable *dhūṃ* is declared to be the seed.
*Svāhā* is the power (*śakti*), and its application (*viniyoga*) is proclaimed for the purpose of eradication (*samuccāṭa*). || 21-55 ||
With six *dhū* syllables, the six limbs [are formed]; listen to the visualization, O fair-faced one:
she is mounted upon a crow, extremely black in luster, with broken teeth, and devoid of passion. (21.56)
With disheveled hair and smoke-colored eyes, afflicted by hunger and thirst, overcome by fear, fickle, and tormented by excessive lust, she was distressed, yet her limbs were full and languid.
The supreme Dhūmāvatī is to be meditated upon as being soiled, red with the blood of a śramaṇī, manifesting a fetus, antagonistic, and holding a snake by its head in her hand.
O Maheśānī, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times to effect the eradication of the world;
because it is employed in all tantras, it is considered here in brief.
Since it is a different mantra, it has been told—what else do you wish to hear? (59)

Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, titled "The Concise Ritual for the Amusement of Dhūmāvatī," in the third section of the latter part of the *Śrīśaktisaṅgama-mahātantrarāja*, within the dialogue between the venerable Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. || 21 ||
